Viirabhúmi means viirácárińáḿ bhúmi in Sanskrit, and its altered name is Viirabhúma, or Varjyabhúmi in Vedic. Its altered form is Varrabhúmi and also Viirabhúma. Biira means “forest” in Austric language. Biirabhúmi means “land abounding in forests”. If the word is taken to mean “forest”, then undoubtedly this creates an awkward combination because the word biira is Austric and the word bhúmi is Sanskrit. Birbhum was undoubtedly covered with forests at one time. Mamudbazaar Tháná, Rajnagar Tháná, Khayrasol Tháná, southwest Dumka, east Deoghar and west Pakur, which until 1855 was a part of Birbhum, were all heavily forested. The word ráŕhá or ráŕho, which we find in Austric language, means “land of red soil”. Similarly, if we accept the meaning “forest” for the Austric word biira, then it can definitely offer an explanation behind the name Birbhum, Ráŕhʼs own cultural territory. More research is required on this subject.
Place-names ending in Báŕi/Báŕiyá/Beŕe

It should be mentioned in this regard that with one or two exceptions, one does not come across any place in the environs of Kolkata with the name d́ihi-d́ihá, but one does come across d́áuṋgá and beŕe. The Bengali word báŕi comes from the Sanskrit word vát́i and the word báŕiyá or beŕe comes from the word vát́iká. Thus baḿshveŕiyá or báṋshbeŕe comes from the Sanskrit vaḿshavát́iká. In north Bengal, báŕiyá has changed into báŕi instead of becoming beŕe, for example, Khaŕibáŕi, Khágaŕábáŕi and Nakasálbáŕi. A reed forest (nalkhágŕá – ikŕá in old Assamese) is called Khágŕábáŕi. Khaŕibáŕi is where there is a jungle of wood suitable for use as fuel (khaŕi means “firewood”). Also there is Bagŕibáŕi (Sanskrit badarii, bagaŕi, meaning “plums”), Sháluniibáŕi (shál tree, in Assamese sháluni) and Nalbáŕi (reed jungle).

In southern Bengal we find places with the suffix beŕe such as Ulubeŕe (Uluberiyá), Cakrabeŕe, Gaoriibeŕe and Láuṋgalbeŕe. ( 7 ) Beŕe has another meaning. Villages surrounded by jungle were named after the predominant tree in that jungle. For example, the village that was surrounded by a gol tree jungle was given the name Golábáŕi. There are still villages by the name Golábáŕi in Howrah and 24 Parganas.

It was mentioned earlier that Kolkata was once submerged under water. After those regions rose up from the water, trees that favoured salty soil began to grow, for example, sundari, hentál [a type of palm], mangrove and báin. Many places, such as Garánhát́á, Hentálii, were named after such jungles. The area of Kolkata known today as Entally was formerly called Hentálii. It was comprised of a jungle of huge hintál trees with thorns. Tigers used to hide in [the trees] hoping to catch deer. In distorted British pronunciation Hentálii became Entally. At that time different varieties of crops grew in different areas of Kolkata. These areas were also named according to the local crop; for example, the area where betel grew was named Guvábágán (the Sanskrit word for “betel” is guváka and from this is derived the Bengali gubá). Similarly we obtain Nebubágán and Hartukiibágán.
Place-names ending in Kháli

In southern Bengal there are many places with kháli in their name, for example, Pat́uyákháli, Sandeshkháli, Hánskháli and Dhanekháli. In southern and eastern Bengal there were not so many roads or land routes. People used to travel from one place to another by canals, rivers and swamps. Generally girls would travel to their fatherʼs house when the rivers and creeks would fill with water, which made boat traffic convenient and plentiful.
Náo laiyá sháon másere bandhu náiyar laiyá yáio.
[Take me (the bride) to my fatherʼs house by boat in the month of Shrávańa.]
–Mymensing

It was Emperor Sher Shah who originally constructed the long road from Dhaka Districtʼs Suvarńagrám to At́t́ak in The Punjab. He did not name the road after himself. It was the people who gave it the name Badshah Road. Later the British extended the road up to Peshawar and renamed it the Grand Trunk Road. It should be mentioned here that the word saraka [road] is not a foreign word. It is actually a Sanskrit word. Sr + ńaka = saraka, that is, “that which exists for moving (sará)”, not for standing, sitting or lying down. Due to mass confusion, the word saraka was replaced by saŕaka. Saŕak in chaste Hindi is a feminine gender word. Many people well-versed in Hindi do not realize that the correct form of the word saŕak is saraka. The words sarańa, sarańii, upasarańii and sáráńa in Ráŕhi Bengali all come from the verbal root sr. Incidentally, it is worth mentioning here that the builder of the Badshah Road, Shershah, came from Sasaram, formerly of Sahabad District and today of Rohatas District. The word śasárám has also undergone distortion. It was named Sahasraráma or Sahasarám after a famous local celebrity (mánuś ( 8 )) named Sahasrarám Singh. The place is still called Sahasarám in local Bhojpuri language.

Bear in mind here that the words sará and hat́á are not identical in meaning. The word hat́á or hat́ná in Hindi means “to move from the front” and sará means “to go on moving”, so the work of sará cannot be done by hat́á or hat́ná, although the work of hat́á can be done by sará. Another meaning of the word sará in Bengali is “to bring into use”, for example, ghát́t́á sará hacche ná [the quay is not being used], básant́á sará hacche ná [the container is not being used]. In the domestic life of Bengal, the container or utensil used frequently for regular tasks is called sará in Bengali and not any other word.

Southern Bengal did not have sufficient roads for land travel. People used to travel nearly everywhere by water with the exception of a few areas near Tripura. ( 9 ) Imagine, for instance, that someone wants to go to Bhát́igrám in Barishal. First they have to travel some distance by steamer from Khulna. ( 10 ) Thereafter, once the depth of the water decreases, they have to leave the steamer behind and travel by launch boat. ( 11 ) Then, after travelling a little further by boat, they have to continue by footpath to Bhát́igrám. A steamer can travel down a large river or canal but not down a small river or canal; a boat is required to travel down the small rivers and canals. Now, the villages formerly connected to the main waterways through canals (khál) were given the name kháli; examples are Pat́uyákháli, Dhanekháli, Jelekháli and Sandeshkháli. When you see the name kháli, you can assume that there is now or was a canal near the village, and that the canal joined a large waterway.
Place-names ending in Kholá

The name kholá is attached to those villages that have no relation with any khál but have very large trees full of birds, for example, Sharańkholá and Harińkholá. Kholá is a native word that means “bird”. The Sanskrit synonyms for pákhii [bird] are pakśii, vihaga, vihauṋga and vihauṋgama. Similarly, the Sanskrit equivalents for “deer” are kuraga, kurauṋga and kurauṋgama, and for “horse” they are turaga, turauṋga and turauṋgama.

The word kholá has other meanings in Bengali. The first is the covering of a fruit or something similar. You must have all seen a kholá ghar [house with a pantile roof] and also used the word. Here also the word kholá means “covering”. Two words are commonly used in Bengali to refer to the covering of a fruit – kholá and khosá. If the covering is hard, then it is called kholá, as in the kholá of a coconut; however, if it is soft, then it is called khosá. For example, a banana has a khosá. However, in Kolkata Bengali a banana skin and a coconut shell are both called kholá. Of course, there is a special word for coconut shell – málá (nárkoler málá).
Place-names ending in Mocá/Muci/Ghát́/Ghát́i

Bengali has its own words for “flower” – mocá and muci. The word mocá means “large flower” and muci means “small flower”. Since a banana flower is large in size it is called mocá, but a coconut flower is quite small, so it is called muci. The jackfruit flower is also called muci. In these kinds of philological discussions, one learns not only the history of names but many other things as well, and in this way it becomes easy to demarcate history.

Boats were once used throughout Bengal, except for certain areas bordering Tripura, the far north of Bengal and western Ráŕh. ( 12 ) During that era rivers and boats played such a prominent role in everyday life that people imagined there was a river of life lying between the physical realm and spiritual salvation. ( 13 ) A poem from twelve hundred years ago says:
Sońe bharitii karuńá návii Rúpá thoi náhika t́hávii.
[The boat of compassion is overloaded with gold.]
[There is no room for silver.]

Be that as it may, boats plied up and down the rivers and were moored at quays along the way. In some places where there was no quay, boats were tied to a large tree. Today if a dishonest person takes advantage of his or her friendship with a famous person to carry out misdeeds, and no one else dares to say anything to them about it, then we say “They have tied their boat to a large tree.” In Midnapore, Howrah, 24 Paraganas, Khulna, Noyakhali and other places ghát́ [quay] is called ghát́á and hát́ [market] is called hát́á, for example, Páthureghát́á, Gariyáhát́á, Beleghát́á, Murgiihát́á, Darmáhát́á, Káliighát́á, Gáighát́á and Harińghát́á.
Footnotes
Place-names linked to English names

The names of specific settlements in this country are inextricably linked to certain English names. After the British occupied India, they imposed the “policy of subsidiary alliance”. As a result of this policy certain kings in the country accepted the authority of the British, for example, the kings of Tripura, Coochbihar and Mayurbhanj. They had a contract with the British. The British took their army into all those kingdoms where the kings or large landowners did not accept their authority. They allowed those who surrendered to them out of fear to keep their zamindarship, but they snatched away the kingdoms of those who did not accept their authority and fought against them. Then they installed their own obedient zamindars in their stead. They managed to find something to name after all those British officers who achieved success in these campaigns. For example, after the kingdom of Palamu was defeated, the district headquarters was named Daltonganj after Mr. Dalton. The Octorloney Monument in Kolkata maidan was built in the name of General Octorloney. Nowadays the Octorloney Monument has been renamed Shahid Minar. This is not proper since it is a distortion of history. Something new should have been dedicated to the memory of the Shahids. Similarly, they have created Pamarganj, Macluskeyganj, Leslieganj, and so on.
Distorted pronunciation of English words

Incidentally, it should be pointed out the English word “general” has undergone a distortion of pronunciation to become jáṋdrel in Bengali. We call powerful (jabardast) people jáṋdrel lok. Bear in mind that the word jabardast is Farsi. Dast means “hand”, and if that hand is applied forcibly to something or possesses something forcibly, then it is jabardast. In Panjabi “general” became járńál. If you look around a little, you may able to find a couple of Járnál Singhs present [in the audience].

Even though the English word “colonel” does not have an “r” it is pronounced karńel. From this comes the Panjabi word kárńáil. Similarly, the English word “recruit” has become raḿrut́ in Panjabi and the English “surrender” has become sáláńd́ár.
‘Mumbai’, not 'Bombayʼ

As a result of the Britishersʼ distorted pronunciation the names of many famous cities in this country have become distorted. I have already talked about the distortion of the name Kalikátá (Kolkata) in this regard. A similar situation took place with the city Bombay. Many fishing families were living in the suburbs of the modern city of Bombay. These fishing families were the old inhabitants of the city before it became Bombay. Their traditional deity was the goddess Mumbávatii. Vatii becomes bái in Maharastrii Prákrta, so accordingly Mumbávatii became Mumbábai and, with the passage of time, Mumbái. The word mumbái has been common in both Marathi and Gujarati since that time and remains so today. The British, however, turned Mumbái into Bombay and this “Bombay” became Bombái in Hindi and Bengali. Kothákár jal kotháy ese dáṋŕála [“Where does the water come from; where does it end up?”] ( 1 ). Recently the government of Maharashtra changed the name Bombái to Mumbái. This is a praiseworthy action. Kolkata should promptly be changed to Kalikátá in English. Why should the same proper noun be called differently by different people? This destroys the sense of value of a proper noun. If you ask someone named Sardar Hazara Singh his name, will he reply that his name is “Leader Thousand Lions”? Should we call Krishnanagar “Black City” in English? Someone who gets a kick out of calling Krishnanagar “Black City” should follow suit and call Kolkata “Lime and Rope”. Only then will their penchant for imitation be complete.

The old Sanskrit the word áditya means “one who collects what is due to them”. After the death of a living being, their quinquelemental existence – that is, solid, liquid, luminous, aerial, ethereal – these five factors collect what is due to them. The stars, planets, atoms and molecules, these luminaries and particles, are an aggregate of twelve factors. Since each one of them collects what is due to them, they are called “the twelve ádityas”.
Now, this garland of rajaniigandhá [tuberose] that you see here – how did this flower get its name? Rabindranath has written in one of his poems:
Rájár kánane phut́eche
vakul-párul-rajaniigandhá.
[Vakul, párul and rajaniigandhá flowers have blossomed in the kingʼs garden.]

However, during the historical time period depicted in this poem, that is, during the era of the king of Magadha, Bimbisar, there was no such rajaniigandhá flower in India. It was only four hundred and fifty years ago that the Portuguese first brought the rajaniigandhá from Mexico and planted it in the garden of their Bandel church. The original home of this flower was Mexico in Central America. Its English name is “tuberose”. Like the shiuili flower [night jasmine], the tuberose is full of fragrant pollen. During the day the breeze becomes light in the heat of the sun. As a result it cannot easily carry the fragrant pollen of the rajaniigandhá. But during the night the breeze becomes strong and easily carries the scent; for this reason the tuberose brought by the Portuguese was given the name rajaniigandhá [literally: night-scent] in Bengali. One can also smell the rajaniigandhá during cloudy days and solar eclipses.
Sanskrit influence; Vátávipura is Batavia

The bestowing of Sanskrit names is not only confined to India; in many countries outside India the given names show the influence of Sanskrit. At one time the Sanskrit language was used throughout the entire region extending from southern Russia all the way to Suvarńadviipa. The southern region of Russia – what is today Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and Tajikistan – was earlier called Shákadviipa [Scythia], and the combined name of India and Afghanistan at that time was Jambudviipa. You must have heard the mantra jambudviipe bháratakhańd́e [In jambudviipa and within the Greater India]. Of course, at that time Afghanistan was a part of India. The name for Burma and all of Southeast Asia was Suvarńadviipa. Sanskrit is still used to speak with the king of Thailand; however, it is pronounced differently. For example, in Thailand ja is pronounced like d́a and ńa is pronounced like d́ha, and both ya and ya [with dot] are pronounced like ya [ja]. The name of the kingdom of Kamboja is pronounced nowadays Kambod́iyá by the people. At that time, the kingdom of Kamboja was much larger than the present Cambodia. At one time a huge Shiva temple existed there called Ouṋkárabhat́t́a. Its modern name is Ouṋkár Bhát́. Today the temple is practically in ruins.

When I was in Thailand, my driverʼs name was Krśd́had́ás; that is, his real name was Krśńadás. But since ńa is pronounced like d́ha in the Thai style of pronunciation, if you asked the driver his name, he would reply, “Krśd́had́ás”.

One also sees the influence of Sanskrit pronunciation in Indonesia. One famous city in Indonesia is Jakarta. Its Sanskrit name in the past was Yogyakarttá. Thus, according to the local style of pronunciation, it became Yogayákarttá, or Jakarta for short.

The Sanskrit name for the land we now call Java is Yavadviipa. Its capital was Vátávipura. The modern name Batavia comes from Vátávipura. When the Dutch [Olandáj] came to India in the last part of the Mughal era, they brought a variety of lemon with them from Vátáviipura, which they first planted in the present city of Chinsura [Cuṋcŕo]. ( 2 ) The Dutch had a factory in Chinsura and they christened the city “Chinsura”. The modern Dutch pronunciation was syánsurá, and in Bengali it became cuṋcuŕá, cuṋcŕo in spoken Bengali. When I was staying in Holland, I spoke with a few scholars regarding Cuṋcŕo, and I found that none of them were conversant with Cuṋcŕo. One of them said: “I have never heard anything about Cuṋcŕo in history, but the word cuṋcŕo is from our language.” I have seen a place in Cuṋcŕo called “Dutch Villa”.

The Dutch imported into this country a type of legume from Yavadviipa similar to peas (karáishuṋt́i). In Kolkata Bengali we call mat́arshuṋt́i [peas] as karáishuṋt́i. Although they are not as good as regular peas for making d́ál [pulse], they are quite tasty when eaten fresh in the pod. At one time the village people of Hooghly District used to love eating the pods with puffed rice. They cultivated them as well. They named them oŕandá shuṋt́i (that is, “Dutch peas”). They look somewhat like regular peas.

The Batavia lemon [pomelo] that I mentioned earlier is a well-known name in Bengal nowadays. It does not have any true Sanskrit name; however, the Sanskrit name for the somewhat smaller, sweet and sour lemon already common in this country was mahálauṋga [Citrus grandis]. Today the mahálauṋga has become lost in the abundance of Batavia lemons. The Sanskrit name of the lemon that is somewhat smaller than the mahálauṋga and slightly elongated, and which was already in this country, is jambiira; its modern popular name is jámir, jámerii or jamburá.

The jambiira did not come from outside India. It has also become lost nowadays in the crowd of Batavia lemons. Keep in mind that although the Batavia lemon came to this country from Java, it is native to all of Southeast Asia, that is, Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines (this countryʼs Sanskrit name is Mahárliká or Mahárliińá). The Sanskrit name shiitanimbu is given to the sweet and juicy lemon called maosambii [sweet lime; Citrus sinensis] in Urdu, and sharvatii in Bengali. It is smaller than the jambiira and quite plentiful in India. Today the name maosambii is more common in Bengali; however, it would not be right to forget the Bengali name, sharvatii nebu. The sharvatii nebu belongs to the nebu family, not the kamalá family. Nebu in English is “lemon”; in Sanskrit it is nimbu; in Hindi niimbu; in Angika nemu; and in Bengali nebu – some people mistakenly say lebu. Kamalá in English is “orange”. In Sanskrit it is kamalá or nágarauṋga, in Urdu náráungi, in Marathi sántará and in Bengali kamalá. The main difference between the nebu family (sharvatii or sweet lemon, jambiira [citrus lemon], mahálauṋga, Batavi or lemon pomelo, páti [lime], kágjii (small, green lime)) and the kamalá family (orange – Sanskrit nágarauṋga group) is that the rind of the nebu is not easily removed. It is cut with a knife. But the skin of the kamalá family (Sylheti kamalá, Assam kamala, Meghalay kamalá, Darjeeling kamalá, Nagpurii kamalá or khokákamalá, gonŕá nebu, gonŕá kamalá) is easily peeled [by hand] and the sections inside come apart. The keno nebu [a kind of lemon], quite common nowadays, is a mix between the lemon and orange families. In those days India was producing less sugar so it was imported from Batavia in Indonesia. Hence, the colloquial name for sugar [ciinii] among the people became bát́á ciinii. (During our young days bát́á ciinii and Barishalʼs bálám rice were very common in Kolkata).
Shyámdesh is Thailand; Siḿhapur is Singapore; Shákadviipa is Scythia

It is said in Thai folk tales that Sahasrarabáhu, the crown prince of Ráŕh, defeated Thailand and gave it the name Shyámadesha [siam]. The land is very green and lush, so the name Shyámadesha [verdant land] is both fitting and beautiful. He established a vast empire in Southeast Asia. At that time the capital of Ráŕh was Siḿhapur. The former name of the place called Siuṋgur in present-day Hooghly District was Siḿhapur. The crown prince, Sahasrarabáhu, founded a city in Southeast Asia and named it after Ráŕhʼs Siḿhapur; its modern name is Singapore. Just as the British established another city called London after going to America, the same practice has occurred many times. There are cities and towns in many places with the same name.

We have already mentioned that the Sanskrit name for the southern part of Russia was Shákadviipa. The Greek name for Shákadviipa was Sacdonia. “Alexander” is also a Greek name. Its Arabic equivalent is Sikándár. There is a port in Egypt named Sikandria. Its Greek as well as European name is Alexandria. Alexandria was home to a historically renowned library. The poet, Satyen Datta, has written these lines about the scholar, Acharya Harinath Dey, who was master of many languages:
Yácche puŕe desher garva smashán shudhu hacche álá,
Yacche puŕe nútan kare sekendriyár granthashálá.
[The pride of the country is burning, The grave is
illuminated, It is burning anew, Sekendriaʼs library.]

The people of Shákadviipa were followers of the Árśa religion [religion of the Rśis]. Since they were unwilling to embrace Islam during the age of the first expansion of Islam, they left the region and took shelter in India. In Indian society they became known as the Shákadviipii Brahmans. They mostly kept themselves busy studying astrology and Ayurveda. They used to wear loose pyjama pants with a jacket on their upper body and a Fez cap. Although they were followers of the Rśis, they did not always follow the Vedic customs in their sacrifices and rituals. Furthermore, they were worshippers of the sun god. So the images of the sun god they worshipped that are found in the different sun god temples are also dressed in loose pyjama pants with a Fez cap on the head and a rosary in the hands, which we call jápámálá in Bengali. Thus people say that it is more of a non-Hindu sun god. This kind of sun god temple is found in several places in India. There is a famous temple of this type in Gaya District (present-day Aurangabad District). Today the sun god temple at Końárk is in ruins and its idol has vanished.

The Shákadviipii Brahmans spread (prasár) Ayurveda throughout northern India. ( 3 ) In Bengal, however, there was little use of Ayurveda; rather, the Vaedyaka system was primarily in vogue. In contrast to Ayurveda, the Vaedyaka treatises provided for the dissection of corpses; that is, Bengali physicians did not limit themselves to Ayurvedic theories. They paid attention to the practical side also. Later on, the demonic dogmas of the Shákadviipii Brahmans in north India extended their repressive influence over Vaedyaka physicians as well, and slowly the Vaedyaka practitioners abandoned dissection of cadavers. When Shrii Madhusudhan Gupta began practising western medicine during British rule, the caste injunction against touching dead bodies made him a social outcaste.
Place-names ending in Daha

A large portion of Bengal is watery land. In the areas where big rivers flow, those rivers take a bend at certain places and as a result eddies are created at the bottom of the river near the bend [váṋk]. ( 4 ) Such places are dangerous for boats or ships. There was one such eddy in the Jalangi River where it takes a bend [vánk] (Sanskrit vakra > vaḿka > váṋká) near Krishnanagar. At that time one used to go by water down the Jalangi River from Kolkata to where it met the Padma River and from there to Dhaka [Dacca]. The steamers used to take special care when approaching the eddy. The settlement that sprang up near this eddy [ghurńii] was named Ghurńii. Three places – Ghurńii, Goyári and Krishnanagar – collectively developed into the cultural centre of Bengal at the time, Krishnanagar. During the reign of Maharaja Krishnachandra, some sealing wax artisans were brought from Ilambazaar of Birbhum to reside in Ghurńii. They were the forefathers of Krishnanagarʼs renowned modern-day clay sculptors.

The Bengali name for this whirlpool or eddy at the bottom of the water is daha, so when one hears the word daha in the name of any village or town, one can know that there is or was a large river nearby and that it has or once had a daha or eddy in it.

There was one such eddy in the Mahánandá River also. There are two rivers mentioned in the Atharvaveda called the Paránandá and the Aparánandá. These two rivers joined near Kiśańganj and thereafter became known as the Mahánandá. When the king of the Malla Kśatriyas occupied this region, it was renamed the Máldah. In other words, the kingdom of the Mallas and the nearby Mahánand daha were combined to create the name Máldah. Similarly, in Rajshahi District you find Sardaha. Cákadá in Nadia comes from Cakradaha. At one time the Bhagiirathii River used to flow past Cákdá. At present the Bhagiirathii has moved in a westerly direction.

The Saraswati River passed by Mogra to the west of the Bhagiirathii, and the Yamuna passed by Kalyani. The lands of these three rivers, the Bhagiirathii, Saraswati and Yamuna, is a triveńii [confluence of three streams] – an open triveńii or open stream. In other words, the three rivers flow off in three different directions. The triveńii at Prayág near Allahabad is a closed triveńii or closed stream, because it is at that spot that the three streams coming from different directions unite.

The open stream of the Yamuna merges into the Ichámatii. At that time the Vidyádharii River used to emerge from the southern outlet of the Yamuna in midcourse; today it flows into the Bay of Bengal after passing the eastern outskirts of Kolkata, south past Canning, then joining with the Bhagiirathiiʼs tributary, the Piyálii, where they assume the name Mátlá and thereafter pass through the Sundarbans. The British had planned to build the port of Canning on the banks of the Mátlá, but the Mátlá is actually no longer actually a river. It is an ordinary estuary [kháŕii]. An estuary is also called a “backwater” in spoken English. Although in Bengali and Oriya kháŕii means “estuary” or “backwater”, in Urdu it means “bay”. For example, the Bay of Bengal is báuṋgál ki kháŕii in Urdu. So seeing that the proposed Canning port was ruined by the flooding of the Mátlá, the plans for the Canning port were abandoned.

The Vidyádharii that flows from this southern outlet used to change its course practically every year. Later the area turned into a salty swamp so the British named it the Salt Lake area. This area was full of trees and plants that favoured salty soil. There was a jungle of gol, báin [Cynometra polyandra], hintál [marshy date tree; Phoenixar Elate paludosa], mangosteen and mangrove. The salty seawater inundated the area during flood tide and made it even more frightening. There were a number of eddies. Packs of jackals used to roam there in broad daylight. The people used to call the entire area Shiyáldaha [the jackal eddy].
Tales of Kolkata

When the British occupied [India], Kolkata was part of the northern outskirts of the Sundarbans. In order to save Kolkata from the Maratha invasions, they dug a canal to the northeast which was known as the Maratha Ditch. Mr. Tolley joined the Maratha Ditch to the Ádigauṋgá. In olden times the Ádigauṋgá was the original Ganges River and it used to flow past Maháprabhu D́áuṋgá in Báruipur towards Chatrashál. On his way to Shyámpur, Maháprabhu would keep the Bhagiirathii on his right at Khaŕdá, then rest for a little while at the modern Maháprabhu D́áuṋgá in Báruipur, and then cross the Ganges near Chatrashál. From Shyámpur he would take the Gopiivallabhapur road to Puri. This part of the canal was named after Mr. Tolley and part of the Ádigauṋgá as well; it was known as T́alii Nálá [Tolley Canal]. It was an unhealthy saltwater area full of mosquito-infested jungle and undergrowth. Agriculture there was not very successful. Afterwards, when a new settlement was founded there it was named Tolleyganj. It cannot take pride in its antiquity the way in which Behálá and Baŕiśá can.

If you take a look at a map of Bengal, you will see innumerable estuaries in the south by the Bay of Bengal. They are full of saltwater and are home to ferocious crocodiles. These ferocious crocodiles are called “Crocodile gangelitis” in English. They are not the alligator variety of crocodile. Although the alligator variety of crocodile lives in various regions from the Tropic of Cancer to the equator to the Tropic of Capricorn, their primary home is the Amazon River basin in Brazil. In other words, they are not gangelitis but rather amazonika. At one time there were huge numbers of the gangelitis variety of crocodile on the shoals of the Rupanarayan River basin near Shyámpur, Báganán and Geṋyokháli, especially during wintertime. ( 5 ) During the middle of the day in winter, they would lie on the river shoals with their mouths gaping open, and small birds would enter their mouths to pick out the pieces of meat stuck to their teeth and eat them. There was an unwritten alliance of mutual self-interest and doing each other a good turn between the birds and the crocodiles. The crocodiles used to get their teeth cleaned and the birds found their food there. The crocodile would not close his mouth while the birds were inside.

At that time the Rupanarayan was a huge river. During the rainy season it was full of ilish (hilsa) fish and during the winter it was full of tapse. ( 6 ) The word ilish means “glossy” or “glittering”. In spoken Bengali it is called ilshá or ilshe in some places. The word is derived from Prákrta. If the ilish loses its taste, then it is called viilish [vi-ilish – without ilish]. When the ilish would become separated from the main river and end up in someoneʼs pond or pool due to flooding of the sea or of the Ganges, then they would grow large in size, no doubt, but they would be less tasty because the amount of oil would decrease. This kind of ilish was commonly known as viilish.

When they came to this country for the first time, the British took three settlements from the Nawab for 2700 rupees – Kalighat, Sutanuti and Govindapur. Sutanuti was a village of weavers to the north. ( 7 ) Their trade involved sutá [thread] and nut́i [“bobbin” in English], so naturally the name of the village become Sutanut́i. What is now South-Central Kolkata, from Dalhousie Square to the southern outskirts of the fort field, was Govindapur. ( 8 ) The name Govindapur probably comes from the name of the zamindar Govindaram Basu. Kalighat was to the south of Govindapur.

It has been said that Sutanuti was principally a weaversʼ settlement. The old textile merchants of Kolkata used to live in the area between Sutanuti and Govindapur. Now it is known as Baŕabájár. Actually its old Bengali name was Buŕá Bájár – from the local name Buŕo Shiva. The place was probably under the ownership of Baŕiśáʼs Sávarńa Choudurees. They were the forefathers of Baŕabájárʼs merchants. The area beginning where Sutanuti touches the bank of the Ganges straight south up and until the bank of the Ganges to the west of Kalighat was the home of the fisherman community, or jelepáŕá. Jelepáŕá was divided into three localities – Sutanuti, Govindapur and Kalighat. We should keep in mind that this does not mean that the city of Kolkata was formed from only Sutanuti, Govindapur and Kalighat. Kolkata was founded over a vast area to the north and east of these three villages comprising primarily another twenty-seven villages and secondarily thirty-five villages. The villages of Pat́old́áuṋgá, D́ihi, Hentáli (Entally), Citrapur (Chitpur), Hogalkunŕe, Pat́uyápáŕá, Bágmárii, Mogalbágán, Beleghát́á and Táltalá, all became part of Kolkata as well. The neighbourhoods of Garáńahát́á, Áhirit́olá, Mohanbágán, Hartukibágán, Hálsibágán, Hát́kholá, Kumárt́ulii and Shobhábájár were incorporated later; however, they are also not very new.

Kalighat was a small, temple-centred village to the south. A few Brahman families and pat́uyá [painter-caste] families lived there. The pat́uyás were the artists responsible for the renowned Kalighat canvases. It was Jamini Raiṋjan Ray, a resident of Bankuraʼs Beletoŕ, who recognized the excellence of the Kalighat canvases. No written history exists to tell us how old the Kalighat canvases are, but the pat́uyás were living there at the beginning of the Pathan era. They came from the areas of Arambag and Ghatal. In those days the people of Bengal would buy paintings (pat́as) along with other items when they went to market. There used to be an especially brisk trade in the paintings of different Hindu gods and goddesses. The women who worshipped Lakshmi all the year round performed it with paintings. When Durgápúja [worship of Durga] began during the Pathan era, only the zamindars used to make idols for their worship. The middle class people who celebrated Durgápúja at home would use paintings. Those who could not afford to buy paintings would celebrate it with earthen pots. Even as recently as onehundred years ago, worship of Saraswati was performed primarily with earthen pots. The performance of Saraswati pújá with idols was introduced later, with inspiration from the British.

The temple at Kalighat has been ruined and rebuilt many times. Ultimately a large temple was constructed by the Sávarńa Choudurees. Certain Ráŕhii class Kushárii Brahmans from the Jagannathpur area of Jessore came to Jelepáŕáʼs central area and began living along the banks of the Ganges. They were the forefathers of the renowned Tagore families of Jorasanko and Pathureghata. The fishermen used to call them T́hákur out of respect, and thus they became famous as T́hákurs (Tagore).

At that time Kayasthas lived in the Govindapur area. Later, when the Maratha cavalry invaded Ráŕh, the wealthy Kayasthas of Murshidabad, Birbhum and Dumka districts left and sought shelter with the Datta zamindars of Bhagalpur Districtʼs Dattavat́i, the Ghosh families of Campánagar, and the Ghosh zamindars of Jhauyákut́hi. They began to live in hundreds of villages in Bhagalpur and Monghyr districts. Descendants of Ráŕhii Kayasthas bearing the surnames Ghosh, Mitra, Datta, Das and Singha still live there. They brought with them their own Ráŕhii class Brahman priests as well. During the invasion of the Maratha cavalry, the wealthy Kayasthas of Bankura, Hooghly, Howrah and Burdwan areas sought safe shelter in British Kolkata, the city of officialdom and business. However, for whatever reason, they did not take up residence in Govindapur. They went to Hát́kholá, Shobhábájár, Shyámbájár, Shyámpukur, Kambulit́olá, Kumurt́ulii, and Chitpur.

After the fall of Saptagrám port, the Suvarńa bańiks [a business community] and Gandha baniks residing there migrated primarily to Cuncŕo, and secondarily to various cities along the banks of the Bhagiirathii. When the British built up their business interests in Kolkata, many of Cuncŕoʼs Suvarńa bańiks moved there. They started living in the cityʼs western district by the bank of the Bhagiirathii River. In those days Kolkataʼs trade goods were moved principally along the Bhagiirathii. One famous personage of Cuncŕo at that time was Gaorii Sen. He was famous throughout the land for his wealth, his generous heart and his liberality. People still say, “If you need money, Gaorii Sen will give it to you”. These fisher folk, Piráli Brahmans, Kayasthas, weavers, textile merchants and Suvarńa baniks were the old residents of Kolkata.

With the exception of the Piráli Brahmans, many of the other Brahmans who had come to Kolkata at the beginning left for the great Brahman-predominant village of Bálii in Howrah District after the hanging of Maharaja Nandakumar [1775]. ( 9 ) Since a Brahman had been hanged in Kolkata they left for the western bank of the Ganges (“Gauṋgár pashcim kúl varańasii samatul” [the west bank of the Ganges is parallel to Varanasi]); that is, they went to Ráŕh and began living there. Afterwards, although they would still go to Kolkata for work purposes, they would not touch food or water while they were there, nor would they spend the night. They would go in the early morning and return back in the evening.

There was a dense forest between Govindapur and Kalighat. No one dared travel that path alone, even in broad daylight, what to speak of at night. When they would go to perform Kali pújá in the Kali temple they would travel in groups of forty or fifty persons and take their staffs and cudgels with them. Otherwise they would be killed by highwaymen. It is said that the highwaymen used to kill people in broad daylight and hang them from trees. The ashram of Caoraungii Bábá was in the Govindapur area (the Nátha yogi Caoraungiináth). Caoraungii Bábá was pained to see the distress of the pilgrims, so he had his disciples carve out a road through the jungle to Kalighat. For a long time this road was known as Caoraungii Bábáʼs road. I cannot understand why those who have completely or partially changed the name of this road ( 10 ) have done so.

Dharmaráj T́hákurʼs place was slightly to the east of Caoraungii Bábáʼs ashram. Dharmaráj was another name for Buddha. The worship of Dharmaráj or Dharmat́hákur began in Bengal towards the end of the Pál era. There is a Dharmarájtalá or Dharmatalá in Howrahʼs Shálikhá also, as there is in Kolkata. ( 11 ) I also do not understand why the historical name Dharmatala Street in Kolkata has been changed at present to Lenin Sarani. I am unaware of any kind of connection that the noble Lenin had with this part of Kolkata. Would it not have been possible to name a new or non-historical street or park after him? At the end of the Buddhist era in Bengal, the Buddhist followers of Dharmaráj flourished alongside the Nátha cult. It is very likely that the Carak pújá [worship] also began at this time. ( 12 ) There were and are still many Carakd́áuṋgás in our Kolkata. I am waiting for that auspicious day when the name Carakd́áuṋgá will also be changed!

I was talking about Dharmaráj pújá. Dharmaráj pújá was common to some extent in central Bengal and throughout Ráŕh. In Birbhum and Bankura, Dharmaráj was regarded as non-Brahman and was worshipped as Shiva right from the beginning. In certain parts of eastern Ráŕh and central Bengal, Dharmaráj acquired the appellation Buŕo Shiva. In many villages and towns of this region there is a Buŕo Shivatalá as well as a Dharmarájtalá. The difference was that the majority of worshippers of Dharmaráj were non-Brahmans, that is, people belonging to the ját [original] Bengalees [traditional Bengalees], chiefly Kaevarta and Sadgopa. They were generally known by the name Deváḿshi. The worshippers of Buŕo Shiva, however, were predominantly Buddhist Brahmans with the surname Cakravartii. In subsequent times, this Buŕo Shivaʼs Buddhist colour changed and he was transformed into Paoráńic Shiva.

Due to the pressure of increasing population in northern Kolkata, a famous local person, Bhavani Prasad Bandopadhyaya, cut down the jungle to the southeast and established a new village. (There is some difference of opinion regarding this.) The Bhawanipur area was built in his name. At that time the ancient Padmapukur of Bhawanipur already had a long history. Towards the end of his life, the poet Hemchandra Bandopadhyaya used to live on Padmapukur Road. You may be familiar with the invitation that he wrote to his son-in-law:
Tapta tapta tapse mách garam garam luci,
Ája máḿsa báṋdhá kapi álu kuci kuci.
Shiiter dine esab yadi khábe thábá thábá,
nambar padmapukure shiighra eso bábá.
[Hot tapse fish and hot lucis, goatʼs meat, cauliflower and potato chips,
If you would eat handfuls of all this on a winterʼs day,
Then come soon, my good man, to such and such number Padmapukur.]

The poet Hemchandra Bandopadhyaya became famous for his Vitrasaḿhár Kávya. One mistake of the poet Hemchandra has now infected the majority of Indian languages. He used the word káyá to rhyme with cháyá. There is no such word as káyá in Sanskrit. The word is káya (derived from the verbal root ci + ghaiṋ). Although the word káyá is a mistake, it is used extensively today.
Names ending in Gáchá/Gáchi/Geche

In Bengal there are many places named Gáchá, Gáchi, Gachiyá (Geche). We should know what the origin is of the Bengali word gách [plant, tree]. The Sanskrit synonym for gách is vrkśa. Be that as it may, the Bengali word gách does not come from the Sanskrit word vrkśa. In other words, gách is not originally a Sanskrit word. The word gách comes from the Mágadhii Prákrta word gratsa. Gratsa means “that which does not move”. Gratsa > gaccha in Demi-Mágadhii > gacchá in old Bengali > gách in modern Bengali. There is a twelve hundred year old Bengali poem:
Oggar bhattá rambháa pattá,
Gáikka ghittá dugdha sajattá,
Diijjai kantá kháy puńyavantá.

It means: “Hot rice served on a ripe banana leaf, with cowʼs ghee and boiled thick milk, nálte (jute) greens and maoralá [Aspidoparia marar] fish. The lovely wife is serving and the virtuous husband is eating.” It is worth pointing out that tastes of Bengalis with regard to food have not changed much in twelve hundred years.

Have you noticed one other thing? When fish is mentioned here, it must be understood that if the author is from Vauṋga-D́abák, then by fish they mean fish curry with the fish mashed in its juices. If they are from Kolkata then they mean a fish soup with ground cumin, pepper and green coriander leaf. However, if they are from Ráŕh, then they are certainly referring to a sour fish broth prepared with tamarind, because when the people of Ráŕh obtain mature fish they cook it this way. People from Kolkata take fish soup and people from Vauṋga-D́abák eat fish curry.

However, in such an excellent food list there is no mention made of d́ál. If so, then what about Ráŕhʼs intoxicating black gram? What about Nadiaʼs thrilling golden mung? What about Barishalʼs masoor d́ál [lentils] with chilli paste? What on earth is happening? Did the people of Bengal not eat pulse? Perhaps in the olden days, Bengalis ate pulse and perhaps not, but there is no mention of it in the literature. In Bengali literature these words are even attributed to Shiva:
Shák nái, shukto nái, vyaiṋjanao jadi nái,
Cáulo báŕanta, tabe phyán-bhát cái.
[If there are no greens or bitter soup or even curry
And a shortage of [uncooked] rice, then give me watery rice.]

Here also there is no mention of d́ál. The first mention of pulse in Bengali literature comes much later at the beginning of the Pathan era. The Bengalis of that time used to prepare mug-sháuli [one delicious preparation with mung] with mung d́ál. Modern ladies who cook are unfamiliar with the way mug-sháuli was actually prepared, but I would guess that it was prepared by boiling the whole mung in milk after removing the husk and then frying it in a little ghee with cloves, sugar and cassia leaf. Mugkhańd́a was prepared in those days in a similar fashion. The consumption of mung burfi as a sweet had probably not become common yet. Suriʼs artisans began making Suriʼs renowned morabbá [fruits soaked in sugar-cane syrup] approximately four hundred years ago. ( 13 ) The local preparation of mung burfi probably dates back to that time as well. At that time Suri was simply a large village in Birbhum, comprised mainly of learned Brahmans. The vital centre of Birbhum during that era was the now nearly extinct Rájnagar.

Let us return to the subject of pulse. Whether or not it was used in old Bengal, there is little doubt that pulse was not a favourite food of the people. However, greens [shák] – gacchá in the Bengali of that time – were certainly a favourite. Gimá shák [Hydroctyle rotundifolia], titá shák [a kind of bitter leafy vegetable], heleiṋcá shák [Hingtsha repens] (hiiṋce shák in Kolkata Bengali) were popular foods. Some names of these various greens are Sanskrit-derived and others are native Bengali. Nat́e shák [Petsaii; Brassica chinensis] (tańd́uleraka in Sanskrit; this green grows spontaneously in putrid water left from washing rice, thus the name tańd́uleraka) and d́euṋgo d́áṋt́á (that d́áṋt́á which is cultivated in d́áuṋgá [elevated] land) are native Bengali words. Nálte Shák [jute leaves, a variety of Ipomea reptans] (in Sanskrit nálitá). The name of Nálitábáŕi village in Mymensing District means “where nálte shák can be found in abundance”), punko (a kind of leafy vegetable; Sanskrit puńyaká – the famous sweet greens of Burdwan), hiiṋce [Enhydra fluctuans] (heleiṋcá in Ráŕh, hilamociká in Sanskrit), betho shák [goosefoot; Chenopodium album] (vásttuka in Sanskrit), kalmii [water spinach; Ipomoea reptans] (Sanskrit kalambii), puṋi [Basella lucida] (in Sanskrit putiká, potakii, upadiiká, amrtavallarii; in Vedic: potakyupadiiká svátu mánavamrtavallarii), pálaḿ [Spinacia oleracea] (pálaunkyá in Sanskrit) and shushnii [Belpharis edulis Pers.] (shikhii in Sanskrit), thánakuni [Hydrocotyle Asiatica] (bráhmii in Sanskrit) are all Sanskrit-derived words. Some people believe that pálaḿ shák [spinach] may have come originally from outside India, but that is not correct. Pálaḿ shák is native to India. It is mentioned in old Sanskrit. In Ayurveda it has been said:
Pálaunkyá madhurá svádu shleśmalá hitakárińii,
Viśt́ambhińii madashvása-pittarakta-viśápahá.

That is, “Spinach is sweet and tasty, increases the mucus element to some extent, has a beneficial effect on the body, removes constipation, relieves heart disease, is a remedy for bilious blood and counteracts poison.” The Hindi word pálak and the Angika word pálakii both come from the word pálauṋkyá. There is no relationship, however, between the word pálaḿ and the famous Pálauṋ village in Faridpur District. At one time the people of this village in southern Vikrampur were very hospitable, or extremely pálankári [caring], so the name of the village became Pálaunkyá, which in turn became Pálauṋ later on. Anyhow, we can see that shák is not something insignificant. One can compose an entire literature based on greens; however, our subject of discussion here is the word gacchá.

The modern Bengali word gách comes from the old Bengali word gacchá. Many people think that the word gách comes from the word gratsa and that gratsa means “that whose nature is to move”, but this idea cannot be accepted because when are plants ever mobile? It becomes a kind of oxymoron. It is as if it wore an anklet on its wrist, a bracelet on its ankle and a nose-ring in its ear. This reminds me of a response Kabir once gave, although it is not actually inverted in this way.
Caltii ko sab gárii kahe jvaltii dudhko khoyá,
Rauṋgiiko nárauṋgii kahe yah Kaviir ká doṋhá.

Gáŕii means “that which has been planted”. How can we call something that moves on wheels a gáŕii, and how can we say that thickly boiled milk, which is so enticing to the tongue, is khoyá, that is, spoiled? ( 14 ) But we do indeed say khoyá-kśiir [condensed sweetened milk]. And that fruit which is such a beautiful bright colour should be called ráuṋgii but instead we call it ná-rauṋgii (in Urdu oranges are called náráungii).

The old Sanskrit for “orange” is nágarauṋga. From this comes the word náráuṋgii, even though the orange is a Mediterranean fruit; that is, it is native to Europe. Nevertheless the English word “orange” is neither originally English nor European. Its origin is the Urdu word náráuṋgii. Ekt́i náráuṋgii in English is “a narangi”. With the passage of time the “n” became displaced. “A narangi” became “an orange,” and through distortion “an orangi” became “an orange”. Similarly “an apkin” became “a napkin” through displacement of the “n”. A gámchá used to be called “an apkin” in old English, not “a napkin”. Its family member, the word “apron”, is still in good health; it has not become “napron”. There are many examples of such changes on this earth, not only in the spelling of words.

In certain compositions it can be seen that the outer meaning is not the same as the inner meaning. For example, twelve hundred years ago poetry was written in [the genre of] twilight language. At that time the inner essence of spirituality was not openly stated. For example, in one place Kabir has said kambal varśe bhiuṋge páńi. Here kambal does not mean “a woolen blanket”. One of the many names for water is kambalam. Thus, in this case kambal varśe means “shower of water”, that is, water is seeping from the eyes. And in bhiuṋge páńi, páńi does not mean “water” but rather “palm”. The spiritual aspirant is seated as usual meditating on God, and the flow of tears from their eyes is wetting their palms. Many poems were written in this twilight language in the old Bengali of twelve hundred years ago.
T́álata ghar mor náhi paŕiveshii,
Háṋŕita bhát nái niti áveshii,
Eveuṋ saḿsár baŕa hil jáy,
Duhila dudhuki veńt́e sámáy.

Its apparent or external meaning is: “My house is on a hillock and I have no neighbours. There is no rice in my pot so I have to fast daily. My family is growing like that of a frog. Can the milk that has been milked from a cow go back into her teat?” Its real meaning is something else altogether. Similarly, there is another poem written in twilight language.
Dulii duhi pit́há dharańa ná jái,
Rukher tenttulii kumbhiire khái.

Its outer meaning is: “So much milk was obtained by milking a turtle that it could not be carried on the back, and a crocodile is eating the tamarind on the tree.” Needless to say, its inner meaning is different. The rukh here comes from the Sanskrit word vrkśa. Sanskrit vrkśa > rikśa > rukśa > rukh. Generally, whenever r is joined to a consonant in Sanskrit, then in Mágadhii Prákrta it is taken as if the r were not there. For example, nrtya becomes nacca, vrddha becomes vad́hd́ha > vud́d́ha > buŕá > buŕo. If there is only r, then it becomes i in the Yajurvedic style. In the Atharvavedic style it becomes u. For example, rśi becomes isi and rju becomes uju. In the aforementioned verse it would have been more correct had vrkśa been changed into vakśa, but since the pronunciation of antahstha va is akin to a vowel, vrkśa in the Atharvavedic style becomes rukśa and from that comes the old Bengali rukh. Of course, there are also exceptions. For example, the Sanskrit vakśa becomes bukka in Prákrta, and from that buk in modern Bengali. The name of the place where Lord Buddha initiated his first five disciples was Sárauṋganáth; now it has become Sárnath. The sages made a deer park in Sárauṋganáth so the place was renamed in Sanskrit as Rśipattana Mrgadáva, which later became Isipattan Migdába in Prákrta.

In any case, we were talking about the names Gách, Gáchá, Gáchiyá, Geche and Gáchi. The name of a place where there is more than one gách [tree] is gratsii in Prákrta, gacchia in Demi-Prákrta, gáchi or gáchiyá in old Bengali, and gáchi or geche in modern Bengali, for example, Belgáchiyá (Kolkata), Kalágáchiyá (Dhaka), Bámungáchi (Howrah), Kánkuŕgáchi (24 Parganas) and Sántarágáchi. To indicate more than one or also a specific one, the words gáchi, gáchá, chaŕá are used in Bengali, for example, hárgáchit́á or háte tule dáo [put the necklace in his hand]. Here both hárgáchá and hárcháŕá can be used. Similarly, the word gáchá is found in village names. For example, Muŕágáchá (Nadia), Muktágáchá (Mymensing) – where there is a collection of objects as valuable as pearls or fit to be welcomed like a pearl, or a golden opportunity for speaking. Gáchi is also added to place-names in the languages of Bihar, such as Nagpurii, Maethilii and Angika. In other words, gáchi is also used to mean “a collection of gách”, for example, Ráńiigáchi (Rátu, Ranchi) and Mańigáchi (Mithila).

A small king who is subservient to a greater king is called sámantarájá in Sanskrit. Sámanta rájá > sánotta ráá > sáṋtaráyá in Prákrta > sáṋtará in modern Bengali. Many people in southern Bengal have the surname Sáṋtará. None of them are kings any longer, but they continue to use the surname. The name of a settlement built around a Sámantarájáʼs garden or bágáń (that is, where there are many gách plants) is Sáṋtarágáchi. Sámantarája gratsii > sáṋottaráa gacchia > sáṋtarágáchi. Thus the spelling is Sántarágáchi; Sátrágáchi is an erroneous spelling.

In fact, the words gáchi, gáchá and gáchiyá were commonly used before the Farsi-derived words bág, bágán, and bágicá were imported into India. In other words, people used to call an area with a Bel tree garden as “Belgáchiyá”.
Place-names ending in D́ahari/D́ahar

There are many villages or places in Bengal as well as in many other parts of India called D́ahari. In old Bengali, the word d́ahar was used to mean “street” or “road”. D́ahar is an Austric word. Betho shák [Chenopodium ambrosioides; a type of leafy green] is found by the side of the road; that is, it is found by the side of the d́ahar, so its name is bethuyád́ahari. ( 15 ) Since buffalo graze by the ponds on both sides of the road, their name is mahiśád́ahari.

Nowadays we scarcely use the word d́ahar. It is used a little in certain parts of Bihar. We have abandoned the use of the word d́ahar and accepted the Farsi word rastá in its place. We have not accepted the Farsi word ráha instantly; it has had to travel a long and winding road before being accepted. For example, ráhá-kharac means “expenses for moving along the road”. Someone travelling by road is called ráhii in Hindustani, and a travelling companion is called hamráhii. The descendants of those government officials in Bengal during the Middle Ages who were responsible for supervising the roads (that is, they worked in the Public Works Department) still use the surname Ráhá today. Although the word ráhii is not used much in Bengali, it has been in use for nearly seven hundred years. Of course, the Sanskrit-derived word ráhi means rádhiká > ráhiá > ráhi > rái.
Shyám rúp dhari áj eseche marańa
Práńapákhii ár máne ná,
Cal ráhi cal marań yamunáy.
[Death has come today in the form of Krśńa; the bird of life refuses to linger any longer. Let us go, Radha, and plunge into the river of death.]
From Rádhikágaiṋja comes Ráigaiṋja which we mistakenly pronounce Ráygaiṋj.
Another example of the use of the word rái is:
Nava ghana cikan kála
Rái ki báseni bhála,
Tái rádhár rúper bháṋte gumor
Bujhi káṋcá soná mákhli gáy.
[Is it true that Radha has not liked The dark clouds
of the early rains?]
[Is it true that you have covered your body With a
golden hue just to put Radha to shame?]

When Mahaprabhu came to personally deliver his spiritual teachings during the time of Nawab Hussain Shah, he began his work at Rámkeli (Rámkeli is a place in Malda District). As a result, quite a few place-names related to Rádhá-Krśńa could be found in this region in subsequent time periods, for example, Káliyácak, Káligaiṋja, Ráigaiṋja and Rádhikápur.
Place-names ending in Báthán

One can also find many places in Bengal with the name “Báthán”. Báthán means “where cattle are raised extensively”. Let us say that in some place there are many cattle or buffalo being raised. Such places have been given names such as Gorubáthán and Mahiśabáthán.
Rajgir, Monghyr and Patna

At one time there was a very large village in the far north of Magadha. The name of the village was Kusumpur. The famed Indian scientist of the Middle Ages, Áryabhat́t́a, was from Kusumpur. After Kusumpur was destroyed, Pataliputra was built on the same spot. Pataliputra was destroyed in the floods of the Ganges and Shon rivers, and time and again it was rebuilt.

Girivraja or Rajagiri was the capital of Magadha during the time of Bimbisar and before that as well. The place called Rajgir nowadays is the same Girivraja or Rajagiri of that era. Many people think that the word rájgir comes from the word rájagrha, but it does not. The Sanskrit word grha became the word ghar through distortion. If the name of that place had been Rájagrha, then its modern form would have been Rájghar. Actually Rájgir comes from Rájagiri (Royal Mountain). Rájagiri is surrounded by mountains; for that very reason, its name has become Girivraja or Rájagiri.

Magadha never had a city by the name of Rájagrha. The giri has become gir through corruption, so the cityʼs present-day name is Rájgir. Similarly, Mudgagiri was the name of a giri or mountain that looked like mung (mudga > muunga > muḿg > mug), or else the name of a place which was like a mudgar (“club” in English). The name of this place in Angadesh underwent change and became Monghyr. In the Pathan era, its distorted name became Mungher. Monghyr was the last capital of Bengal during the Mughal era. Its nawab was Mirkássim. The fort from those days and the arsenal bazaar originally made for muskets and cannons still exist in Monghyr. There is a Kasimbazar named after the nawab as well as the Kaŕeyá parade grounds for military parades. Rest houses called Sarái could be found throughout the city for travellers. At that time travel lodges, where long-distance travellers would take rest, were called sarái in Farsi. In Indian languages they were called cat́i. It was where long-distance travellers would take rest. In some places the kings or nawabs made arrangements to provide food and in other places almshouses were available. In some places rice, pulse, salt and wood were stored, and the travellers would cook their own food. Sophiyásarái and Púravsarái were near Monghyr and Lakśmiisarái was slightly further away. Burdwan was also the capital of Bengal at one time. Nai-sarái was near Burdwan. At one point Patna was the capital of Bihar province during the reign of Akbar. ( 16 ) Núrsarái and Sohsarái were near Patna and Láheriyásarái was in north Bihar. Earlier I mentioned that sarái is called cat́i in Indian languages. Many villages still exist today along the roads to pilgrimage spots with the name Cat́i, such as Durgácat́i and Niirasácat́i (old Manbhum District and modern Dhanbad District).

So we were talking about Mudgagiri, which was the last capital of Bengal during the era of the Nawabs and the second capital of Anga in olden times. At that time, the Rashtrakuts were a dominant force in western India. They took possession of Monghyr for a short time and they also designated it as their second capital. This was most probably during the time of Mahendra Pal. Monghyrʼs history dates back to the Mahábhárata when Karna was the king of Angadesh. The capital of Angadesh then was Campaknagar (present-day Campánagar near Náthnagar). Although there is no connection between the historical Karna and Monghyrʼs historically famous Karńacúŕá palace, the hillock on which the palace is situated is named after Maharaja Karna. During the time of the Pala kings, Bengalʼs impenetrable fort was on the south side of the Ganges. The fall of Monghyr accelerated the fall of the Pala kings and opened the doors for the Pathan invasion. As a result, the historically renowned Vikramshila University located to the east of Monghyr near Bhagalpur (in nearby Antichak village) was destroyed.

With so much going for it, why compare the mountain to mung d́ál? As far as we can tell, mung d́ál was the favourite pulse of people in eastern Bengal. Golden mung has been cultivated in the clayish soil of Central Bengal for a very long time; it is incomparable in taste, aroma and sentience. However there is no way of knowing if the mung mentioned in Bengali literature of the Middle Ages is the śát́há variety of golden mung or some other variety of mung, because in the Ráŕh region ghoŕá mung or gheso mung is cultivated more than golden mung. They grow well even in infertile soil.

Mung is a pulse of the tropical and equatorial regions. Like lentils and peas, it does not like cold weather, so it is noteworthy that while there are English synonyms for masur and mat́ar (“lentil” and “pea” respectively), there is no proper English synonym for mung. It has been grouped in the gram family. For example, mung is called “green gram”; biri kalái or máś kalái (in Kolkata we say biuli) is black gram; kurthii kalái or kulattha kalái is “horse gram”; cholá is “Bengal gram” (chickpea; buńt́ika or cańaka in Sanskrit; but́ in Ráŕh and Bihar; rahilá in Bhojpuri; cańá in Hindi; harbaŕá in Marathi). The British first came into contact with cholá on both banks of the Kunur River, which begins in the Budbud jungle and merges in the Ajay [River] near Kográm. Since the river was in Burdwan District, they named it “Bengal gram”. Many people mistakenly use the word “gram” only for cholá. “Gram” is the name of a family [of legumes], so if one says “gram” it refers to all grams – biri kalái, mung, cholá, etc. One should use the English synonym “Bengal gram” for cholá.

Actually [ásale], the common Bengali word cholá is Farsi. And most interestingly, the word ásal [real, actual] is also a Farsi word, and so is nakal [imitation, counterfeit]. Now bal má tárá d́áŕái kothá [“Tell me, mother, where do we stand?”]. Without Farsi there is hardly any scope for moving even a single step. There is no proper English synonym for aŕhar d́ál [pigeon pea; Cajanus cajan, syn. Cajanus indicus; toor d́ál], but in Sanskrit it is kandula. In southern Oriya and in Telugu (Sarkar region Telugu) it is called kandul.

A little while ago we were discussing Kusumpur. Girivraja or Rájagiri was the capital of Magadha during the time of Bimbisar, that is, during the age of Buddha. It suffered from a lack of water, so there was need for an ample water supply in the capital. Once Buddha stood at the place where the Ganges and Shone rivers meet and said that if the capital were there, it would be advantageous in every respect. Among the disciples of the Buddha present was a merchant by the name of Pataliputra. At that time there was a synthesis between the matrilineal and patrilineal systems with respect to giving names. The motherʼs name was Rúpasári so the son was named Sáriputta. The motherʼs name was Mahámaodgalii (Mahámaggali), so her son was named Mahámaodagallan Arahań (Mahámaggallan). Similarly, his motherʼs name was Pát́alii so he was named Pát́aliiputra. Pataliputra took on the responsibility of building a city at that spot, and thus the city was named Pataliputra after him. Kusumpur was destroyed and Pataliputra was built in its place. Time and again the Shon changed its course, and time and again Pataliputra was destroyed. When one Pataliputra disappeared, another was founded atop its ruins. As a result of constant reconstruction, the name of the city, which was so often destroyed and rebuilt, became Patná or Pat́ná. ( 17 ) In Bengali and Marathi we write Pát́ná (Pát́ńá in Marathi) but in the local language, Magahii, it is written as Pat́ná. It seems to me that the spelling of Pat́ná is more correct than Pát́ná or Pát́ńá.

The flooding of the Shon River is even more destructive than that of the Ganges. This great river takes birth in the Baghelkhandi region of Madhya Pradesh and flows past the borders of the former kingdoms of Kashi and Magadha until it merges in the Ganges. Its waters are golden-coloured like the soń [flax] flower; thus its name is the “Shoń”. Although according to Hindi grammar most rivers are feminine, the Shoń is masculine. For example, Gauṋgá vahatii hae [the Ganges flows] but shon vahatá hae [the Shone flows.]

As with Patna there were or now are other cities in India which have risen from the ruins of former cities, for example, Masaliipattanam, Shriirauṋgapattanam, Bhavániipát́ná and Siḿhalapát́an (a small village near Siuṋgur in Hooghly District). At one time the village of Siḿhalapát́an, situated at the confluence of two small rivers, was a port in Ráŕh. It was from this port that the crown prince of Ráŕh, Vijay Siḿha, started his journey towards Siḿhala (its name was Lauṋka at the time).
Names and characteristics of rivers

In olden times rivers were named according to their special characteristics. For example, the river whose waters were as clear as the eyes of a kapota, or dove, was named Kapotákśa [dove eyes]. The river whose eyes were like those of a peacock was called Mayúrákśii. That river that had fire [dáma] in its belly [udara] was called Dámodar. Since there were charcoal or coal deposits beneath the Damodar, the fire-related word dáma was used. The cruel river that causes terrible harm to a community through sudden flooding is named Kasái (butcher). At present this terrible, cruel-natured Kasái River has been attired as a woman of leisure in a Benares sari and given the name [goddess] Kaḿsávatii. One should bear in mind that there is no relationship between this river and kánsá [bell-metal]. Moreover, the Sanskrit for kánsá is kaḿsya or bharańa, not kaḿsa or kaḿsá.

The river that takes birth in Midnapore and whose waters are comparatively black is called Káliyághái (Keleghái). The Keleghái River merges in the Kánsái River slightly downstream from Midnapore. After joining together, their combined flow has been given the name Haldii. This Haldii River flows into the Bhagiirathii a little upstream from the mouth of the Bhagiirathii. The small village called Haldiyá that stood at that time at the place where these two rivers meet is not connected in any way with diyá or dviipa. The village was named Haldiyá because it was situated on the banks of the Haldii River.
Qualities of villages

Villages are often named for their qualities. There are many snakes in the villages and market centres of Bengal and there are a great many cobras in Ráŕh. Their name in Ráŕhi Bengali is kharis. The village that has a very huge number of snakes is called Sarpalehaná (Birbhum). Similarly, in Manbhum District there is Mańihárá, and in Bankura District there is Mukut́mańipur.

Formerly people were given names to signify manliness. At present there is a tendency towards giving sweet names. Formerly, girlsʼ names used to have six or seven syllables, for example, Viirendramohinii, and Shatad́álavásinii. Thereafter they were shortened to around four syllables, for example, Viińápáńii, and Saodámińii. Later on it became three syllables and nowadays just two, for example, Viińá, Riińá, and Rtá. Since the very long names of earlier times presented difficulty when calling people, a tendency arose to give nicknames. A woman whose name was Kirańashashii used to be called Kenná. Today short names are the custom, so there is no longer much need for nicknames. As names keep becoming shorter, perhaps one day they will become one syllable. However there are not many one-syllable names in our storeroom. Several come to mind – Áh, Uh, Ki, Chi, Thuh, Ca, Khá. I hope that in future many meaningful one-syllable words will be created in different languages of the world; then no one will laugh if these kinds of names are given.
Place-names ending in Chaŕá/Kándi

When many are taken together to make a single whole, then it is a guccha [bunch]. This guccha is called chaŕá in Bengali. What is spread about (chaŕiye deoyá) is also called chaŕá. Rural girls sprinkle (chaŕá dey) cow dung water in the threshold of the courtyard. Many guccha or chaŕá together make one kándi or káṋdi (the words chaŕá and káṋdi are pure native Bengali words), for example, a káṋdi of bananas, a káṋdi of palm fruit, a káṋdi of coconuts or a káṋdi of betel. There are many chaŕá in one káṋdi of bananas. Many villages forming a cluster in this fashion are also called chaŕá; in north Bengal it is called guŕi, for example, Lakśmiichaŕá, Durlabhchaŕá and Kaláchaŕá. As with chaŕá, villages are also given the name Kándi or Káṋdi for the very same reason, for example, Chátinákáṋdi, Káṋdi, Jemokáṋdi (Murshidabad), Pátharkáṋdi (former Sylhet District) and Háilákáṋdi (Kachar District).
Differences between Kándi and Káṋthi

There is no relation between the names Kándi or Káṋdi and Káṋthi. The name Káṋthi comes from Kánthika, which means “shawl” [cádar] or “covering”. The word cádar, however, is Farsi. In Urdu cádar is feminine; that is, merii cádar rather than merá cádar. Since the British pronunciation of Kándi in Murshidabad District and Káṋthi in Midnapore are extremely similar, they used the word “Contai” for Káṋthi. There are two hidden reasons behind the origin of the name Káṋthi. One is the famous Káṋthi textile industry – [which produced] clothes and coverings. At one time, woven cloth was exported from Káṋthi outside India. The second reason is the renowned erudition (erudition is also a covering) of Káṋthi. At one time Káṋthi was one of the centres for the cultivation of knowledge. A good number of Sanskrit Pandits used to live there. Even though Sanskrit pandits are now few in number, Káṋthi has not completely lost its lustre.

After government records were taken away from Leguyá, Káṋthi expanded. Today the city in many respects is more developed than other district cities. In those days, unlike many other district cities, Káṋthi had a college. I know many elderly people in Orissa who learned to read and write in Káṋthi College. Amongst the five districts in Orissa at that time (Cuttack, Puri, Baleshwar, Sambalpur and Aungul-Khondamahal), Cuttack alone had Ravenshaw College, so Káṋthiʼs educational importance must indeed be recognized.

I along with many of my friends were forced to go to college in Kolkata due to the scarcity of colleges in the provinces of Bihar and Orissa at that time. The Sanskritic and cultural importance of Káṋthi cannot be denied. It would not be a bad idea if a Sanskrit university were established there. It is my firm opinion that the poet Kalidas was a resident of Káṋthi region. The all-round development of Káṋthi would afford many opportunities and benefits. I would like to direct the attention of all concerned parties to [this region.]

It would be very good if a railway line were extended from Haldiyá to Dántan via Káṋthi-Diighá. ( 18 ) This would bring the luster of a new day to the city of Káṋthi and at the same time would foster the development of Haldiyá port. The sandy town of Diighá would become a favourite of the people and south Midnapore would be bathed in a new light. Not only that, it would enable the local fisher folk, banana farmers, betel farmers and flower farmers to expect a proper return for their commodities. If arokedia (Japanese tamarisk) trees are planted by the ocean, their lustrous growth would also assist matters by providing protection against ocean storms, since this tree species has the capacity to serve as an obstacle to cyclones. It would be even better if a marine drive were built along the ocean from Haldiyá to the mouth of the Suvarnarekha River. This would not only prove attractive to travellers, but would also foster the development of smaller and larger trade centres and towns on the roadside. It would promote the economic prosperity of the local people. Many sea-dependent industries should be developed in the region lying between Káṋthi [Contai] and Junput́. A small port should also be developed near Káṋthi at the mouth of the Rasulpur River. Since it could take advantage of natural amenities, the port would not entail much expenditure.
Place-names ending in Talá/Talii/Banii

The area below any large tree is called talá or talii. Many places also have names that include talá or talii, for example, Nimtalá, Keoŕátalá, Táltalá (Kolkata), Ágartalá (Tripura) and Bádámtalá. Some examples of talii are Ámtalii, Kultalii, and Phultalii. If a particular place is used for some particular purpose or activity, in that case talá is used. Talii, however, is not used in such cases. Some examples are: Cańd́iitalá (Hooghly), Káliitalá, Paiṋcánantalá (Chandannagar), Mácántalá (Bankura), Poŕámátalá (Navadviipa), Śaśt́hiitalá (Krishnanagar) and Buŕo Shivatalá (Chandannagar). Besides this, many places have a Hát́talá and a Rathtalá.

If large numbers of a certain object or certain tree are found spread over an extended area in a certain locality, then the villageʼs name is formed by adding vanii after the name of the tree or object, for example, Ásánvanii, Paláshvanii, Shálvanii (Midnapore) and Madhuvanii (Mithila).
Tales of Nayávasán

If new people make a settlement or are newly established in a place, then those places have the name Vasán attached to the end of the name, for example, Rájávasán, Nawábvasán, Mukundavasán and Nuyávasán. Many people mistakenly say Nayávasán, but this is incorrect. “New” is nuyá or noyá in southern Ráŕh and northern Orissa. Nayá is a Hindi word. Nayá-related words in the Bihar languages include nayká or navká. Nowadays many people mistakenly call the town of Noyágrám in Midnapore District as “Nayágrám”.

When the British turned Mayurbhanj, Tripura and Coochbihar into native kingdoms, feudatory kingdoms or vassal kingdoms in accordance with their subsidiary alliance policy, they summarily included significant portions of them in British India. The former kings were thereafter considered as the zamindars of those areas and they would deposit their land revenue in the collectory. They were not considered native kings in those regions but instead became zamindars. In the remaining portions of their lands they were considered native kings.

The British left the mountainous eastern portion of Tripura in the hands of the Maharaja. In that region the Maharaja of Tripura was a native king and he had his capital there. The densely populated, fertile areas in the western part of his kingdom were incorporated into British India. In this manner, they formed the Brahmanbaria Subdivision from part of the former Kingdom of Tripura and part of the former Sylhet District; along with this they formed British Tripura or Tipperah out of Chandpur and Comilla district headquarters. Since British Tripura or Tipperah District was densely populated, there was no need to colonize it anew, but the Maharaja of Tripura remained the zamindar of a substantial part of this district. He used to deposit the land revenue in the Comilla collectory. He remained the native king for the remaining portion, which was part of Tripura. The spoken Bengali of the Kingdom of Tripura is Sylheti Bengali in the north and Noyákháli Bengali in the south, which is a blending of Chittagong Bengali and Sylheti Bengali.

Similarly, the British incorporated a vast region from the former kingdom of Coochbihar (its former name was also Kámtápur) into British Bengal. They left only eight thánás (Coochbihar, Máthábháuṋgá, Dinhát́á, Shiitalkuci, Haldibáŕi, Mekhligainj, Sitái and Tuphángainj) under control of the Maharaja. Rangpur District in the province of Bengal was formed from the areas taken over by the British. Since this region was also more or less densely populated, there was no need to make many new land leases. However, in the northern part of this region, private lands, or in a few cases leased lands, were appropriated for numerous tea plantations without paying loss compensation, or paying compensation in name only. Since the eastern part of Rangpur District was less populated, many farmers were brought in from outside and land tenures were drawn up. After Rangpur District grew very large, it was divided into three parts. The name of the southern portion remained Rangpur. The north was made into a new district, Jalpaiguri, and the northeast portion became Northeast Rangpur District. When the Province of Assam was created in 1912, Northeast Rangpur District was incorporated into it. Rangpur remained in Bengal Province and Northeast Rangpur was made part of Assam Province. Being somewhat incompatible, Northeast Rangpurʼs name was changed to Goyalpara. Dhubŕi was made the district headquarters. The spoken language of Dhubŕi is Rangpuri Bengali. The spoken language of Coochbihar and Jalpaiguri is also Rangpuri Bengali. However, in different parts of the two districts, different branches of Rangpuri Bengali are prevalent.

The mountainous regions in the western part of the Kingdom of Mayurbhanj were allowed to remain in the hands of the maharaja and the relatively level regions to the east were incorporated into British Bengal. The maharaja of this region became a zamindar of the British. His land revenue was deposited in the collectory at Midnapore. In the remaining areas he remained a native king. The capital of the kingdom was Báripadá. The portion incorporated into British Bengal was somewhat sparsely populated at that time. There was a small jungle but no mountains to speak of. The British brought in new tenants so the region became known as Nuyávasán, that is, “where tenants have been newly installed”. The spoken language of the western and southern parts of Mayurbhanj is northern Oriya, and the spoken language of the northeast part is Kerá Bengali.

Kerá Bengali is a blending of Oriya and Bengali. Many people are aware of the fact that the Oriya and Bengali languages are extremely close cousins. To a great extent their history is also the same. Their social functions and community mores as well as their anthropological identities are almost the same. It is impossible to completely separate the two, thus it is meaningless to weary oneself trying to decide whether Kerá Bengali is a dialect of Bengali or of Oriya. No matter what the leaders or philologists say, I would affirm that since this dialect is equally related to both Bengali and Oriya, the people there can claim either Bengali or Oriya as their mother tongue, as they desire. It is only natural that they should do what appeals to them the most.

Another native kingdom situated in the far west of Bengal was Seráikelá. The spoken language of the southern portion of this kingdom (the south bank of the Saiṋjay River) is Kerá Bengali.
