The spoken language of the northern part (the areas of Ádityapur, Gámáriyá, Sini, and Kándrá) is Ráŕhii Bengali. There is scarcely any difference between it and the spoken language of Bankura.

If a village has a well-known pond [pukur] or large tank [diighi], then it may also be named after that, for example, Tálpukur, Táldiighi (Táldiighi > Táldihi > Táldi), T́ungidiighi, Tapandiighi, ( 19 ) Bilvapuśkarińii (Belpukur – Nadia), Bámunpukur (Bráhmań-puśkarińii – Nadia), Pátrasáyer (Bankura), Ráńiibándh (Bankura), Rájbándh (Burdwan), Ságardiighi (Murshidabad) and Dattapukur (24 Parganas). ( 20 )
Footnotes
Four races

There were originally four races on earth: Caucasian, Mongolian, Austric and Negroid. Many people, of course, do not wish to include the Semitic race among them. Like these races, the Semitic people are also a separate race, the people of the Middle East. In some peopleʼs opinion they are a mixture of the Caucasian and Negroid races.

The Caucasian race has three branches – Nordic, Alpine and Mediterranean. The meaning of the word “Nordic” is “northern”; it comes from the Latin word nord. The Alpine people lived neither too far north nor too far south, that is, they were residents of central Europe, the table-lands of the Alps.

Nordic people have high noses, blond hair, ruddy complexion and are tall in stature. Alpine people are relatively short in stature. They are not as ruddy in complexion, have bluish hair and blue eyes. Mediterranean people are fair-complexioned with black hair, black eyes and are somewhat shorter than Alpine people. The collective name for these three branches is “Aryan”. The English word “Aryan” comes from German and originally from the Vedic word árya. As far as can be determined, the word árya comes from the

Vedic verbal root r, which means “to cultivate” or “to plough”, so the meaning of the word árya becomes “that person or community whose culture thrives through husbandry”. The original homeland of the Aryans was Europe and the areas lying near the Caucasus Mountains in Central Russia. In northwest India and in Kashmir there are a good number of people of Aryan lineage; however, their population in the rest of India is quite insignificant. The few present are mostly of mixed blood. An attempt to search and locate them would be quite difficult.

As a result of [the prevalent] Caucasian-centred aristocracy of colour, an erroneous conception has become embedded in the mind which, if clearly pointed out, might cause many people to become uncomfortable. In other words, in order to avoid this uneasiness, short-statured people will have to be accepted as Aryan, dark-complexioned people will have to be accepted as having come from Aryan origins and flat-nosed people will have to be accepted as Aryan – what kind of situation is this? I will hearken back to my original remarks and reiterate that apart from Kashmir and the northwest areas, people in other parts of India are not of the Aryan race. The Caucasians came to India from far away. They belong to the Mediterranean branch, not the Alpine or Nordic. Many people consider them to be the original inhabitants of Kashmir, but that is not correct. The original inhabitants of Kashmir belong to the Kash or Khas clans. They were people with slightly earthen complexion, short stature and snub noses.

The word kashmir comes from the word kash or khas. In old Sanskrit the word meru was used to mean “country”; for example, ajeya meru > ajamiira. The original word is kashmeru. Kashmir means “the land or meru of the Kash people”. Many people write Káshmiir instead of Kashmiir.

This is incorrect. The word káshmiir is derived by adding the suffix śńa to the word kashmiir, and it means “inhabitants of Kashmiir” or “concerning Kashmiir”. Saffron is produced in Kashmiir, thus saffron is also called káshmiir. The Hindi word keshriyá comes from the word káshmiir and it means “ochre colour”. We can call the Brahmans of Kashmir as Káshmiir Brahmans, not Káshmiirii Brahmans. Káshmiirii means “women from Kashmiir”. In the Rájataraunginii of Kalhan there is a description of the border of Kashmiir:
Sáradámat́hamárábhya kuḿkumádrtat́aḿtaka,
Távat kashmiira deshasyád paiṋcáshat yojanátmakah.

That is, Kashmiir is the land which measures fifty yojana [a distance measure ranging from four to ten miles] from Sáradámat́h to the Kumkum Mountains. India has a rich literature, especially in Sanskrit, but there is very little historical literature. Due to philosophical confusion, there was a particular apathy towards history among the people of India. It is due to this apathy that the inhabitants of India were averse to writing history. It has to be pondered by scholars to what extent, apart from the Rájatarauṋginii [Twelfth Century A.D.], can the Rájamálá of Tripura and the Assamese Buraiṋji be classified as history. The greater portion of what we consider to be the history of the Indian Middle Ages had to be collected from the diaries of foreign travellers. In order to write even a single page of history we had to look up Fá-Hiyen, Meghásthinis, Iuḿ, Chuyáḿ, or Ivanavatutá. During the Pathan and Mughal eras some history was recorded in the collections of different sovereigns, but it is difficult to say just how far they are authoritative. However, we can say that even if not all was lost, something certainly was.

The Negroid race has three branches: western, northern and southern. There are differences in their facial appearance and hair. Their hair is similar, but there are differences in the curls. The Mongolian race has five branches: Nippon (Japan), the original Chinese, Indo-Tibetan, Malaysian and Indo-Burmese. The script of the Chinese and Japanese branches is pictorial script. Each respective sound is represented by a particular picture. For example, instead of writing “tree” as we do, a mark is made to signify “tree”. Two of these marks mean “park”. A forest has many trees so three marks are used to mean “forest”. The framework of the Japanese alphabet is also fundamentally Chinese, that is, pictorial. Since the sun first rises over Japan, the name of the country is Nippon. The first syllable is ni and the second syllable is ppon and together they make nippon. Some people pronounce nippon as nihon. In this case they read the second picture hon instead of pon. In Chinese ni is pronounced ji and pon is pronounced pán, thus the pronunciation of nippon in Chinese became jipán. The distorted pronunciation of jipán in English gave rise to “Japan”. The people of the Nippon branch are large in size with flat noses and high jawbones. The Chinese branch is somewhat yellow in complexion and rather short in stature.

The Caucasian alphabet is read from left to right. English, Latin and Greek, are all read from left to right. The Semitic alphabet is read from right to left as are the Arabic and Israeli alphabets. Negroid people do not have their own script. They use Roman script. The people we call Dravidian in India are a mixture of Austric and Negroid. The word támil comes from the word dráviŕa [dravid]. Their script is Indo-Aryan.
The people of the Indo-Tibetan branch are somewhat earthen-coloured and medium in stature. Their script is also Indo-Aryan. In this group are found the Tibetans, Laddakhis,

Bhutanese, Sherpas, Lepchas, Guruḿs, Newars and Thárus. The Gorkhas do not belong to this branch. The Gorkhas are a mixture of Aryan and Tibetan. Their language, Gorkháli, is not an Indo-Tibetan language; it is a Sanskrit-derived language. Nowadays many people call the Gorkháli language “Nepali”. Actually “Nepali” does not refer to any specific language, but rather to all the languages of Nepal. These languages are Gorkháli, Newári, Rái, Tháru, Guruḿ, Sherpa, Bhutanese, Lepcha, Magar, Limbu, Limpá, Bhojpurii (western Madeshii), Angika (Moráḿ), Maethilii (central Madeshii) and Bengali (Jháṋpá District). “Nepali” does not refer to a particular language any more than the word “Indian” does.

The Gorkhas have adopted an Indo-Aryan script. Indo-Aryan scripts begin with a and end with kśa. The Indo-Aryan languages of Nepal are included in the same group as Bengali, and approximately twelve hundred years ago all of these languages were one and the same. The Caryápada or Caryácaryavinishcaya was written in this language. It should be remembered here that the Caryácaryavinishcaya was discovered in Nepal and it was written in the Bengali script of that time (Shriiharśa script). The language of the Caryácaryavinishcaya can just as well be called old Angika or old Maethilii as old Bengali. Their script was also the old Bengali script, or Shriiharśa. It should also be remembered here that during the time of the Newári kings, Maethilii, written in Shriiharśa script, was the court language of Nepal. Gorkháli gained acceptance as the court language of Nepal during the reign of the Gorkha kings (Prthviináráyańa Sháh), and it is this Gorkháli that is mistakenly called Nepali. Of course this is a partial error, not a complete error, because, like Nepalʼs other languages, Gorkháli is also a Nepali language. Gorkháliʼs old script is also Shriiharśa script. Later on Nágrii letters were introduced into Gorkháli. Old letters and records are all written in Bengali script (Shriiharśa). Thus the discovery of the old Bengali manuscript, the Caryápada, in Nepal is not at all surprising because Nepal is a land of Bengali script. When Lolitapat́t́an (Lolitapát́an), and Bhat́t́agrám (Bhát́gáon) were the capital of Nepal, they used Shriiharśa script exclusively.

The fourth branch is the Malay branch. Included within this branch are the Philippines, Indonesia and Malaysia. Chinese, Kachin, Shan, Burmese and Arakan (Mag) fall within the Indo-Burmese branch. None of these languages use pictorial script. They use Indo-Aryan scripts, that is, they are written from left to right.

Next is the Austric branch. At one time there was one vast expanse of land which stretched from old Gondwanaland to Australia. The original inhabitants of this vast region were the ancient Austrics. They are black but not jet black. They are shorter in stature than Negroes and their hair is not as curly. Indiaʼs Kols, Bhiils, Muńd́as, Hars (Santhals) and Biirhoŕas, and the aborigines and Maoris of Australia and New Zealand all belong to the Austric branch; however, the native inhabitants of the Andaman Islands do not. They are a mixture of Austric and Mongolian. The Jarvadiis who live along the Bengal-Burma border are also more or less of the same blend.

The Austric branch did not have its own script. They became familiar with Roman script when Christian missionaries came in contact with them while proselytizing. Indiaʼs Kols, Bhiils, Muńd́as, Santhals and Biirhoŕas also belong to the Austric branch; they do not have their own script. The “Ol” script that some Santhals like to use was invented by Pandit Raghunath Murmu, a man of modern times.

The script of the Dravidian group is Indo-Aryan; however, here and there they have an extra letter or two, or perhaps one or two less. For example, Tamil has fewer letters while Telegu has more. While it is true that the lack of those few letters in modern Tamil makes it difficult to write Sanskrit properly, it is even more true that the particular kind of Tamil script that Tamil pandits use for writing Sanskrit works perfectly fine. This script goes by the name of Granthalipi or Granthákśaram [book script]. The authorʼs professor in the Vedas, Pandit P. K. Ayar, was able to write very proper Sanskrit in this script. ( 1 ) The script has neither disappeared nor become completely obsolete today. In modern Tamil the numbers one and two are written alongside several letters to indicate a particular pronunciation. Others want to use certain Singhalese letters for this purpose, but there is no necessity. Tamil has its own closely related script. By using book script, Tamil will gain added respect.

The Singhalese are a mixture of Aryan and Dravidian races. They are fair-complexioned and short in stature. Their language has a large number of Sanskrit words. It is also a mixture of Aryan and Dravidian and most likely originated from a blending of Tamil and Bengali in ancient times; however, more research into this issue is required. The Oráon sub-caste in the Chottanagpur area is also part of the Dravidian group, not the Austric group. Their language, which is called Kuruk, is a Dravidian language. However, Kuruk does not have its own script. The Oráons take their surnames from the names of different birds and animals, for example, Kacchap [tortoise], T́oppo and Miinz. Miinz means “fish” in Kuruk. In Tamil it is miinam. Many people think that miina is a Sanskrit word, but actually it is not. It is a Dravidian word that was absorbed into Sanskrit.

In Bengal there is a mixture of Austric, Mongolian and Negroid stock. The further west and southwest you move, the greater the Dravidian (Austric-Negro) influence, and the further northeast you go, the greater the Mongolian influence. There is a great Mongolian influence seen in the Bengali Cákmás. The Cákmás live in the mountains of Chittagong, certain parts of Tripura and in the Demagiri region of the Lusái Hills (its modern name is Mizoram). The Mongolian influence is also pronounced in the far north of Bengal among the Bhutanese, Mech, Boŕo and Poliya communities. ( 2 )

Hebrew and Arabic

Hebrew is a close contemporary of Latin. It is a Semitic language, that is, it is between an Aryan and non-Aryan language. The Semitic lands stretched from Eastern Europe to Western Asia, that is, from Turkey in the north to Eritrea in the south (ancient Abyssinia, modern-day northern Ethiopia). The crown jewel of this Semitic land was the Hebrew language. In subsequent times, Hebrew was divided into two branches. One was medieval Hebrew and the other was old Arabic. However, we do not have a modern Hebrew language developed from medieval Hebrew because, for certain reasons, those whose mother tongue was medieval Hebrew abandoned their homeland and scattered to various parts of the globe. For this reason, their original mother tongue disappeared. Their descendants, who returned to this Semitic land, have resuscitated medieval Hebrew and now use it in their everyday activities. They have also brought back to life the Semitic script [Hebrew] of that era. In addition, they have made significant strides towards the creation of a new literature. I was very happy to see these efforts to create a new literature when I was in Israel.

Israelis are using the old Hebrew script. As with the language, the script is also Semitic. Arabic and Hebrew scripts belong to the same family, just as the two languages do. Moreover, the old Greek script and ancient Roman script were formerly used for Latin, which is indicative of the connection between the two. One difference is that the old Greek and Roman scripts are read from left to right, while the Semitic scripts are read from right to left. There is also similarity in the names of the letters. One says áliph and another says alpha. One says be and another says beta. Arabic script has diphthongs. In this system the diphthongs are written by joining the head of one letter to the tail of the other. Although this system remained in old Roman script, it is not found in modern Roman script.

I was speaking about the Arabic language. Arabic is a moderately developed language. At present, several states, especially Iraq and Egypt, are making full-fledged attempts to create a new Arabic literature. In Egypt one sees the clear influence of French literature over Arabic literature. Egypt was under French influence for quite some time. Thereafter British influence increased, and consequently it benefited from the constructive literary work of both the British and the French. Although Iraq did not have this opportunity, it is moving ahead rapidly.

Farsi is written today in a changed and expanded version of Arabic script. In other words, it has increased the number of letters according to its needs. Old Farsi, however, was not written in Arabic script. This [custom] has only prevailed in the last one thousand years. Prior to that Farsi was written in the Bráhmii and Kharośt́hii scripts. Farsi is not a Semitic language. It is an Aryan language and a distorted form of the southern branch of Vedic. Some of the Indian languages belong to Vedicʼs southeastern branch and distortion, just as Latin is Vedicʼs western branch and distortion. Medieval Farsi was a developed language and its literature achieved significant development. While modern Farsi literature has also moved forward on the path of development, its speed is comparatively less than that of medieval Farsi.

There is some Negroid influence and some Aryan influence in Semitic countries, but Vedic influence is negligible, though it cannot be altogether discounted. The Old Testament was first written in Hebrew. Later it was translated into Latin. ( 1 )
Semitic script

Today Hebrew, Semitic is the official language of Israel, though it is not [completely] the day-to-day conversational language of the people. This language ceased to exist in Israel quite a few centuries ago. Since then, the Jews residing in different lands attempted to keep Hebrew alive as their language of religion and culture, but they could not revive it as their customary language. In recent times, converging from different lands, the Israelis are using Hebrew, the language of their culture, as the official language of their nation. After a long hibernation, the language has been resuscitated and is gradually turning into their customary conversational language. The three chief Semitic languages are (1) Ottoman Turkish, (2) Hebrew and (3) Ancient Arabic. A great similarity exists among these languages, with only a few disparities. Though the official Hebrew language has changed to some extent from the language of the Old Testament, the change is minimal. If the Hebrew language had remained alive for three thousand years and evolved accordingly, present Hebrew would certainly have changed substantially from the language of the Old Testament. However, that did not happen due to its long hibernation.

The original Semitic letters were written from the right side to the left; however, despite close linguistic affinities, this tradition is no longer observed in modern Greek language. When the Turks used Arabic scripts they did follow this rule. However, since the days of Kemal Ataturk, Turks have been using Roman script for their language. The context of their language has somehow deviated from the Semitic family and come closer to the Aryan family. Prior to their returning to Israel, the Jews living in any particular land would accept the local language of that land as their mother tongue. In some countries they used Iaáaáltiish [Yiddish] as their domestic language.

In synagogues, (places of Jewish worship) we saw that Hebrew was pronounced in its ancient intonation. Now that Hebrew has become the official Jewish language, or at least of those residing in Israel, there might be some impact of modern pronunciation on the language used in their synagogues. Jews have lived in the state of Kerala, India since very ancient times. They used Malayalam as their conversational language. Malayalam had a considerable impact on their pronunciation of the Hebrew language in the synagogues. Of course, a few of them attempted to pronounce Hebrew with the correct intonation. At one time in Armenian churches of Turkey, services were given in Hebrew instead of in Latin. Perhaps now they are offered in Latin or in Armenian Turkish. Even in Kolkata, there were once many Armenians. They had their own churches (perhaps they have them even now). I had no opportunity to know what language is used in their services today. Of course, the pronunciation of the first letter a in Armenian is very close to that of Greek, which is slightly different from that of Semitic. In Hebrew, Arabic, Ottoman and Iaáaáltiish [Yiddish] languages the first letter has two pronunciations – a and áya.

The second pronunciation is fairly prolonged. In other words, the pronunciation of aya must be sufficiently elongated – somewhat like the extra long sound (pluta) in Vedic language – for example, the Vedic word agnimiile. It must be read as a-a-a-g-ni-mii-i-i-l-ra-e. ( 2 )

Hebrew and ancient Arabic were languages belonging to the same Semitic lineage – both were Semitic. Hebrew was uprooted from the land of Israel several centuries ago. Like ancient Arabic, it also died a natural death. Yet while ancient Arabic took on a new and transformed appearance, Hebrew did not, since the people speaking Hebrew were dispersed to many different lands. In certain parts of Europe, due to blending of Hebrew with local languages, Yiddish language took birth; however, it cannot be described as a transformation of the Hebrew language. After the establishment of the new state of Israel, Hebrew was made the state language and [at present] it is flourishing. If one looks at the revival of the Hebrew language in Israel, one has to wonder and reflect on the enormity of mental strength and stamina required to revive and resuscitate a language. Those conceited pundits who satisfy themselves by declaring that Sanskrit is a dead language should ponder and draw lessons therefrom. The time has come to reconsider the extent to which one is justified in declaring a language such as Sanskrit to be extinct. [Indians] not only borrow words several hundred times a day from Sanskrit but also borrow constantly from its style of expression, artistry and idioms.

Hebrew and ancient Arabic belong to the same family and hence are sister languages. Thus the present author had the advantage of learning ancient Arabic while pursuing the Hebrew language. During my stay in Israel, I saw how nicely and commendably the Hebrew language was being cultivated. However, to my regret, I also noticed that ancient Arabic was not being pursued and cultivated with the same zeal in any country, even in comparatively developed countries such as Iraq, Lebanon and Egypt. Today, ancient Arabic not only lies veiled behind a dark curtain but is also in a mist of neglect and disregard. ( 3 )

Emanation also affects script and letters. I have already mentioned that a language survives approximately one thousand years. Individual scripts, however, last about two thousand years. Written script did not exist at the beginning of the Yajurvedic era. Written script was invented in India towards the end of that era, that is, about five thousand years ago. At the time when script was invented the sages thought that the creation was a composite of a-u-ma, that is, creation, preservation and destruction. However, the manifest universe is a result of the influence of the guńas of Prakrti over consciousness – the supremacy of the binding faculty over the cognitive faculty. In other words, Parama Puruśa comes within the jurisdiction of the binding power of Prakrti. This manifest universe is called saḿvrttibodhicitta in the Buddhist nomenclature and káryabrahma (expressed universe) in Aryan nomenclature. In order to indicate this state of Puruśa and Prakrti a vertical line is used for Puruśa and a horizontal line is used for Prakrti. Together the two form a cross (+) which signifies káryabrahma or the created universe. The biija [seed] mantra of káryabrahma is ka, so this cross became ka in the Bráhmii script. Through the process of writing the Bráhmii ka quickly it became transformed through distortion into todayʼs letter ka. For example:

Hence we see that in the case of written script emanation also remains intact. The name of the first script invented by the people of India is Bráhmii or Kharośt́hii script. With the passage of time this Bráhmii-Kharośt́hii script evolved into three separate scripts. The name of the distorted script to the southwest of Allahabad is Náradá script. The distorted form to the northwest of Allahabad is Sáradá script. The script that arose in Allahabad and the lands east of there is known as Kut́ilá script.

The area where Náradá script was used included the western areas of modern Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Sindhu, Gujarat and Maharashtra. The Nágar pandits of Gujarat wrote many Sanskrit compositions in Náradá script. Later the script was named Nágarii after them. When they wrote their local language in this script they used to call it Deshii Nágarii or Moŕi. When they wrote Sanskrit (devabháśá) they would write with conjuncts by joining the upper lines [mátrá]. Then they would call the script Devanágarii. Although the modern Gujarati script is Deshiinágarii and does not have mátrá, it does have conjuncts. Among the Moŕi scripts that were used to write the different languages of Rajasthan (Marwari, Mevárii, Háŕaoti, D́hund́háru, Meváti, etc.), western Madhya Pradesh (Málavii, Bundelii), and Maharashtra (Marathi, Varáŕi, Khándeshii, Koḿkanii), Maharashtraʼs Moŕi has conjuncts in certain circumstances. However the remaining Moŕi scripts did not and do not have conjuncts. Although modern Marathi books and so forth are printed in Devanágarii script, Devanágarii is not Maharashtraʼs script. The Moŕi scripts of Rajasthan (Curuwalii, Yodhpurii, Jhunjhunwalii, etc.) are still commonly used by the general public, especially by merchants. Sindhuʼs script is not used for printing modern-day books and so on. Books in Sindhi are now printed with Farsi script, however the old Sindhi script, or Láháńd́ei, is still prevalent among merchants.

The northwestern Sáradá script evolved into several branches. The T́ekŕi, T́egŕi or T́eḿŕei (this script is a close relative of Tibetan script) scripts of the Himalayan mountain regions, Laddaki script (it is also a close relative of Tibetan script), Kashmiri Sáradá (the script in which the modern-day Kashmir pandits write Sanskrit), and D́uggardeshii Sáradá (the script of Jammuʼs D́ogri language), etc. are all distortions of the ancient Sáradá script. The script in which modern-day Panjabi is written is known as Guŕmukhii script. It is not a natural distortion of Sáradá. The Sikh guru, Arjanadeva, introduced this script (there is some difference of opinion regarding this). This script does not have full conjuncts either, however if some effort is made conjuncts can be introduced. This will eliminate the need to write words such as skul, st́ap, st́eshan, etc. as sakul, satap, sat́eshan.

The pandits did not write down the Vedas for a long time, even after the invention of script. They used to believe that the Vedas should not be written down since their forefathers had not done so. Had they looked into it a little more deeply they would have realized that the Vedas were not written down in ancient times because written script did not exist. Later, when the Vedas could no longer be committed to memory, the Kashmir pandits were the first to write them down and they did so in this distorted Sáradá script. ( 1 )

Although the scientific name of the script that arose in the lands east of Allahabad is Kut́ilá, it is better known as Shriiharśa in the annals of history. The gold coins of the emperor Harśavarddhan were inscribed with this script. It has been found in Kaoshámbi near Allahabad. Modern Bengali, Maethilii, Manipuri, Assamese and Oriya are written in this script. The scripts of Angika, Bhojpurii, Magahii, Chattisgarhii and Nagpurii are also Shriiharśa scripts, but since the people have forgotten their mother scripts and have not been able to create a developed literature of their own up until now, they do their writing and reading nowadays in Hindi. Since Hindi books are printed in Devanágarii script they are more familiar with Devanágarii script.

Oriya script is also Shriiharśa script but the people of those days used to write on palm leaves with a type of iron spud. In order to keep the palm leaves from being torn by the iron spud they rounded off the corners. Thus the modern-day Oriya script looks somewhat circular. Actually Bengali script and Oriya script are the same. The letters of Bengali script have corners, that is, they are angular, while Oriya script is circular. So in the olden days Bengali script used to be called the Gaod́iiya [Bengali] style of Kut́ilá script and Oriya used to be called the Od́ra style of Kut́ilá script.

The effect of emanation can also be seen in Bengali script. For example, in old Bengali ya used to be joined to the original letter in order to indicate a conjunct with ya. Formerly, all ya-conjuncts were written the way dya is written today (). In other words a kind of curved ya was written after the letter. This is no longer done in modern Bengali. Previously, kya, dya, tya, bhya, etc. used to be written:

In old Bengali one ta was written underneath the other to indicate tta. Nowadays, however, the tail of the upper ta does not extend back up and the hem of the lower ta begins where the tail leaves off; the letter looks like the letter o. The difference is that tta has an upper line [mátrá] while the o does not. Similarly, the conjunct tra was written with a ra below the ta. Nowadays the tail of ta does not extend back up and the hem of the ra begins where it leaves off. The letter looks like the letter e, the difference being that the letter e does not have a mátrá while the conjunct tra does. If you look at any of the Bengali compound letters you will find that they are actually a proper blending of the original letters. This blending results from taking the path of emanation.

We were talking about the Sáradá, Náradá and Kut́ilá scripts. The Sáradá script developed from the Bráhmii script; it achieved its full form about thirteen hundred years ago. Similarly, the Kut́ilá script achieved its maturity about eleven hundred years ago and the Nágarii script about eight hundred years ago. Thus very old Sanskrit manuscripts can be found in this Sáradá script. Moderately old manuscripts are found in Kut́ilá or Shriiharśa script. Nowadays those who are involved in deciphering obscure passages of old Sanskrit texts and reprinting those texts cannot avoid taking the help of scholars versed in the Sáradá and Shriiharśa scripts. During British rule, when arrangements were made for the study of Sanskrit in universities, there was a need felt to print the textbooks in a specific script so they began printing them in Devanágarii script. The use of Devanágarii script instead of Shriiharśa for Sanskrit in Varanasi, the then centre of Sanskrit study, became common at that time despite the fact that the local script was Shriiharśa and that Shriiharśa is found on stone engravings recovered there. However the pandits at Sanskrit schools in different parts of India used to write Sanskrit in their customary local script and still do so today. So no one should harbour the conception that Devanágarii is Sanskritʼs only script. Actually Sanskrit does not have its own script. Every script commonly used in different parts of India is Sanskritʼs script. Among these, the Sáradá, Shriiharśa and the south Indian scripts are older than Devanágarii. ( 2 )

Shriiharśa Script

Many of you know that what passes for Bengali script today is traditionally known as Shriiharśa script. In ancient India, Saendhavii script was a bhávátmaka lipi [a script based on bháva, that is, ideas]. In the context of its lineage, it was somewhat related to Chinese pictorial script, though it did not belong exactly to the same family or type. In Saendhavii, one single idea was represented to a certain extent in the form of a single letter with the help of pictures. Bráhmii-Khorośt́hii ( 1 ) script was its metamorphosed form. Bráhmii script was prevalent in eastern India until the time of Ashoka, when the stone edicts of Ashoka were inscribed in Bráhmii letters. Now, is the oldest form of Bengali script, known thus far as Shriiharśa script, actually Shriiharśa script? Does Shriiharśa script in fact belong to the period of Emperor Shriiharśa? Did the script not exist before it came to be inscribed on the seals of King Harśavardhana? Has the Bengali first letter a or other letters of the present Bengali language come indirectly from Bráhmii script or directly from Shriiharśa script?

When examining the first Bengali letter a, one understands its indirect link with Bráhmii script as well as with Shriiharśa script. As a result, scholars came to the conclusion that the present Bengali resemblance to Shriiharśa script is about eleven hundred to twelve hundred years old. The appearance of Shushuniyá script in Bankura district (the deed of King Chandravarmaʼs gift, which is inscribed on the walls of Shushuniyá hills near Chatna police station in Bankura District) suggests that it is definitely the old Bengali script, and that this script is very close to Shriiharśa script. From the language and ideas revealed in that script, it can be understood that in Bengal (especially in Ráŕh) at that time, a new Hindu religion (not the ancient Puranic religion, that is, religion based on Bráhminism, and not the Vedic/Árśa religion or the Jain religion) was prevalent. So it is not difficult to surmise that the edict was inscribed during the Gupta age [from 320 A.D.] or some time later.

When the people of Bengal, especially of Ráŕh, came into the realm of [recorded] history, they were devotees of Lord Shiva. This definitely occurred after the emergence of Sadáshiva – significantly less than seven thousand five hundred years ago. From this very period, it can be reasonably surmised that the people of Western Ráŕh were known as Máhátos. Today certain people claim that the Máhátos are descendants of Shivajii, since they introduced the system of agriculture in Western Ráŕh with the help of bullocks and ploughs. Others used to address them reverentially as Mahátman, which later turned into Máhátos. The Máháto civilization is at least seven thousand years old. They are the sons of the soil of Western Ráŕh. However, the emergence of Shivajii [1627] took place towards the end of the Mughal period. So by what logic could they be the descendants of Shivajii, who appeared only a few hundred years ago? How could more than fifty lakh [5,000,000] Máhátos be the descendants of Shivaji, who emerged only a few hundred years ago? The idea is antithetical to history and illogical. In reality, Máhátos are [among] the original Bengalis, such as Siḿmuŕá, Kháuṋgármuŕá, Kheriámuŕá, Ho-muŕá and Kushmet́muŕá of Western Ráŕh. They never originated from outside Bengal. Rather, the intellectual and wealthy people originated from within their own ranks. Attempting to pass themselves off as a distinct and separate race, they have turned themselves into so-called upper-caste Bengalis. Hence I have designated Máhátos as the ját báuṋgálii [original Bengalees], meaning that most communities of western Ráŕh have descended from this community.

This description is applicable not only to the Máhátos of western Ráŕh. Even the Kaevarta-Máhiśya of southern Ráŕh, Gope-Sadgopes of Central-North Ráŕh, Ráj-Baḿshii of North Bengal, Kot́ál-Namashúdras of Central Bengal and Cákmás (shákyamás) of Eastern Bengal are from this original Bengali community [Máhátos, Siḿmuŕa, etc.]. They did not originate from outside Bengal. Rather, they are the actual foundation of Bengali civilization and its upholder, its vehicle and nurturer. It is true that the so-called upper-castes have enhanced the glamour of Bengali society, but they are not its primary foundation. Since these original Bengalis have been neglected for so long (the pure Bengali equivalent for ‘so long’ is etadin, but we pronounce it ayáddin, according to the local Kolkata dialect of Bengali), the all-round development of Bengalis who followed Shaeva Dharma was not possible.

After a long period of time, that is, about two thousand five hundred years ago, Vardhaman Mahaviir, founder of the Jain religion, came to Astinagar with the goal of giving instruction on dharma. Earlier known as Atthinagar, the town was given its current name Vardhamán [Burdwan], in honour of Varddhaman [Vardhaman is also correct] Mahaviir. It was the central hub of activities of Ráŕh in those days. It is there that he preached his religious ideas. From that time onwards, the people of Ráŕh embraced the Jain religion, but they did not forget their ancient Deity, Lord Shiva. The situation was very much like that of the green plating on a golden ring. The gold was Shaeva Dharma, and the plating was that of the Digambar Jain religion.

Due to the impact of the Jain religion, the people of Ráŕh, though advanced in courage and valour, became averse to giving battle. They have silently [endured all sorts of] wrongs and injustices as they considered that to protest was an impious act. [However], the teachings of Shiva did not conform to this [ideology.] Even today, in the rural areas of Ráŕh, festivals like gájan, caŕak, jhṋápán and bolán [all local festivals related to Shiva], which have no relation to the Digambar Jain religion, are observed.

By examining stone inscriptions, one could surmise that Shushuniyá script was about eleven hundred to twelve hundred years old, which tallies with the period of the new Hindu [Puranic] age. Yet prior to that in Ráŕh was Shaeva dharma or a blending of Shaeva dharma with Jainism. The symbol of Jain Shiva was the huge Shiva-liuṋga, known commonly as Jyotirliuṋga, and the gigantic Gaorii-pat́t́a, which is found in various ruins. The worship of these Shivas was not performed by Brahman priests of the new Hindu age but by native Bengalis known as láyá or Páńd́e-Brahmans. (They worked as priests amongst the tribals or so-called lower caste Hindus.) The priests of the D́om community still use the title of “Pandit” and the priests of the Sadgope community use “Deváḿshii” (deváḿshii > deáḿshii > deáshii) as their title. It may be that they use it even today. Traditionally, the stone idols of Lord Shiva, known as Jyotirliuṋga, have been found in Ráŕh in large numbers, especially in Western Ráŕh. Some time ago this Jain Shiva idol was found even in Burdwan, and is presently being worshipped as Vardhamáneshvar.

Since the time of Harśavardhan, in Ráŕh as well as all of Bengal, there emerged the Maháyánii Buddhist religion. Due to the presence of Jainism in Ráŕh since early times, Buddhism could not strike as deep a root there as it could at Samatat́ [South Bengal], Davák [Dacca and adjacent districts of Bangladesh] and several other parts of Bengal. The Buddhist Shiva idols or Kúrma Shiva idols look somewhat like kúrmas [tortoise] or like the letter “zero,”which symbolizes the Buddhist concept of shunyaváda [nihilism.] Shankarácárya said, Yathá Shúnyavádináḿ sunyaḿ Brahma Brahmavidáḿstathá [“What Shúnya is for the followers of Shúnyaváda, Brahma is for the followers of Brahma.”]

When the Puranic religion was sweeping across Bengal, Kúrma Shiva was transformed into Dharmaráj or Dharmat́hákura, and elsewhere into Buŕoshiva. The priests for these deities were primarily native Bengalis. Some of these priests who followed the Puranic religion used threads of copper. Close to Kolkata (in the Shálkiyá area) is Dharmatalla, where the god Dharmat́hákur is also found. Dharmatalla Street of Kolkata is named after this Buddhist Shiva or Dharmat́hákur (I have already mentioned earlier and I say it again that by changing its name, a desecration of history has been perpetrated. I am certain that before committing this act, the wrongdoers did not consult any historian.) From the above-mentioned facts ( 2 ), it can be understood that before the existence of Shushuniyá script in Ráŕh or Bengal there existed Shaeva Dharma, Digambar Jainism influenced by Shaivism and Maháyánii Buddhism. However, Maháyánii Buddhism was prevalent throughout Bengal. Hinayánii Buddhism or sthavirváda (Theraváda) existed only in Chittagong, where it still persists to some extent.
Dálmá script – a new discovery

A good number of relics from the Jain period have been found recently in Bhulá-Pávanpur village of P. S. Patamda as well as in the adjoining Báiṋgurdá village of Kamalpur P. S. and Jáydá village of Chandil P.S. [in Singhbhum District – Ráŕh], to the southwest. Along with these relics, the Bengali script of that period has been found. That script must be seventeen hundred years old or more, because during that entire period Ráŕh witnessed the golden era of Jainism mingled with the Shaivite cult. The broken idols that can be found are all those of Digambar Jain gods. The script that has been discovered must be older than that of Shushuniyá script. It could even be older than the Shriiharśa script found in the seals of Harśavardhan. The script belongs to the family of Shriiharśa script, but it is far more ancient. It is probable that this script has evolved from Bráhmii script, or perhaps it has not; it might be the original eastern Indian script.

During the rule of Ashoka, Ráŕh was included in the Magadha Empire. Even after the demise of King Shasháuṋka, Ráŕh was part of the Tháneshvar (Harśavardhan) dynasty. It does not mean that the particular Shriiharśa script found in the seal of Harśavardhan, was also prevalent in the distant land of Ráŕh. Of course, it could be surmised that the script of Ráŕh, though similar to that of Shriiharśa script, is much older. Ashoka used Bráhmii script in his stone inscriptions, but no such stone inscription in Bráhmii script can be found in Ráŕh, and Ráŕh was under the rule of Ashoka. There was no dearth of hills, nor was there any scarcity of stone; in fact, many broken stone idols have been found. Then why did Ashoka not erect stone pillars bearing religious instructions in this region?

There are two strong possibilities. First, during the rule of Ashoka Ráŕh ceased to use Bráhmii script and introduced its own script and began using it. That is why Ashoka did not use Bráhmii script. The second possibility is that in Ráŕh, Buddhism was not as predominant as it was in Magadha during the rule of Ashoka or even later. At that time Jainism was the dominant influence in Ráŕh, and that is why no Buddhist edicts were inscribed on the rockwalls of Ráŕh. Consequently, the scripts found in the Bhulá-Pávanpur-Báiuṋgurdá-Jáydá areas were the relics of the Jain-cum-Shaeva golden age ruins. Based on these [considerations] one can conclude that Bengali script was at least seventeen hundred years old, if not more. After this discovery there is little doubt that Bengali script is not just eleven hundred years old. Rather, it is far older. It is the oldest among the [modern] Indian scripts. Since this discovery, the script called Shriiharśa script, which hitherto was considered the oldest Bengali script, is now proven to be more recent. Under these circumstances, it would not be possible to pretend that the Bengali script is Shriiharśa script, as Bengali script, though similar to Shriiharśa script, is in fact much older.

Most of these scripts have been found in the river valleys surrounded by the Dálmá hills of Western Ráŕh (the southeastern part of the Vindhya mountains that end at Shavarbhúm). Hence, in my opinion this script should be called “Dálmá script”. There is ample scope to research whether Dálmá script originated from Bráhmii script. In other words, the Bengali language was written not in Shriiharśa script, but in the much older Dálmá script, which belongs to the Shriiharśa lineage.

It has taken a long time to discuss the history of the first letter a. There is a slight connection between the Bengali letter a and the Bráhmii letter a. It also has a strong similarity with the same letter in Shriiharśa script. In reality, it is the latest manifestation of the letter a in the Dálmá script. ( 3 )

The alphabet – Akśamálá

The word akśa has several meanings. The first letter of the alphabet is a and kśa is its last letter. Between a and kśa there are forty-eight other letters. The total number of letters is fifty. So akśa denotes the fifty letters of the [Sanskrit] alphabet. So in place of varńamálá [alphabet], the compound word akśamálá is also used. In the description of the goddess Bhadrakálii in the Atharvaveda, it has been said that Mahákálii or Bhadrakálii, the deity of time, holds these fifty letters. People of that era did not have any idea of scripts, but they had knowledge of letters or words. Disciples used to receive their mantra from the gurus by hearing them. In Sanskrit the ear is called shruti. Hence the Vedas learnt through the ears were called the shruti.

Indeed, the people of those days did not know how to write. So in place of fifty letters, they used to imagine fifty faces. They would ideate that the first letter of creation a was in the hand of Bhadrakálii. They believed that the remaining letters were in her garland, although there was no distinct entity called Mahákála. Hence, in philosophical analysis the entities Mahákála or Mahákálii can find no logical support. Time is created at every moment from the mental measurement of the motivity of action. Yet the people of those days believed that [one day] there would be a calamity that would destroy everything. In the absence of adequate knowledge of science, they imagined a final cataclysm – that one day everything would be annihilated – this is the kind of fear that was expressed. During such a cataclysm (pralaya), it was believed that Bhadrakálii would save the letters, even though philosophical and scientific logic might be against the idea of a final cataclysm. There can be no thermal death of the universe. Perhaps a particular entity may undergo thermal death, but even in that case, entities transformed into hard, solid matter due to internal clash and cohesion would fragment in a fierce explosion, as a result of which immense thermal energy would be released from the broken structures, the fragments. This would prevent the thermal death of the universe from taking place. In any case, we are relating what the people of those days believed. They believed that Bhadrakálii would save the sounds [of the alphabet] during such a cataclysm. Since they had no knowledge of letters, they used human heads to represent the letters. That is why the people finally conceived of the alphabet as a wreath of human heads. By accepting Bhadrakálii as the symbol of welfare they gained peace of mind.

In this connection it is worth mentioning that those who created the Vedas did not write them. By orally creating the rks or shlokas of the Vedas, they taught their disciples by singing them out loud. That is why they contained melody, rhythm, grammar, kalpa, and nirukta; however, nothing existed in writing. The six parts of Vedic learning, such as chanda [science of rhythm], kalpa [explanation of religious rites], nirukta [etymology], vyákarańa (grammar; there are differences of opinion on this), jyotiiś [astrology] and ayurveda (medicine; there are even differences of opinion here; some say not ayurveda but dhanurveda) were called vedáuṋga. Vedáuṋga was unwritten, since humans at that time had no knowledge of script. In the absence of script, people of those days retained the Vedas as shruti (learnt through hearing; one name for ear is shruti). When people later learnt about scripts, even then they did not want to put the Vedas into written form. By that time they had piled up such mountainous superstitions in their heads that they believed the Vedas were not meant to be written! They did not carefully analyze that their ancestors did not write the Vedas only because they had no knowledge of script. Surely had they known a script, they would have put [the Vedas] in writing. Mogul/Mughal

You have certainly heard about the word iyuichi, which is from the ancient Mongol language. You are probably familiar with the word ‘mongol’. It is the ancient language of the [northern] part of China, that is, Mongolia. Mongolians are residents of primarily inner and outer Mongolia. In ancient times, the people of both regions spoke in Mongol language. At present [that original language] has split into several regional languages. Mongolian is a mixture of Aryan-Vedic and Chinese languages. From “Mongol” has come the word “Mughal,” and through verbal transformation this word has become “Mogul”. The muglái parat́há [a special kind of flat bread containing spicy ingredients and fried in ghee or butter] is a speciality of this very area. In medieval India, there were several invasions originating from this region. Babar [1526–1530] was born from this ancient Mongol race, as was also Tamerlane [1336–1405]. The land of the Mongols was also the fatherland of the Shakas [A.D. 78]. The early habitation of the Huńas ( 2 ) was in the southwestern corner of the Mongol lands. (Mihirkul [Mihirgul – 505 A.D.] descended from this Huń dynasty.) Kujula Kadphises or Kujul Kadphises (he is not recognized as a king but rather as a leader in history) was the leader (sardár) of the Kushan sub-branch of the Iyucii branch of the Shakas [Sakas]. His successor (according to some, his son, and according to others, his son-in-law) Vimá Kadphises, or Wima Kadphises, was also a Kushan leader recognized in history. King Kanishka [A.D. 120], who belonged to the Kushan dynasty [A.D. 48–220], became the lord of a vast area of northwestern India. It is worth noting that Kujula Kadphises and Vimá Kadphises are two names that occur in the early Mongol language, but the name Kanishka belongs to Sanskrit. This change of language in Kanishkaʼs name took place when he came to India and embraced Buddhism. The names of the successors of Kanishka [Kańiśka], such as Vashishka, Huvishka and Vasudeva, are genuine Sanskrit names.

Hiuen Tsang (Yung Chuang) spoke in Chinese and was an ancient historian and traveler. According to most pundits, Mang-daring or Mang-daing Chinese was his vernacular mother language. Whether his vernacular language was Mang-daring, Cantonese or Sang Haiese Chinese, the present Chinese languages had not have appeared at that time. In addition, it is worth remembering that the letter r is hardly pronounced in Chinese. In ancient Chinese also, the same practice was observed. It can be emphatically asserted that during the last six thousand years, the letter r has been pronounced almost silently in Chinese. From my own knowledge of Chinese, I have no hesitation in making this statement. ( 3 )
The Vedic word Naptá

Even today in northwestern India, Punjab and parts of Afghanistan, the daughterʼs son is called dohatar, which is derived from the Vedic word daohitrá. The Bengali word náti [grandson] is derived from the Vedic word naptá – the words nápit or nápte are derived from the same source. The word nápit [barber] is a pure Vedic word. The word naptá, meaning nápit, is also a Vedic word that stands for both náti and nápit. The true meaning of naptá is one who prevents downfall. A barber prevents the downfall of society through [personal] grooming; a grandson [according to Vedic belief] prevents downfall through offering of food to the manes. From this belief emerged the word napta. To a modern person it narrates a tale of ancient history.
Meaning of Prabara or sub-clan

Pra – br + al/ac = prabara, meaning the best leader or the most respectable person. In certain regions of ancient India, along with the system of gotra there was the system of prabara. For instance, let us take the case of someone whose gotra was bharadváj. It indicates that the forefather of that person lived on a hill on which Bharadváj was the leader. I have mentioned in an earlier book that in ancient society, when matriarchal society and matrilineal order were in vogue, people used to identify themselves through their mother – through the name of the mother, through her mother, and again through her motherʼs mother. Identity was not determined through the fatherʼs side. The meaning of the word mátá [mother] is one through whom a family earns social respect. However, later on, due to certain unique needs of the extant social order, the patriarchal system was introduced. Amongst those special needs of the social structure, the primary one was that in the matriarchal system the mother had full responsibility towards the child and the father had very little responsibility. However, in the patriarchal system the motherʼs responsibility remained almost the same, but it was supplemented by the responsibility of the father. It created an advantage in raising children. Although the motherʼs responsibility persisted, she also received the aid of her husband. In this system, the social structure became much more solid.

In any case, in the patrilineal system the gotra (clan) was determined by the name of the leader of the hill on which they lived. The meaning of the word gotra is “hill”. Now, a very large number of people used to take shelter on a big hill. Hence, under the leader of the gotra, there were also some local leaders. They received greater respect than anyone else. In fact they received the highest veneration, and from this evolved the word prabara. ( 4 )

Gondwana ( 1 )

About 8,000 million years ago, there was no solid structure in the world and the earth was a [ball of] glowing gas. The land mass was formed only about 2,330 million years ago. [Eventually] Gondwanaland was created. At that time, the middle portion of the earth was in a state of liquid composition.

In those days there was no Arabian Sea, no Bay of Bengal or its present islands, no Indonesia and no Australia. There was no North India, no Tibet and no Himalayas. There was only one contiguous land mass from what is now the eastern portion of Africa, including South India and Malaysia, up to Australia. This landmass – the oldest landmass in the world – consisted mainly of a long island in [the form of] an archipelago. What is now Canada and Argentina also existed at that time. The territory that covered what is presently the Arabian Sea, the Bay of Bengal, the Indonesian Archipelago, the Deccan Plateau, Southeast Asia and Oceania – has been named Gondwanaland by [geologists] because the Gond people of the Austric race lived in the central portion, although this portion was not the oldest part of the land. Even today the descendants of the Gond people still live in the [Chattisgarh region].

Ráŕh – the oldest part of Gondwanaland that has remained above the sea – was the birthplace of human beings. The hills of Ananda Nagar in Ráŕh are also at least 300 million years old. At that time there were no Himalayas.
Ancient Earthquake

At least 30 million years ago, a plutonic earthquake occurred. The land that presently comprises the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea was submerged under the ocean and the present North India emerged. In the same earthquake, those parts which were previously hills became islands in the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea after the earthquake. In this way a group of 503 oceanic islands, comprising Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines islands, was also formed. All of this, including the emergence of the Himalayas, took place about 30 million years ago. The Himalayas are therefore approximately 30 million years old, but Gondwanaland and Ráŕh are far far older.

The fossils of ocean creatures can be found in the Shivalik Range, which provides proof that at one time the Himalayan ranges were under water. The Indo-Gangetic plains were formed from the alluvial deposits of the Himalayas.

The Sahara desert and Thar desert of Sind and Rajasthan were previously under the ocean, thus their sand dunes are of marine origin. These dunes provide proof that at one time these regions were under the ocean. ( 2 )
Ancient land of Ráŕh

There was a great ocean, its surface agitated by rows of towering waves, an ocean which had neither name nor gotra [clan]. Who was there to name it, who was there to tell others about it? No one was there, since human beings had not yet emerged onto this earth. This was about 300 million years ago. ( 3 ) [And as regards the land mass,] there was no name yet on earth for that arid, mountainous terrain, nor even a single grove of trees to which a name could be given. ( 4 )

After a long time this very terrain, this nameless, mountainous terrain, was given the name Ráŕh. The word ráŕh originated in the ancient Austric language and means a land of red (laterite) soil. In the world of those days there was no Áryyávartta; ( 5 ) there were no plains of Bengal or of the Deccan, nor were there the deserts of Rajasthan and Gujarat. The northern part of the Arabian Sea did not exist either; what existed was its southern part, which linked the Deccan peninsula with Africa, the Andamans, Malaysia, Indonesia and Australia. They were linked by [land] that lay sometimes a little above the water level, sometimes a little below. ( 6 ) In that world, uninhabited by human beings, the Ráŕh of those days was older than any other land. The snow-covered mountains of Ráŕh gave birth to numerous rivers. Those rivers, fed by melting snow, flowed some to the east and some to the southeast, towards the ocean.

Days passed, time passed, from beginninglessness to endlessness. Rainstorms and thunderbolts struck the mountains, and gradually the mountains diminished. Their snowy crowns fell off their heads, their height decreased. As the mountains became smaller and smaller through erosion, each river basin lying between two mountains became more elevated. The undulating red soil that we see today in western Ráŕh, the undulation that advances ahead of us till it mingles in the remote blue [horizon], the undulation that gives a hint of some lost address as it recedes behind us – that undulating land is our Ráŕh.

The mountains were gradually eroding and being transformed into sand and silt. The sand and silt, carried by the rivers of Ráŕh, formed eastern Ráŕh. This was lakhs and crores ( 7 ) of years ago.
