Characters of Rámáyańa

I have mentioned earlier that one meaning of the word khara is rákśasa. It seems that the Aryans of ancient times used to label people belonging to the Austric-Negroid group or Dravidian group as Rákśasas. Their own [Aryan] writings indicate that the Rákśasas had a developed civilization. They established large cities and towns, practiced dharma and were devotees of Lord Shiva. With the blessing of Shiva they came to possess enormous talents, power and wealth. Unwarranted comments have been made in a number of books so as to portray them in a poor light. It is true, of course, that they were antagonistic to the Aryan Vedas and their rituals, such as religious sacrifices – possibly because vital food supplies were wasted in these rituals. Wherever they saw such rituals being performed, they would storm the site and spoil the function. Ravana was described as a Rákśasa, most probably because he was opposed to the Vedas, although it was accepted that Ravana was a descendant of the sage Pulastya (according to some, a descendant of Vishvashravá). His mother Nikaśa, or Kaekesii, was born to a Rákśasa family. The character of Rama has been declared as the Maryádá Puruśottama, to signify that [according to the Puranic religion], if Puruśottama [Supreme Entity] Himself ever appeared on earth in human form, all the potential contributions He would have made have been portrayed in the Rámáyana text.

It is indeed difficult to say how successful the Rámáyana was. Nor is it possible to describe it with a single stroke of the pen. To say or write something about the Rámáyana requires careful study.
Rama was deceitful towards Ravana. His conduct was reprehensible and should be denounced. Similarly, so were certain acts of Ravana, such as the abduction of Sita.

Why did a character like Maryádá Puruśottama [that is, Rama] want to assassinate an innocent man like Bali? In his plot to kill Bali, why did he seek the help of a weak person like Sugriva? Maryádá Puruśottamaʼs behaviour can be likened very much to that of present-day politicians – castigating someone when convenient, casting off another, but when in difficulty or in a tight corner, hobnobbing with them the very next moment, even secretly conspiring with those persons. Furthermore, both parties will have a clandestine agreement to criticize and blame each other in public but “would be very close like brothers with no division between them at all in private.”

Ramaʼs act of putting Sita through the ordeal of [walking through] fire can never be condoned. His desertion of a pregnant Sita by sending her to Valmikiʼs hermitage was another despicable deed. Finally, to ask that Sita undergo the ordeal of fire a second time was sheer inhumanity. In the Rámáyańa, there are three examples of truly developed characters – Sita, Urmila and Lakśańa. Jatáyu is another character who is illumined with sacrifice and nobility. In contrast, Rama again displays his vile nature when he indiscriminately slaughters the Rákśasas. According to the Rámáyańa, the reason why one of Ramaʼs Sanskrit names is Khardhvaisin or Kharadhvaḿsii is because he annihilated the Rákśas, also known as the Khars.
In protest against the murder of her innocent husband Bali, Tara cried:
Vipadavárańa tumi Náráyańa,
Loke bale tomáya karuńánidhán.
Tave kena háy luńt́hita dharáy,
Svarńacuŕá svámiir bhutale patan.
Je anale prabhu jválále ámáya,
Sei anale tumi jvalive nishcay.
Jánakii páibe, punah háráibe,
Keṋde keṋde habe divá avasán.
[O, Savior from danger, You Narayana, People call You
the bestower of mercy Then why, alas, was he swept to
the dust, My gold-crested husband, fallen to the earth!]
[The fire with which you have blighted me Will indeed
one day burn you still.]
[You will regain Janakii, yet lose her again.]
[Your days will end in tears.]
About Tara, it has been said:
Ahalyá-Draopadii-Kuntii-Tárá-Mandodarii tathá,
Paiṋcakanyásmarennityaḿ mahápátakanáshanam.
[Remembering these five women, men can rid themselves of the sins of different births and purify their minds.]

The word khara or rákśasas has a derogatory implication. It was used by the Aryans to indicate extreme cruelty or horror; it also signified ugliness in men. The condescending Aryans (indeed, their noses had high bridges) could not accept the Austric and Dravidian civilizations. They were reluctant to recognize them as civilized. They were accustomed to thinking that they alone had the capacity for good taste and culture. That was why they called themselves Aryans, which means 'progressive peopleʼ and ‘cultured ones.’

Since Buddhists and Jains were free to some extent from the influence of Aryans, they did not discriminate between Aryans and non-Aryans. Hence, they retained their respect for Ravana. You all know that although Valmiki was the official author of the Rámáyańa, earlier versions existed – the Buddhist Rámáyańa, the Jain Rámáyańa, the Cháyá Rámáyańa, the Giitá Rámáyańa and the Adhyátma Rámáyańa. The Válmikii Rámáyańa portrayed Aryan ideology. In those days, whoever opposed the Vedas or Árśa doctrine were considered by Aryans as Rákśasas, as barbarians and infidels. Perhaps due to the influence of Aryan superiority complex (evinced in the Páiṋcálii literature of Válmikii Rámáyańa and in the Rámcaritamánasa composed by Tulsidas), a differentiation was made between vipras and shúdras. Tulsidas called his Rámáyańa Rámcaritamánasa instead of Rámáyańa – meaning the character of Rama as conceived in his mind. He could not remove his prejudice against the shúdras. His Rámáyańa, albeit a treasure-house and a gem deserving of manifold praises, was not devoid of Aryan arrogance. Here too, the Rákśasas were denigrated. About the shúdras it was said:
D́hol-gábár-shúdra-pashu-nárii,
E sab tárańa ke adhikárii.
[Drum-beating peasants, lower castes, animals and women – All these must be treated roughly in every place.]
This means that drum-beating, rustic people, shúdras, animals and women must always be treated roughly; otherwise, one will not get maximum output from them.

The Buddhists and Jains revered Ravana for his qualities. Thus, Manasarovar Lake [near Mt. Kailash, Tibet] came to be divided into two sections: the large and shallow section, which the Buddhists named Rávańa Lake, and the narrow, deep section that belonged to the Aryans and [Vedic] traditionalists. Ravana Lake was a place of pilgrimage for Buddhists who took holy baths therein; similarly, the Aryans and traditionalists considered their section of the lake sacred and also bathed there.

Various writers of the Puranas maintained that the rákśasas and dánavas [so-called demons] practiced advanced meditation. They did not have yajiṋas, nor did they perform the ritual of offering haviih [butter-oil]. The nikumbhilá yajiṋa offered by Indrajit, the son of Ravana, was quite different from those offered by the Aryans. These writers also claimed that, blessed by Lord Shiva, many Rákśasas and dánavas became strong and powerful. It became clear from these stories and legends even if there was no similarity of thought or ideas between Aryans and so-called rákśasas and dánavas, the latter were in no way inferior to Aryans. So the name Kharadhvaḿsii for Rama did not reflect any worthy quality in him; rather, according to certain people, it reflected his intolerance.
In the Rámáyańa, Rama deserted Sita. As a result, many parents in Bengal are reluctant to name their daughters Sita. At the end of the Rámáyańa, Sita said to Rama:
Janma janma tumi dev haiyo mor pati,
Ár kono janme hena koro ná durgati.
[For birth after birth be my husband, my lord, But please do not ill-treat me thus.]
In the Vaeśńava religion, followers were not allowed to touch wine, what to speak of drinking wine. Knowing this, how could one say:
Jadyapi ámár guru shuṋŕii báŕii jáy,
Tathápi ámár guru Nityánanda Ráy re Nityánanda Ráy.
[Although my guru goes to the wine sellerʼs place, Yet my guru is Nityananda Roy, he is Nityananda Roy.]

I have sufficient regard for Rama, but why should I therefore withhold my criticism of the way that the author of the Rámáyańa has portayed the characters? I shall speak frankly, using the words of Iqbal, the poet of Skekowa:
Nitya járá tomár náme paŕche namáj,
Táder mukhei kutsá kichu náoná shuńe rájádhiráj.
[Those who offer prayers in your name at the mosque, Hear from their lips some words of abuse, O king of kings.] ( 1 )]
Karkat́ii Rákśasii and cures for cancer and diabetes

The word khasátmaja (khas + átman + jan = d́a) means the son of Rákśasii, who may not necessarily be a Rákśasa. There are many stories about this in the Puranas. According to the Puranas, Rákśasii women give birth to gods and to intelligent men. One such story is about Sutanuka, the son of Karkat́ii Rákśasii, Karkat́ii Rákśasii discovered the medicinal cure for cancer. Her husband Anuvasen was a human being. Sutanuka was an ideal character; he was a generous, caring physician. Although he was the son of a Rákśasii, Sutanuka was not a Rákśasa; he was a Khasátmája. In the scriptures, the word átmaja means the first child (a son or daughter); other children are called kámaja, not átmaja. Earlier it was mentioned that Karkat́ii Rákśasii had discovered the cure for cancer. Unfortunately, that medicine has been lost to posterity. In order to diagnose diseases and find their cures, Karkat́ii Rákśasii used to dissect [and examine] corpses. Since people in those days were very undeveloped, they concluded that she was a cannibal in search of human flesh. It is said that ungrateful men burnt Karkat́ii Rákśasii to death and that both a curse – the disease bisuciká (cholera) – and a blessing – the medicine madhumeha (for diabetes) – emanated from the burning flames. Bisuciká is the Sanskrit name for cholera. In Bengali it is called oláot́há, in English cholera, and in Farsi hyáyajá. The cure for cholera has been lost; administering saline is not an actual remedy. Humanity will have to rediscover the medicine for cholera. It is beyond human understanding how worship of the goddess Oláicańd́ii (Olábibi) can alleviate this disease. ( 2 )
Caucasian Aryans, ancient Iran and wheat

Gandha + v – hval + ac. In the etymological sense, it means whoever moves or causes others to move because of a smell or at whose smell others move or stir. You know, the entire human race did not evolve at the same time in all parts of the world. Different human species with different skulls developed from tailless animals in various parts of the world. It is surmised that human beings first emerged from the western corner of Ráŕh and then from the central region of Gondwana. The first human species that appeared in Ráŕh, though belonging to the Austric race, had longer noses than those of the present-day Austric race. The first group of humans that originated from central Gondwana – Sumatra, Balidviip, Javadviip – were also Austrics, but their noses were slightly flat. It is difficult to say anything with certainty about their physical complexion. However, the land of Ráŕh was chiefly within the Karkatakranti [temperate] region. Hence it is believed that the physical complexion of these people of Ráŕh was dark blue or slightly dark. And since central Gondwana was situated in the equatorial region, the people of that area were comparatively dark-complexioned and slightly flat-nosed – but not entirely flat-nosed. It is surmised that later, people belonging to the Mongoloid group or Chinese race came there in great number in search of a livelihood, and due to the intermingling of these newcomers with the earlier Austric race, the Mongoloid-Malaysian branch of humanity was created.

There is a great amount of similarity between the skulls of the people of Ráŕh and those of the present-day Bengalis of Ráŕh. Though there is a blending of the blood of exotic Aryans or Caucasians therein, the Kayasthas of Ráŕh continue to bear a physical resemblance to their ancestors. As a result of Aryan genes, they are tall and have a brighter complexion. Nonetheless, the imprint of the ancient Ráŕhiian breed is clearly shown in their bodies. Other people of Ráŕh, especially original or native Bengalis, are bearers of that ancient skull. Amongst the Oráoṋs, due to the admixture of Negroid blood, substantial transformation has taken place in their skulls, akin to what happened among the Gońd́s and Satnámiis in Madhya Pradesh and among the Oriyás in Orissa However, in Ráŕh most of the native Bengalis – the Gopes, Sadgopes, Máhiiśyas and Kurmiis – have that ancient Ráŕhiian skull. The Brahmans, Kayasthas and Vaedyas of Ráŕh, no matter how much they consider themselves outsiders, are also the sons of the old land of Ráŕh.

Due to the blending of blood between Caucasians and Mongoloids, a definite change has come about in their physical complexion and features. Despite this, their appearance still indicates that they belong to Ráŕh. Using gold as an analogy, if the native Bengalis are pure gold, then the so-called upper caste people, especially the Kayasthas, are enameled gold. The Aryans who are known today as Caucasians originated from Switzerland. To escape from the snow in Switzerland, they turned eastwards to the Caucasus region to seek refuge in the first lap of their journey. The Negroid people made their first appearance in the central region of present-day Sahara. Due to earthquakes, the Sahara was elevated higher than sea-level; in its higher regions there was scarcity of water, though in the lower regions water was present – and could be brought up like fountains through artesian wells even today. The Sahara region appeared to lack water; hence, most of its inhabitants moved to the south. The remaining population migrated to the north and northeast. Through intermingling of this population with Caucasians, the Semitic population was born. Some of these Semitic people resemble Negroids and others Caucasians. Some have fair skin while others have brown skin; quite a number of them are curly-haired and an equally large number are straight-haired.

The second home of the Caucasian Aryans was Caucasus Ural and part of the Volga River Basin of the Volga River. As the land was full of pebbles and excessively cold, these Aryans were forced to remain idle for the major part of the year. They constantly worried about where their next meal would come from, and were compelled to hunt wild animals for food. In order to survive, they had to leave in search of new lands and new horizons. This time they moved southwards. The branch of Caucasian Aryans that moved westwards are the Europeans or Euro-Aryans of today. Those who traveled southwards became the Aryo-Iranians or Aryan-Persians. They settled for some time in Persia. Owing to their physical proximity to the Caucasian branch [of Aryans], the Aryo-Iranians retained most of their Caucasian looks and appearance. Though the lustre in their physical complexion disappeared, it did not turn blue-black or dark. Another group of Caucasian Aryans traveled to the east. They went to the basins of Gauṋgá and Yamuna, to the Brahmaputra and Brahmariidesh via Gándhára [Afghanistan], Kashmir, Saptasindhu (Punjab) and Haritadhánya (Haryana). They continued moving eastward and left their physical imprint on the Kayasthas of Ráŕh. After crossing Padma, the kayasthas of Ráŕh became the Bauṋgaja Kayasthas and, after crossing the Mahananda, became the Barendra Kayasthas (kalitá). All the Kayasthas of Bengal are originally from Ráŕh, but possess a few genetic traits of Caucasian Aryans. If they consider themselves outsiders, they are wrong indeed.

Let us come back to the original topic. The fatherland of Caucasian Aryans was a rocky and infertile region. When the Aryans learnt the art of cultivation, they grew oats and barley (bárlika) ( 3 ), albeit with difficulty. Besides eating oats and barley, they also killed animals and ate their livers, hearts and other parts for survival. Even lions, leopards and hyenas were not excluded from their diet (that region had a cold climate and was not hospitable for tigers, otherwise they would have eaten them as well.) When they came to Persia in search of food, they found paddy and wheat. Remember, the Sanskrit name for paddy is not dhánya but brhii. The word dhánya stands for green vegetation (shaśpa). The word brhii means staple food. After tasting paddy, would anyone choose oats and barley? The Aryans named paddy brhii.

Later, brhii became riihi in Latin. Today, as a result of the oral translation of Scandinavian Anglo-Saxons, it is known as rice in English. Paddy is called brhii because different food dishes could be created from it: muŕi (puffed rice), huŕumba (or huŕumbu), rut́ii (rot́iká), cápát́i (carpat́kiá ), puri (somáliká), nuci (shakkulii or shauṋkulii), parot́á (priyarot́iká or pararot́iká), cṋŕe (cipit́akam), khae (láj or khadiká: khadiká > khaiyá > khae), madiká > maiyá > mae, suji (svádajit), cála ( 4 ) (tańd́ula) and bhát (odanam).

Among you those who know grammar well must be aware of the fact that the kind of compound (samása) in which there are many ideas contained in is called bahuvrhii samása, that is, it is the ‘stock’ of many types (bahu) of foods (vrhii). There remains conjoining words (vyásvákya) like yáhár or yáháte in Bengali and yasys or yasmin in Sanskrit in bahuvrihii samása.

The Aryans fell in love with the land of Persia. When do you love a country? When you find its environment pleasant, its weather congenial, its natural scenery beautiful, its land fertile and in addition there is excellent provision for a feast – is it not? Historians say that the name of the ancient capital of Ráŕh, Astiknagar, is Vardhaman, named after Vardhaman Mahavir; however, according to Khyát́andás Khásnobis [a voracious eater, as per the story of the author], it was given the name of Vardhaman [Burdwan] because of the abundance of food. You can patiently research this! In Persia or Iran, there are many such historical sources. They called this land Áryanya Vraja. The verb vraja means to move about with joy. Compare this with the words vrajabhúmi and vrajaparikrmá.

Here, the Aryans found wheat. Many of you possibly know that one of the words for tongue is go. You must also be acquainted with the word dhumdhám. In North India, when any festival is celebrated with pomp and grandeur, it is said in northern India: baŕe dhumdhámse utsav mánáye gaye. In Bengali, we say: khuv dhumdhámer sauṋge jamidár bábu nátir biye dilen [the zamindar gave his daughter in marriage with pomp and grandeur.]

When the Aryans first ate wheat, their taste buds were filled with relish – mahádhum. That is why they called wheat godhum. The Tamil word godhumái comes from godhum. Due to its golden colour, wheat farmers in Punjab named it kańaka. In Urdu and Farsi, it is known as gondhum, also derived from godhum. In Saorasheni Prákrt it is called gehum, from which is derived the Hindi word gehu. In Mágadhii Prákrt it is called gahum. The ancient Bengali word goham originated from gahum. In present-day Ráŕhii Bengali it is called gaham. When this is quickly and briefly pronounced, it becomes gam.

Should we conclude our discussion of wheat here? No, not yet. There is more – listen. Since there was no instrument for crushing wheat in those days, the Aryans used to crush the wheat with stones and, using their hands to knead the crushed wheat, they prepared cápát́i or carpat́iká (in Hindi cápát́i.) A special smell used to emerge from the crushed wheat while it was baking. They were very much drawn to it – just as bees are drawn to flowers and flies; just as bees are drawn to honey. Thus the Aryans of those days used to sit around the fire waiting for the bread to bake and, as the smell of the baking bread or capati wafted by, they felt thrills of joy and anticipation; they felt exhilarated at the thought that their Áryakanyá (the husbands of those days used to address their wives as Áryakanyá, and the wives used to address their husbands as Áryaputra) was going to put cápát́is with dates (always write kharjúra, not kharjura which means silver) on their plates for them to eat. In order to describe this smell of the [baking] wheat that so excited and exhilarated them, they created a word for it – gandhavihbal. ( 5 )

Previously they were only familiar with barley and oats. They discovered wheat for the first time when they came to India. Wheat is called godhúma in Sanskrit. Go means “tongue” and dhúma means “festival”. When they ate wheat they realized how tasty it was, that is, it was like a festival for the tongue so they called it godhúma.

Lanka – Sri Lanka

Each race has its own special characteristics. The people of one race do not anger easily while those of another [race] keep their anger bottled up. The people of one race are overwhelmed by happiness while those of another express their happiness effusively. The people of one race keep their sorrow inside, while those of another break into tears of sorrow. Some cannot keep their mouth closed while others do not like to open their mouths at all. It must be kept in mind here that these matters are not all due to racial influence; many of them depend on climatic conditions. In countries with a wetter climate, people feel greater need to eat chillies, otherwise there is a likelihood of rheumatic attacks. Even though the inhabitants of those places know that it is not good to eat too many chillies, they continue to eat them in large quantities.

It is worth mentioning here that chillies are not indigenous to India or Bengal. Before chillies were available in India, long peppers (pippali in Sanskrit) and black peppers (kat́ubiijam) were used. When the Portuguese brought chilli [lauṋká] to India, people had a problem naming it. In order to differentiate between chilli and black pepper, they gave it the name gáchmaric and called the other golmaric. (Before the arrival of chillies, black pepper was simply called maric [pepper]). Black pepper is a creeper while chilli is an upright plant; accordingly the name gácmaric was given [gách means “plant” or “tree”]. In old Bengali lauṋká used to refer to any expanse of land enclosed by water, that is, it did not refer only to Sri Lanka or Ceylon. The word viláyet, prevalent in Arabic and Farsi, also means “an enclosed island territory” or “foreign land”. Some people think that perhaps Viláyet or Vilet means “Britain”, but this conception is incorrect. In Urdu and Farsi, Britain is called “Varttániyá”. The British government is called “Hukumate Varttániyá”. Anyhow, lauṋkámaric or chili-pepper came from a foreign land, that is, it came from Lauṋká.
There is a verse in the Caryápada:
Uju re uju cháŕi má leu re váḿka,
Niyaŕi bohi má jáore láḿka.

It means: “Take the straight, O the straight path, do not take the crooked path. Wisdom is nearby; there is no need to go to a foreign land to find it.” Here also the word lauṋká [laḿká] has been used to mean “foreign land”.

With the passage of time, the use of the word gáchmaric declined and the new name for it became lauṋkamaric. Nowadays the word maric has disappeared and only the word lauṋká, meaning “foreign land”, remains. In Ráŕhii Bengali chilli was named ságarapáriyá for a similar reason. From this comes the modern Ráŕhii soṋpre. ( 3 )

The word viláyet means land beside the sea. The Sanskrit word lauṋká also has the same meaning – land surrounded by water. Sri Lanka or Ceylon is surrounded by water. So it became known as Lanka in Sanskrit. ( 4 )

By adding the suffix ań to kula, we obtain the word kaola. The word ku means physical expression, ku means solid factor, ku means folklore, ku means an explicit suggestive expression, ku means earth, ku means something unsocial.
Ku katháya paiṋcamukh kańt́habhará biś,
Keval ámár sauṋge dvanda aharnish.
[Lips are full of foul words, the throat full of poison, With me constantly wrangling.]

Here ku does not mean unsocial or evil. Here ku indicates a clear suggestive expression. The root verb lá + d́a [suffix], thus we obtain the word la. The root verb lá means “to hold”. The word la means one who holds or something that is held. Vijaysingha, the prince of Ráŕh, conquered a country and established his rule there; since he held the kingdom together, the country was called Siḿhala (Siḿha + lá + d́a = Siḿhala). The word Ceylon has come from Siḿhala. Presently its name has been changed and the ancient name Lanka has been restored. Lanka means land surrounded by water. In different parts of India there are dozens of places called Lanka. In Uttar Pradesh near Banda at the foothills of Citrakút́a, a place surrounded by water is still today called Lanka. In the city of Varanasi, that part once surrounded by water is still known as Lanka. Similarly the Sanskrit name of the country which is surrounded by sea, to the east of which is the Bay of Bengal, on the west the Arabian Sea, in the north the Gulf of Mannar, and in the south the Indian ocean, is Lanka.

Though the name of the country is Lanka or Sri Lanka, its [primary] language is Sinhali, and its [largest community] are called Sinhalese. The king of Ráŕh, Singhaváhu, ordered his disobedient son Vijaysingha (then the capital of Ráŕh was Singhapur – Singur of Hooghly district) to leave the capital. With seven hundred of his followers accompanying him, he arrived at Lanka by ship. That was probably in 534 B.C., nearly two thousand five hundred years ago. There was a large port near Singhapur in those days, which in the context of Vijaysinghaʼs conquest of Lanka got its name Sinhalapattanam (presently known as Sinhalpát́an). The sea of Ráŕh was then more towards the north. The port of Tamluk was on the seacoast, and Sinhalpát́nam was very close to the sea. ( 5 )
Bhutan

Bhutan is a small state between India and Tibet. In the last few centuries the capital of Bhutan changed several times. The Bhutias or the tribe of Bhot́s are Indo-Tibetans of the Mongoloid race. Their language also belongs to the Indo-Tibetan group of languages. Their scripts are Aryan-Indian, that is, a, á, ka, kha and so on. Where religion is concerned, they are Maháyánii Buddhists (followers of the Lámás). They regard the D́álai Lama as their religious guru, although they have their own kings. The Bhutias used to fight battles against the kingdoms of Kamtapur (Cooch Behar) and Assam for various reasons. Finally, they reached a consensus among themselves. Since then, Bhutan has been more or less on good relations with these two states. ( 6 )

Nepal is an independent kingdom situated on the border of India and Tibet. In ancient times, Nepal was split into small states. In those days the rulers were the kings of the Newar dynasty. [Today] these Newars reside primarily in the Kathmandu valley of central Nepal. Though there is some Tibetan influence on their language, the influence of Sanskrit is immense. Their own letters are in Shriiharśa script (Bengali). The Gorkha leader, Prithvinaryan Shah, built a single state by conquering the neighbouring fragmented states. That was probably in 1773. The Gorkhas also conquered the kingdom of Udayan and present-day Tarái Aiṋcal of Northeast Himalayas, adjacent to Bihar and Jhapa District of Cooch Behar. Later there were several battles between Nepal and British India over these lands. At last General Ochterlony of British India defeated Nepal. A permanent agreement known as the Sugouli Pact was made between Nepal and British India. Sugouli is a small town in Champaran district. According to this pact, the kingdom of Udayan (present-day Garwal and Kumaon) was ceded to British India, whereupon it became part of Uttar Pradesh (a state that then included Audh and Agra). The southern part of Tarái Aiṋcal in Bihar was surrendered to the British, and the northern part of Tarái (Sattari, Mahattari, Rajbiraj, Morang, Jháṋpá [Jhapa] and Birgaiṋja districts) remained with Nepal. This part of North Tarái Aiṋcal in Nepal is presently known as Madhesha (Madhya desha) and the people are called Madheshiis. Relations between India and Nepal have been very good for a long time. Both countries are culturally linked. As long as it was under the rule of the Newar dynasty, Maethilii written in Shriiharśa script was the state language of Nepal.

After it came into the hands of the Gorkhas, Gorkháli (written in Devanagari script) became the state language. Today this Gorkháli language is called the Nepali language. There are several languages in Nepal – Limpo, Tháru, Magar, Sherpa, Gurung, Rái, Gorkháli, Newari, Tibetan, Bhutia and Lepcha. Apart from these, there are regional Madheshi languages, such as Bhojpurii, Maethilii, Auṋgiká (Morang) and Bengali (Jhapa). Constitutionally, Nepal is a Hindu state and its royal family holds a place of special reverence in several Hindu temples in India. Modern Nepal is advancing fast in education and culture. There is renewed vigour in its society. The modern youth are dreaming of a new life and gazing at the new dawn. [Nepal has now abolished the monarchy and become a full-fledged democratic republic.] Historically, Nepal was a land of Maháyánii Buddhism. Today, however, it embraces a synthesis of Hinduism and Buddhism – a rare occurrence in the world. Idols are worshipped as gods by both Hindus and Buddhists in the same shrines. There is religious harmony and no discord whatsoever between Hindus and Buddhists.

The geographical features of Nepal are similar to that of southern Terai or Madhesh. The manners and conversational style in Nepal are very much like those in India. In the north is the forest-covered, lower Himalayan region. In the social and physical spheres, it is influenced by both Indian and Tibetan cultures. Further north is the Kathmandu valley, which is the cultural centre of Nepal. This is primarily the land of the Newars. In the extreme north lies the snow-covered Himalayan mountain range. Here people are mostly of Sino-Tibetan origin. The language is also of this category. These Sino-Tibetan people are Maháyánii Buddhists. The highest mountain peak in the world, Mount Everest, is located in this region.

Nepal is abundant in natural resources. However, since that wealth was not properly utilized, the people of Nepal had to leave for distant lands in search of livelihood – to Assam, Meghalaya, Manipur, Nefa, Bhutan, Nagaland, North Bengal, and especially to Darjeeling and Sikkim. Hence, during the last 200 years many Nepalese were compelled to travel in different directions. Sikkim and Darjeeling were originally the land of Lepcha-Bhutias. However, so many people from Nepal came to those areas in their quest for a better life that the local, native inhabitants have become a minority. Once the economic structure of Nepal becomes sound, the Nepalese people will not have to migrate any longer. There is ample scope for economic development, as [Nepal has] mineral resources and ample water supplies for the development of hydro-electricity. Forest resources are also in abundance. The Nepalese people are industrious and courageous and are guided by practical intelligence. In its external affairs, Nepal maintains good relations with all countries. ( 7 )

Shyámdesh – Thailand

The word shyáma or shyámá has several meanings. Among them, the most widely used is “green”. You must be aware of the fact that Prince Sahasruvahu of Ráŕh came and conquered a large area of Southeast Asia during the post-Buddhist era and established a Ráŕhiian settlement there. He established the town of Siḿhapur, that is, Singapur (in imitation of Siḿhapur of Ráŕh, which is presently called Siuṋgur) and made it his capital, similar to the then capital of Ráŕh, Siḿhapur (Sinhapur of early Vardhaman district, presently of Hoogly district). Charmed by the lush greenery and natural beauty of Thailand, Sahasravahu called it Shyamdesh. Until today, the name Shyamdesh is still in use, alongside Thailand.
According to some people, shyámá means 'green colour.́
Yaḿ biijaḿ pavanaḿ dhyáet vartulaḿ shyámalaprabham,
Ákásha gamanádyaiṋca pakiśvat gamanaḿ tathá.

[The acoustic root is yaḿ; it is the controlling point of the aerial factor, its shape is circular and colour is green; one who has control over this particular cakra can move in the air like a bird.]

Some people say that shyámavarńa means “deep green colour.” Others say that the physical complexion of Krśńa was this deep green colour, but the complexion of Rama was light green, like green grass.
Mane paŕe ki, mane paŕe ki,
Sei navadurvádala rámarúpa.
[Do you remember, remember That tender green grass-like appearance of Rama?]

According to some people, when Prince Sahasravahu of Ráŕh conquered Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Comboj (Kampucia or Cambodia) and Vietnam in Southeast Asia, he established a large empire and modeled its capital [Sinhapur (Singapur) after the capital of Ráŕh, also called Sinhapur]. He brought the aparájitá and atasii flowers from Malaysia (Malaya) to Bengal.

Once again, let us return to the topic of the colour green. Attracted by the lush green beauty of that land, Sahasravahu gave it the name shyáma [Siam]. It is presently known as Thailand. In all the ancient literature regarding this land, the word shyama is mentioned. When I stayed in Thailand, I saw that the name of the bus company in that country was called “Shyam Bus Service.” So one meaning of shyáma is green.
The explanation for the colour of the atasii flower is given thus:
Shiitkále bhaveduśńá griiśme ca sukhashiitalá,
Atasiipuśpávarńábhá sá shyámá parikiirtitá.

[One whose sweet behaviour enables one to feel warm even in winter and cool in summer, one whose body emits the glow of the atasii flower ([Linum usitatissimum] is golden coloured) is called shyáma.]

What for man is like warmth in winter, like comforting cold during summer, and what golden colour is to the atasii flower, so also is the colour green to Thailand. This explanation of shyámá challenges all earlier explanations. Let the pundits decide which explanation we will accept and which we will not.
The devotee Kamalakanta has used the word shyámá in the sense of blue:
Majla ámár man-bhramará,
Shyámápada niil kamale.
[My mind-bee is absorbed In the blue lotus of mother Shyámá. ( 1 )]
Holland

When the bed of a river or any other body of water is higher than the adjoining land, then the water of that river or body of water can flow out at any time with great force and flood the adjoining area. In such a situation, the bed of this body of water has to be dug with a dredger or something else, that is, it has to be made deeper by removing the sand and silt, or else a high embankment has to be built on its bank so that the water can never flood the adjoining land. The embankment that is built to check the flow of high rising water is called a “dike” in English and certain other European languages. We may call it a stara-báṋdh in Bengali.

In certain places the bed of the Damodara has already become higher than the basin of Burdwan district, and in certain places it is becoming still higher. In this situation, if there is a large outflow of water from the Damodara at some point, then undoubtedly the districts of Burdwan, Hooghly and Howrah will be flooded. In this situation an effective measure would be to remove sand and silt from the bed of the Damodara with a dredger and thereby make the river basin much deeper than the adjacent land. If this is not done in order to avoid the expense, then a high embankment must be raised alongside the Damodara. This is not only to save the left bank of the Damodara but also for the safety of the right bank. Otherwise floods may occur at any time in those parts of the districts of Burdwan,Hooghly and Howrah which are situated on the right bank of the Damodara, especially in the subdivision of Arambagha. This special type of dam on the bank of the Damodara is also a dike.

In Holland, it is difficult to save the country from ocean flooding by deepening the ocean, so there is no choice but to construct high dikes. Having seen those dikes personally, I have often thought that this type of dike is also necessary in certain areas of the subdivisions of Contai and Diamond Harbour in Bengal.

We can also have windmills here as they do in Holland since the ocean wave-driven wind in these coastal areas is stronger than ordinary wind. It is also possible to arrange for production of cheap electricity from those windmills, as it is from the ocean flood tide. At one time these windmills played a very important role in the industrial development of Holland. If constructed they will serve the same purpose in the districts of Midnapur and 24 Paraganas as well.

The word Holland (Olondáj) comes from Hollandas. Earlier, the name of this country was Holland; now it is the name of one province in the country. The name of the whole country has been changed to Netherlands. Most of the work in the capital is done in Amsterdam. Earlier The Hague was the full-fledged capital. Notice that before the proper noun ‘Hague,’ 'theʼ has been used, just as if it is a proper noun. Punjab is also preceded by ‘the’. One must write ‘The Punjab’; otherwise it would be grammatically incorrect. ( 2 )
Germany

Shram + man = Sharman. Presently it is seen that those who perform physical labour are called shramikas. In fact, shram means intellectual labour. So shramika means those who perform intellectual labour. The word parishrama means physical labour. The word mehannat is a Farsi word. For those who perform intellectual labour, shram + man is sharman. For those who safeguard society from invasion like a armour, those who go to battle wearing armour, for those Kśatriyas, use the suffix man to the verb vr (vr + man) and varman is derived, out of which the first person singular is varmá. So in ancient India the Vipra was called Sharmá or Sharmań and the Kśatriya was called Varma or Varman. In North India Kayasthas still use Varma as their title. In Sanskrit, a land having a highly intellectual population was called sharmanyabhúmi. The English word ‘Germany’ comes from this word sharmanya. Germans do not call their country Germany; they call it Deutschland. ( 3 )
Mishar – Egypt

In Sanskrit, the largest number of verbs are for movement (cal, car, vraja,eja and so forth), followed by verbs for eating (bhakśa, ad, ash, kháda) and finally by verbs for seeing (ikśa, drsh, etc.). Why are there so many verbs for movement? The reason is that the Vedic Aryans were nomads before they learnt how to cultivate crops. The Vedic Aryans were not the only nomads; people of all races were initially nomads. Whenever food supplies in a particular region were exhausted, people used to migrate to other regions in search of food. In their quest for food, they roamed the entire world. Those who have this habit of moving are called nomads. In snowbound and desert areas, these nomadic habits are maximally prevalent. The stretch of land between Asia and Europe is called mishrabhúmi in Sanskrit due to its blending of western dynamism and oriental humanism. The expression mishar or mish originates therefrom. Mishar is the symbol of western and oriental synthesis. You must have heard that the Vedic Brahmans, who were influenced by the Tantras after coming to India, used to pass themselves off as Vedic during daytime and wore threads of yajiṋa or upanayana ( 4 ) on their shoulder.

In those days, this land of Mishar was extensively sandy in the south and partially so in the north. Hence the people in this region were more nomadic than people of other regions. The people of Mishar or Egypt ( 5 ) were at that time and even today called Egyptians. The shortened form of this word is gypsy, which means a nomad.

Let us return to the main theme. Aryans were primarily nomads, and this is why they had several verbs for movement. In any case, those Vedic Brahmans who followed the Vedas during the day and performed Tantric meditation at night were known as bearers of both Vedic and Tantric cultures. In those days they were given the title of Mishra. ( 6 )

Indonesia

Garud́a + dhvajá + t́a = garud́adhvaja. According to Puranic mythology, in the dhvaja [flag] of Viśńu there is the symbol of Garud́a [the name of one mythological bird]. So one of the names of Viśńu is garud́adhvaja. Again, it may mean that by watching the symbol of garud́a, one should understand that the rider is Viśńu. It is not only Viśńu – the word garud́adhvaja could be used for any other person whose flag or other emblem carries the symbol of Garud́a. One of the airlines of a Southeast Asian country is known as Garud́ Air Services. It may also be called garud́adhvaja. The name of that country is Indonesia. The religion of most people in that country is Islam, although their social life is immensely influenced by the Rámáyańa, the Mahábhárata and the Puranas. Therefore most Indonesians use names from the Rámáyańa and the Mahábhárata. Their language is also full of Sanskrit words. ( 1 )
Sikkim

Sikkim (Sukhim) was a protectorate; it was not a kingdom. It had no state administrator or king (Rájapramukha). The original inhabitants of Bhutan were the Lepchas and the Bhutias. The Nepalese migrated there later. They were not the original inhabitants. They migrated to Sikkim and Darjeeling during British rule. The British came and appropriated Darjeeling and Kurseong from Sikkim. They also seized certain parts of Kalimpong from Sikkim and other areas from Bhutan. The power of the Dewangiri of Assam was taken from Bhutan. During the rule of the Chinese Chou dynasty, Sikkim and Bhutan were part of China. Subsequently, they regained their independence. Territorially they were always independent. Sikkim and Bhutan did not accept Chinese suzerainty either before or after the Chou dynasty. They had their own chiefs of state, but their real chief was the Dalai Lama of Tibet. The Dalai Lama was both the religious chief as well as the chief of state. The Panchen Lama was a religious chief but not the chief of state. One of the Dalai Lamas (Gepsum Jamphal Nahbang Labson Yengsi Tenzing Gatso) stayed as a guest of India for some time. However the Panchen Lama or Tashi Lama stayed in Tibet.

Tibet was not a sovereign state; it was a buffer state between the large countries of India and China. For historical or other reasons, a small, friendly buffer state was maintained to prevent two large, neighbourly and adjacent states from quarreling or fighting with each other. The British deliberately kept Tibet as a buffer state between India and China. For them, seizing Tibet was an easy task indeed.

The foreign trade goods of Tibet used to pass through the port of Kolkata. The postal and telegraph departments of Tibet were controlled by British India. Both these departments of Tibet were under the control of the Postmaster General of Kolkata. ( 2 )
Hindustán/Hindostan – Hindu

The propounders of different religions were a few great personalities or payagambars (bearers of Godʼs message: payagam means message, payagambar means one who has brought the message.) However, the Vedic religion had no such propounder. Several sages (rśis) worked together to create the Vedas and formulated the Vedic religion; they created humanityʼs first expression of religion. Hence, the Vedic religion cannot be equated with other religions of the world. No one particular sage can be given any distinction for the religion created by the Vedic sages, so since ancient times it has been called Árśa Dharma (rśi + ań = árśa: the word Hindu Dharma is very recent.) When Buddhism became widespread in India, the word Hindu Dharma was not prevalent even then. When Muhammad Ibn Kashem invaded India, the entire country was known as Hindustan, and in time the people of that region came to be identified as Hindus. ‘Hindu’ was not a religious idea; it was not a group of religious people. The direct translation of the word ‘Hindu’ is Indian. Even some time back in America, the word ‘Hindu’ in the sense of 'Indianʼ was used. There can be no objection to this. The name of the land of the people belonging to the Hindu people is Hind, so whatever religious group to which people may belong – Christians, Muslims, Jews, Buddhists – all residents of this land are Hindis or Hindus.
The developed watershed that exists between Punjab and Haryana is called shirhind in Farsi. Those who find communalism present in the word ‘Hindu’ today should seriously ponder this.

Yes, some people can certainly object to improper usage if the word Hindu is used to indicate a particular religious creed. When Tagore received the Nobel Prize [1913], it was proclaimed all over the world that “a Hindu poet of Bengali literature” had won. Though he was a Hindu by virtue of his country, he was not a Hindu by virtue of his religion, as he belonged to the Bráhma [sect]. ( 3 )

A little earlier I was speaking about the árśa creed. The word ‘Hindu’ is not found in Sanskrit to signify what we mean when we use the word today. The people of Central Asia used to term the regions north of the Indus as Hindostan (In fact, during the Moghul period, Hindostan referred to present-day Uttar Pradesh.) They used the word Hindu to describe the residents of the region known as Hindostan and named their religion Hindu. The Sanskrit name for the Hindu religion is Árśa Dharma [creed of the Sages] or Árśa Mata. Whenever people tried to explain that the origin of the word Hindu came from the Meru Tantra – hinaḿ duśate yastu sa Hinduh parikiirtttah – I would say in response that the Meru Tantra is a recent book; hence, it cannot be accepted as proper evidence (ágamik pramáńa). Moreover it does not even offer the proper derivation of the word ‘Hindu.’ There is no such root verb as hind from which we can derive the word hindu by adding suffix un to it. ( 4 )
Gándhára – Afghanistan

Gándh + rak = gándhara, with elongated sound it become gándhár. The etymological meaning of the word gándhára is land in which various kinds of fragrances – the smell of walnuts, pista and raisins, the fragrance of apples and above all of asafoetida – are found in the leaves of trees, caves and rocks. In the colloquial sense, by Gándhára we mean a particular area between India and Áryańyavraja (Iran, whose ancient name is Persia.) Presently, Pakistan, is immediately on the west of India. Gándhára is farther to the west, and then comes Iran. This Gándhár is presently known as Kandahar, a province of the present-day Afghanistan.

The word gándhára also means the art and the techniques of Gándhára. Once upon a time, this land was inhabited by Maháyánii Buddhists. In those days, in its temples, shrines, caves and atop temples, countless idols of Lord Buddha, Bodhisattvas and Buddhist insignia (shakti) could be found. All were created according to a particular style of art, which is known as the gándhára style and technique. It is one of the important techniques in Indian painting. Apart from this, there are also the techniques of Kángŕá, Rajasthan and Gaod́a. By creating idols of Buddha – Buddha touching the knees (jánusparsha mudrá), Buddha in dharmacakra pravartana mudra, Buddha gazing downwards with eyes full of benevolence – a new lease on life was given to the gándhára style. In the past, this gándhára style was welcomed all over the world. In those days there was the famous Taxila University (near present-day Peshawar). Afterwards Darius invaded this land of Gándhára, and Afghans from Persia named this country Afghanistan.

The language of Gándhára is a branch of the Vedic language derived from western Prákrta or known as western Prákrta. The present-day language of Gándhára is known as the Pashto language. The word Pashto stands for western (páscátya or pascimá). A part of Gándhár was brought under Indian control by the British, but kept under military rule. Unlike the rest of India, it was not fully under British rule. Its laws were akin to those of the earlier Gándhára region.

Apart from Peshawar, towns like Dera-Ismail Khan and Deragazi Khan were inhabited by the various tribes of Gándhára. Today the people of Gándhára are known as Pakhtoons. They call those areas Pakhtoonistan. Though the language of the majority of the Afghan people is Pashto, their state language is [Dari] Farsi or Iranian, because the language of those who conquered this land was Farsi or Iranian.

During the time of Shrii Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, residents in some portions of Pakhtoon were converted to the Vaeśńavism of Gaoŕ [Gaod́]; even today they maintain this faith. However, since they have partially accommodated their dress, appearance and food habits to the rest of the Pakhtoons, it is not easy to recognize them. Yes, this is the land of Gándhára.

The word gándhára has another meaning: [the place] where there is excessive fragrance. Literally, the word gándhára is used to indicate asafoetida, the exact origin of which is this land of gándhára.

The western part of Afghanistan was part of ancient Áryańyavraja or Iran, but Gándhára was in Jambudviipa, in Bháratakhańd́a [India]. In the Iranian or Farsi language there are many Vedic words but Pashto or Gándhára language is even closer to the Vedic language. In Gándhára language, as in western Punjabi, there are many Vedic words.

The word gándhárii means a girl of Gándhára land or anything of female gender. The wife of Dhrtaráśt́ra, mother of Duryodhana, was a daughter of this land. That is why she is known as Gándhárii. This spirited lady was like a bright star in the expansive sky of the Mahábhárata. She never made peace with non-righteousness or immorality. This devoted wife was a woman who never compromised, even with her husband, who was corrupt. When Duryodhana conspired to kill the Pandavas in battle, Dhrtaráśt́ra blessed his sons. However Gándhárii did not bless them. She said, Yato Krśńa tato dharma, yato dharma tato jayah. [“Where there is Krśńa, there is victory”] Yet, she was a devoted wife. When news of her marriage with Dhrtaráśt́ra was confirmed, and when she learnt that her husband was blind from birth, she tied a piece of cloth around her own eyes. She was such an austere, devout lady. She removed that piece of cloth only twice in her life: once while blessing her son Duryodhana and secondly in the aftermath of the Kuruksetra battle while cursing Lord Krśńa. About this Gándhárii, the Bengali poet Michael Madhusudan Dutta has written:
Janmándha nrpati!
Tumi e varatá peye,
Dútmukhe, andhá hala gándhárii kiuṋkarii.
Áji hate sei sukh kii sádhe bhuiojiṋiba,
Tomáre je sukhabhoge baiṋcilá vidhátá.
Tumiiyo vidáya náo he rohińiipati,
Cáru candra, tárávrnda
Ár ná heribe kabhu háy abháginii
Tomáder priya mukh
Áji snehahiin haye cháŕinu saváre.
Snehahiin e kii kathá!
Bhulite ki pári,
Tomá Save?
Smritishakti rave jata din
E dehe, smariba ámi tomá savákáre.

[Born blind! When you receive the news From the messenger, you behaved like a blind maid, How could I serve you with that bliss? God has deprived me of that joy. You take leave, O lord of Rohini, Of the beautiful moon, of the stars, Will not once more see, O hapless girl, Your faces anymore. Deprived of affection, I leave all of you, Deprived of affection, what a word! How can I forget All of you? So long as memory remains I will remember In this body all of you together.] ( 5 )]
Malaya/Malaysia

The word girisára stands for the essence of the hills. This is its etymological meaning. Colloquially girisára means the Malaya Mountain. You know, the Bay of Bengal is in the south of Bengal, which in ancient Bengali was called ságara. In those days, the word ságara indicated the Bay of Bengal; the word samudra meant the Indian Ocean. The jálikas, that is, fishermen, of ancient Bengal (jálika > jália > jáli/jele; in Ráŕhii Bengali, both the words jáli and jele are prevalent) used to go to the Bay of Bengal and the Indian Ocean for fishing. Today Gauṋgáságar is still called ságara by the villagers of Bengal. The word ságara (ságar + ań) comes from the name of the king of ancient Samatat́. The kingdom of Ságar extended from the Himalayas to the Bay of Bengal. That is why the extreme boundary of this state, the Bay of Bengal, was known as Ságar.
Ságar jáhár vandaná race shata tarauṋga bhauṋge,
Ámrá báuṋgálii bás kari sei báiṋchita bhúmi vauṋge.
[Where the Bay of Bengal pays obeisance by its endless breakers, We Bengalis live in that cherished land, Bengal].]

On the other side of Ságar is the land of Malaya [Malaysia]. The sound ma is symbolic of destruction or death. With regard to reation-preservation-destruction, the sound a is the seed of creation, the sound u is the seed of preservation, and the sound ma is the seed of destruction. (Malay means eternally alive; one in which ma, that is, death, gets lost; ma + lii + ac = malaya, that is, the place where there is no death is Malaya). In Bengal, especially in south Bengal, the soothing pleasant breeze that blows from the Bay of Bengal is called dakśińápavana or malayapavana in Bengali.

In fact, Kalidas [probably third or fourth century] in his literature has secured a place for this malayánila [soothing breeze]. Kalidas was a man of Bengal. He was an inhabitant of the Contai area in Midnapur district, so his comments on Malaya sprang from his own experience. People used to think that there might be a mountain in the south on the other side of the Indian Ocean. [According to legend] there was a sandalwood forest on that mountain, from whence the soothing pleasant breeze wafted by. By adding the suffix ań to the word malaya we get the word málaya, that is, the land of the malaya breeze is Malaya. To the south of Burma-Martaban is the land of Malaya. Perhaps this southerly breeze comes from that very land of Malaya. Most likely there was once a sandalwood forest there, because the climate is congenial for the cultivation of sandalwood. It may be that since rubber plantations fetch a better profit, cultivation of sandalwood disappeared from this area over the course of time. The word girisára also indicates the [legendary] Malaya Mountain. It is as if the quintessence of all the fragrances on different mountains have converged in this Malay Mountain. Since the early days of Bengal, there was the system of building houses with [their] doors facing south so that the southerly breeze could enter the house. Even now in Kolkata the value and rent of houses with doors facing south are higher than those of other houses:
Púbe háṋs pashcime báṋsh,
Uttar beŕe dakśiń cheŕe.
[Swans in the east, bamboo on the west, The north fenced and the south open].]

The wetlands are in the east; so let there be a pond; let the ducks swim in that water. On the west, let there be a bamboo grove. This kind of arrangement was to prevent the loo gale [hot summer wind] from entering the house from the west. So long as the forests existed in Durgapur region, the westerly loo gale could not enter Burdwan. Due to obliteration of the sál forests in Durgapur in order to make way for steel plants, the westerly loo gale leaving Burdwan is now entering even some parts of Kolkata. In the north there are the Himalayas. During winter, chilly winds come from that direction. So uttar beŕe – meaning the northern part of the house is to be fenced. Dakśiń cheŕe means the southern part is to be left open so that southerly wind or malayánila could enter the house. ( 6 )
Footnotes

The fairly old city of Dhaka has got two Sanskrit names – D́hakkánagarii and D́ákánagarii. This city must be older than 1500 years; it could be even older. As praises of [Dhaka] once resounded across distant lands and countries, it was given the name D́hakkánagarii. The origin of this name does not refer to the demarcation of the boundary of the city by drumbeats. However, it was more widely known as D́ákánagarii. The word D́áká [Dacca] has come from the word d́abák. The root verb d́ab means to go under water. So d́abák means lowland. Since there were lowlands surrounding the city, Bauáṋgabhukti [Eastern Bengal] was called D́abák in those days. Other bhuktis [bhukti means a district] of Bengal were Burdwan bhukti and Dańd́abhukti of Ráŕh, Samatat́bhukti of Samatat́, Kámtápur and Paońd́ravardhanbhukti of Barendra, Bauṋgabhukti of Bauṋga (Bauṋgabhukti primarily meant Mymensingh, Dhaka, Faridpur and Bakharganj districts of undivided Bengal) and Upabauṋga or Shribhúmi (this Upabauṋga stands for Sylhet, Cachar, Tripura, British Tripura, that is, Comilla, Bhulua, that is, Noakhali, etc.). Chittagong was usually known as Chat́t́ala. Most of the time, this Chat́t́ala was part of Upabauṋga or Shriibhúmi. But on occasion the king of Arakan would occupy, and during other periods Arakan would be absorbed into Chat́t́ala. The relationship between Arakan and Chat́t́ala was quite intimate. For a long time the state language of Arakan was Bengali. Every educated man is aware of the name Syed Muhammad Alwal, the medieval court poet of Arakan. The complete works of this great poet, so well-versed in Sanskrit, have not yet been properly compiled. During the British regime, Arakan was made a permanent part of Burma. At that time the Kobe valley of Manipur also became a part of Burma.
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: In any case, from D́hakkánagari has come the word d́háká and from d́abák has come the word d́áká [Dacca]. In Sanskrit, however, both the words D́hakkánagarii and D́ákánagarii are equally correct; in Bengali, D́áká appears to be more correct than D́áká. But the word Dacca is also widely used. ( 1 )

t: Lavapura, Lahore
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: One speciality of dvandva samása is that if two proper nouns ending in a are put together then the ending of the first word of the compound word changes to ii, for example, kusha and lava = kushiilava. In ancient India it was the practice in Sanskrit drama that two small boys would come on stage and one would announce the names of the characters in the drama while the other would announce (ghośańá) the names of the actors and actresses playing them. ( 2 ) Those who used to make the announcements were called kushiilava. Lava was an historical figure [mythologically]. The renowned modern-day city of Lahore bears witness to the historicalname of this person. The city named after Lava is Lavapura > Láhor.
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: At the end of the drama two young girls dressed up as yavanas would come onstage to announce the end of the drama. ( 3 ) The phrase yavaniká patan [curtain-fall between acts or at the end] comes from this word. A great snow [him], that is, snowfall extending a great distance, is called himánii. A great forest [arańya], that is, a forest that extends a great distance, we would call arańyánii. But we would not call a great yavana a yavanánii. The script with which the yavanas write is called Yavanánii. ( 4 )
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: In the Rámáyańa, two sons of Rama are mentioned – Lava and Kusha. According to various and sundry stories, Rama had one son named Lava. According to many people the Lavapura town which is presently called Lahore was set up by Lava. When Sita was living in the hermitage of Valmikii, it is said that Lava once got lost. Sita was utterly stricken with grief. The sage Valmikii, was unable to bear this sight. So by the grace of Brahmá, the Lord of creation, he created another boy like Lava sprinkling the kushodaka ( 5 ) [mythological sacred water.] Since he was created out of kushodaka, he was given the name Kusha. Later, when Lava returned, Sitá did not want to part with Kusha under any circumstances. From that time onwards, Sitá came to be the mother of two sons – Lava and Kusha. ( 6 )
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: Caitya and Cattagram
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: By adding the suffix byauṋg to the word citá, the word caetya has been derived. It was the practice of the Buddhist age for the ashes collected from the funeral pyre of great men to be kept in a stone urn (sometimes even in a clay pot). These preserved ashes were called dhátu. Viháras and Saḿgháráms were built over this dhátu. (Saḿghárám is a Prákrta word which has come from the Sanskrit word Saḿgraham. From the word Saḿghárám has come the word Saḿgha, that is, organization. Saḿgháráms were places where many people used to gather together for meditation, to discuss dharma and philosophy. It has to be remembered that both the words Saḿghárám and Saḿgha are Prákrta words; they are not original Sanskrit words. Those who sometimes say, saḿghe shakti kalao yuge, that is, in the age of kali strength lies with the organization, are possibly not aware that this is not a Sanskrit utterance. ( 7 )) In memory of the ashes of funeral pyres, the Viháras and Saḿgháráms were called Caityas. According to many people, in ancient times, due to the presence of several Caityas, one town of Bengal was called Caityagrám, which in the course of time became Chattagram.
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: According to those people, foreign merchants who came to this town saw many cát́i/sát́i. (In those days, in the spoken language of the ancient people of Chattagram, cát́i/sát́i meant lamps). That is why the place came to be called Cát́igáoṋ or Cát́gáoṋ. Before reaching the shore of Chattagram, from a ship in the Bay of Bengal, one could see this port from a distance decorated with strings of lamps; hence it was so named. Of course, the Portuguese did not use any of these words, that is, Caetyagrám, Chattagram or Cát́igáoṋ. They gave the place the name Porte-de-Báuṋgálá. When the Portuguese came to [India], there were large big ports in Bengal. In the East there was Cát́gáon or Porte-de-Báuṋgálá and in the west Saptagrám or Sátgáon of Hooghly district. Probably to differentiate Cát́gáon from Sátgáon, they did not use those names but called one Porte-de-Báuṋgálá and the other Porte-de-gráṋdi. ( 8 )
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: Potaka means port. Similarly, the banks of the river where boats rest are also called nadiipotaka [river port], and the places where carts and horses gather are known as sthalapotaka [land port]. In the beginning, the spelling of ‘port’ in English was incorrect. The original spelling was porte – its pronunciation should be porte. Still today the spelling porte is the standard spelling in languages of Latin origin. The port Rome is called Porte-de-Romá. The Portuguese named Saptagrám port as Porte-de-gráṋdis and Chittagong port as Porte-de-Báuṋgálá. As per French grammatical rules, if a vowel is not used after the letter t, then t will lose its pronunciation, that is, t will become mute. So if we write porte instead of port, the pronunciation would be ‘port’, but if we write 'portʼ, its pronunciation would be por, just as táṋte is pronounced as táṋt (aunt). However, if we write tant, its pronunciation would be tṋá. In this case t will lose its sound. The French pronunciation for tea is te. Here the pronunciation is correct because the vowel e comes after t. However, vant is pronounced as váṋ whereas vante is pronounced as váṋt – one is the masculine form of selling and the other is its feminine form. Now you understand why in languages of Latin origin, in the sense of potaka one has to write porte for port for the sake of pronunciation. In English there is no need to use the vowel e after t. For this reason, they mistakenly removed the letter e from porte. Today the spelling of “port” is quite normal. The similarity of the two words potaka and porte is significant.
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: Potaka has another meaning. When the commencement of five kinds of actions; namely, the construction of houses, excavation of ponds, planting of trees, building of temples and donation of goods for a righteous cause, are done with the chanting of guru mantra and with the ideation of dedicating these acts for the welfare of the people, then this is called pratiśt́há [firm establishment], and the land where this is done is also called potaka. Presently, the word potaka means ‘compound’ in English. In Bengali it is called hátá; the hát́a of Rambabuʼs house means the compound of Rambabuʼs house; the hátá of the garden means the compound of the garden, the garden compound of Rambabu. The word hátá means compound. Today the word is widely prevalent in Ráŕh. However, this word has come from Hindustani or, according to another source, from the Persian word áhátá. In the course of time á disappeared and the hátá (kalchul) remains. ( 9 )
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: In the Buddhist era in India, there was a famous Vihára [Buddhist monastery] called Gandhakut́ivihára or Mulagandhakut́ivihára. Around that Vihára were muláguru trees. ( 10 ) That is why it was named Mulagandhakut́i vihára. Vi – hr + ghaiṋ, thus we attain the word Vihára [Bihar]. Vihára means the place where a spiritual aspirant remains merged in bliss with Parama Puruśa. Lord Buddha used the word Brahmavihára to describe these Viháras. In a later period, the Buddhist sádhakas preferred to use the word Baoddhavihára instead of the expression Brahmavihára. Vihára is an ordinary word used to describe the Baoddhaviháras – structures built on sites where the remains of ashes of Buddhist sages were kept. These Baoddhaviháras were called Caityas or Caityaviháras. Though there was a Vihára called Baoddhavihára, they were all Viháras.
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: In reality, even Gandhakut́i was a Vihára. At one time in Bengal, especially, in East Bengal, Buddhism was firmly rooted. However, since, along with religious firmness, there was no solidarity in [developing] social bonds, Buddhism perished. Casteism was the main reason for this debacle. Though Jainism existed alongside Buddhism in Ráŕh, Jainism was the more vigorous of the two. However, in one part of present day Hooghly district, Buddhism was strong. It was a kind of triangle, one corner of which was Baṋeci, another corner Mahánád and another Dvárvásinii. Baeṋci was a Baoddha prajiṋávihára. From Baoddha prajiṋávihára has come the word Baeṋci – not from the type of sour and sweet fruit called baeṋci. In a later period, this triangle of Buddhist cities was buried under the sands due to flooding of the Damodar River. The capital of Ráŕh was moved from Mahánád. Pandua, its earlier capital, had also perished under the sands. By excavating the layers of sand, traces of Pandua can still be found today. ( 11 )
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: Batavia (Indonesia)
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: During the first part of the British era, when insufficient coal sugar was being produced in this country, sugar was imported as required from Batavia in Indonesia. During my childhood, this sugar was known as bát́áciinii in the markets in Kolkata. The name bát́áciinii came from the name of the capital city Batavia. The Sanskrit name for the city of Batavia is Vátáviipura. The large-sized lemon that the Dutch brought to this country from Batavia, which has since become practically native, is still called bátávii lemon. ( 12 )
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: Peshawar
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: The people of the kingdom of Kashmiir were not familiar with Farsi script until the time of Kashmirʼs Queen Didda. The Farsi language, and after that the Urdu language, were introduced here at the time of Queen Didda. Earlier I mentioned that Jammu had been an independent, autonomous kingdom since ancient times. It is true that at the time of Kashmiirʼs King Shauḿkarvarmá, and at the time of Lalitáditya Muktapiid́a ( 13 ), that is, every once in a while, Jammu was incorporated into Kashmiir. During the time of Akbar, Jammu and Kashmiir were under the sovereignty of the Mughal court, but in name only. Kashmiir, along with Jammu and Afghanistan, fell under the control of the Punjabi chief, Ranjit Singh. After the last Sikh war, that is, after the fall of Queen Jhindan when Punjab came under British control, the British did not take upon themselves the burden of ruling all of Afghanistan. Rather they kept some part of Afghanistan in their own hands for military reasons. That portion they joined to India and gave it the name Northwest Frontier Territory with its capital at Peshawar (its old name was Puruśapura). The major portion of Afghanistan, however, they returned to the local Muslim Kings of that time; for example, they returned the kingdom of Mahiishúra [Mysore] to the descendants of the former king of that region. ( 14 )
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: Ráwalpińd́i
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: The other meaning of the word kośa is the dining table. Perhaps you may think that the people of earlier times did not sit at a table to eat and that maybe they all sat on a mat or a piŕi [wooden flat seat] and ate on plates on the ground. This is partly true. The common people in those days used to sit either on mats or on piŕis to eat. Women in those days, as today also, used to cook while sitting on piŕis. As this seat was used for preparing food and eating, it was called pińd́ika. Pińd́a means food. So, that which was used as a seat for cooking and eating food was called pińd́ika or pińd́iká. The Bengali word piŕi or piŕe comes from pińd́ika or pińd́iká.
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: In ancient times when the Aryans came to India, they first settled down in Saptasindhu province. Shatadru, Bipáshá, Irávati, Candrabhágá, (Candra and Bhágá are two separate rivers. They later combined and their united flow of waters came to be known as Candrabhágá. To the Europeans of medieval times it was known as the Cenáb), Bitastá, Kabul and Sindhu – they together formed Saptasindhu. Later during the Pathan era, the province came to be known as the Punjab. In Persian, paiṋj means five, ab means water. So the Punjab means “the combination of five waters” (that is, Sutlej, Ravi, Beas, Chenab, and Jhelum).
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: Upon migrating to Saptasindhu they became slowly habituated to agricultural life. At that time, the spots of agricultural land where they used to sit and have their lunch were called pińd́ika or places for taking food (pińd́a). In later times, in Paeshácii Prákrta, the meaning of the word pińd́i became the “village” where people ate and drank. Even today, in Punjabi language the word is used in that particular sense. Rawalpindi means the village of the Ráwáls. During that time, the Brahmans of South India were called Ráwáls. Shankaracharya took along with him several pundits from South India who were well-versed in scriptures to that area. Those pundits came to be known as Ráwáls.
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: People used to sit on mats or piŕis to eat food served in metal dishes, banana leaves, sál leaves or the leaves of lotus plants. Prosperous people, wealthy tradesmen, kings and their officials used to take food either like common people, by sitting on raised wooden seats or across tables [called kaśt́hakośa in Bengali], on normal food plates or on plates of their own choice. On the dining table, they used darbii, srak, d́imbaká, kańt́akapatra and kośasháyiká. D́imbaká means small spoon (teaspoon) and srak means large spoon (tablespoon), darbii means ladle, kańt́akapatra means fork, and kośasháyiká means table knives. Kośasháyiká was known in Central Europe or France as kanif. There was no system of using table knives in England until the reign of King Henry VIII. During the reign of King Henry VIII, table knives made their way into British dining tables. Prior to that, knives were to be found in the hands of attendants only. King Henry VIII was very much a gourmet. He frequently used to stay in Paris, the capital of France, for good wine and food. While returning home, he would carry with him not only tasty food items but also French etiquette and vocabulary. He imported French kanif to Britain. In English the word was transformed into ‘knife’. Because of the presence of the letter “k” in the French kanif, the letter “k” has been retained in the English word “knife”, though it is not pronounced. The Sanskrit word for knife is koshasháyiká. One could very well use this word even in Bengali.
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: In fact, it was King Henry VIII who brought Protestantism in England. He did this since he could not reconcile with the Catholic priests. ( 15 )
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: At́t́ak (Pakistan)
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: Innumerable objects remain in motion. This universe is an endless procession of movement – a huge procession, a panoramic procession, and rich in colour, appearance, idea, thought, sacrifice, perseverance and humanism. In this ever-flowing continuity, some move ahead, while others lag behind. No two entities move in equal rhythm. According to oneʼs own saḿskáras one person moves fast, another somewhat slowly, and another still more slowly. One who moves forward is an individual evolutionary. They come out victorious in evolutionary advancement. One who lags behind is a vikránta [counter-evolutionary] – the seed of counter-evolution lies in this lagging behind. Seven boys are in a race approximately two miles long. They are absorbed in the race, and each one is keen to get the better of the other, to speed ahead of the other. The one who falls behind is drawn back by counter-evolution; and one who moves ahead becomes resplendent in the lustre of the struggle for evolution.
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: In the social, political and economic life of human beings also there is ongoing evolutionary movement (kránti, kramań), a progression forward. The person who gives it a push, striking it with force, thus accelerating its speed (druti) of movement, is an evolutionary – their desire for victory, their genius and their longings become resonant, and attain acclamation. [In contrast], the one who is vanquished hides himself in darkness and becomes drowned in the fathomless depths of blinding gloom. This is the amazing universal order; this is the resonant music of the all-enduring universe.
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: To move while learning is called vrajana or at́ana. The main characteristic of vrajana is to attain pleasure. In at́ana, it may be that one gains pleasure while learning, but whether one derives pleasure or not, this moving while learning is called at́ana. One who learns while moving is called at́aka or paryat́aka. The name of the town of At́t́ak in undivided Punjab was derived in this manner. Sher Shah built his imperial highway from Suvarńagrám (Sonárgáon of Dhaka district) of Bengal to At́t́ak in Punjab. People incorrectly call this town Át́t́ak. When learning something while moving, the verb kram or parikramańa can be used. The word kránti is also used in this sense. ( 16 )
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: Footnotes
chapterTitle: Dhaka, Lahore, Cattagram, Batavia, Rawálapińd́i, At́t́ak

t: Mymensingh (Bangladesh)
chapterTitle: Mymensingh, Mahásthángaŕh, Medimimańd́al, Dhámrári, Vikrampur Mymensingh (Bangladesh)

t: Scholars are divided over the name Mymensingh. According to some, the entire region was known as Momensháhi; however, during the Pathan era, no trace of the name Momensháhi can be found. Even during the Moghul period this name was not commonly used. The name came to be used only during the last one hundred years. It is said that the area came to be called Mymensingh after the name of a Rajput general, Mumin Singh of Isha Khan, one of the twelve Bhuiṋás [feudal princes governing Bengal during the Moghul regime]. In the pre-Pathan era, prior to its being named Mymensingh or Mumensingh, the area was known as Barabauṋga, or the best of Bengal (bara means the “best”). Mymensingh is not a very old town. It came into existence during the end of Pathan rule or in the early Moghul period. The town was founded in the name of a self-sacrificing, religious emperor of Delhi, Nasiruddin, and called Násirábád. To bridge the gulf between Mymensingh district and its headquarters, Násirábád, people named the headquarters also as Mymensingh. For example, if the name of the district was Rajshahi, and the headquarters was called Rampur-Boalia, for the sake of convenience, the people would give also the headquarters the name Rajshahii. Similarly if the name of the district was Jessore, and the district headquarters was called Kasba, then for convenience the people called the headquarters also Jessore; and if the name of the district was Bakhargaunge, and its headquarters was Barishál [Barisal], again, for their convenience, people named the district Barisal (“Where do you live?” “In Baeshál [colloquial for ‘Barishál’] District.”).
chapterTitle: Mymensingh, Mahásthángaŕh, Medimimańd́al, Dhámrári, Vikrampur Mymensingh (Bangladesh)

t: Part of present Meghalaya, which is known as Garo Hills, was once within the zamindary of the kings of Suśanga of Mymensingh district. The Suśanga royal family uses Sinha as their title, even though they are Barendra Brahmans. Since they are kings, they use the kśatriya title Sinha, just like the royal family of Dárbháuṋgá, who, although born as Maethilii Brahmans, used the kśatriya title. Mymensingh district hada special reputation for being a fairly large district during the Pathan and Moghul times, especially during the Moghulperiod.
chapterTitle: Mymensingh, Mahásthángaŕh, Medimimańd́al, Dhámrári, Vikrampur Mymensingh (Bangladesh)

t: In those days, since Sylhet (Shriihat́t́a), Mymensingh, Birbhúm, Purnea and Jessore districts of Bengal were very large, they used to be under the rule of a governor (baŕá hákim). The remaining districts were each ruled by a magistrate (hákim).
chapterTitle: Mymensingh, Mahásthángaŕh, Medimimańd́al, Dhámrári, Vikrampur Mymensingh (Bangladesh)
