t: The size of Mymensingh district was reduced when the Garo Hills were excluded from its territory. In 1912 when Vauṋgabhauṋga [partition of Bengal] was radd [modified] Mymensingh was included in the province of Bangla. The Garo Hills became part of the newly constituted Assam province with its district headquarters at Tura. Had the Garo Hills been within Mymensingh district, the Házangs and the Garos would have revived the embers of a renewed vitality, which they had already initiated. Upon separation from Mymensingh, they were deprived of this opportunity. Even today the Bengali dialect, which the original residents of the Garo Hills – the Garos, Házongs and Koches – generally use among themselves, is the dialect of Mymensingh. The sweet cultural link that evolved between Mymensingh and Garo Hills, even after change in the political situation, is inseparably tied, even today, in an eternal bond of gold. ( 1 )
chapterTitle: Mymensingh, Mahásthángaŕh, Medimimańd́al, Dhámrári, Vikrampur Mymensingh (Bangladesh)

t: Maháśt́hángaŕh – the capital of old Paiṋca Gaod́
chapterTitle: Mymensingh, Mahásthángaŕh, Medimimańd́al, Dhámrári, Vikrampur Mymensingh (Bangladesh)

t: In old Sanskrit, any large geographical territory was called dviipa [island]. An island is not necessarily surrounded by water. Jambudvipa, Shakadvipa, Subarńadvipa – none of these is surrounded by water. We can certainly call these kinds of special islands continents. If any island has water on its three sides, it is called upadviipa (peninsula). The southern part of India or Deccan is a peninsula. That part of a peninsula which tapers sharply downwards into the water is called antariipa, in English “cape”.
chapterTitle: Mymensingh, Mahásthángaŕh, Medimimańd́al, Dhámrári, Vikrampur Mymensingh (Bangladesh)

t: Actually, if any island develops several peninsulas, then these peninsulas are called separately anudviipa or sub-continents. India, Pakistan, Nepal, Bhutan, Burma, Sri Lanka and a few other countries constitute an island. This island is called Asia. Its old Sanskrit name is Ásiká – Ásiká > Ásiá > Asia. India, Pakistan, Burma and Sri Lanka, when conjoined, form a sub-continent or anudviipa. A region with special geographical features could be part of a sub-continent or may not be – that is, from a geographical standpoint.
chapterTitle: Mymensingh, Mahásthángaŕh, Medimimańd́al, Dhámrári, Vikrampur Mymensingh (Bangladesh)

t: If surrounded by various mountains and rivers, it is called Maháśt́hán or Mahábhúmi in old Sanskrit. The valley of the Mekong River in Southeast Asia and the Bauṋgálistán region of India and Bangladesh are examples of such a Maháśt́hán. To the north of Bauṋgálistán are the impenetrable Himalayas, and to the south is the Bay of Bengal, in the west the Ramgarh Hills, which are part of the Vindhya Mountain range, in the east lies the Arakan-Iyomá [mountain range], and in the center is the land of alluvial soil carried by the ever-flowing Gauṋgá, Brahmaputra and the rivers of Ráŕh, including the Damodar River, surrounded by its tributaries. Possibly for these reasons, during the Vedic age, Báuṋglá was called both Vauṋga and Maháśt́hán. In the Buddhist age, Paiṋca Gaoŕ was clearly identified as Ráŕh, Samatat́, Vauṋga, Barendra and Mithila. They were more clearly defined by Maháśt́hángaŕh, the name of the capital of Paiṋca Gaoŕ in that period. The ruins of that capital can still be found along the sandy shores of the Karatoyá River in Bogurá district. ( 2 )
chapterTitle: Mymensingh, Mahásthángaŕh, Medimimańd́al, Dhámrári, Vikrampur Mymensingh (Bangladesh)

t: Medinimańd́al, Dhámrái, Maynámati, Vikrampur (Bangladesh)
chapterTitle: Mymensingh, Mahásthángaŕh, Medimimańd́al, Dhámrári, Vikrampur Mymensingh (Bangladesh)

t: Medinimańd́al is a well known village in Dhaka district. During the Buddhist period, this village was a famous holy center for the Buddhist Maháyánii Tantrika cult. The Tantrika practices of the Saḿgháráms of the land were controlled from this village. The Vajrayána Buddhist cult was controlled from Vajrayoginii village and Buddhist Tantra was controlled from Medinimańd́al. These two sacred centers of Buddhism were situated in Dacca district.
chapterTitle: Mymensingh, Mahásthángaŕh, Medimimańd́al, Dhámrári, Vikrampur Mymensingh (Bangladesh)

t: In this context, it is good to remember that Matsyendranath returned from Nepal by ratha [chariot]. That was the first chariot of Bengal or of eastern India. In commemoration of that chariot, the residents of Dharmarájiká Vihára, a vast center of Mantrayán Buddhism of Bengal, introduced the rathajátrá festival. In Nepal a wooden chariot (sojá ratha) was built for the onward journey of Matsyendranath, and an iron chariot (ult́o ratha) was built for his return journey. In those days, Dharmarájiká Vihára was renowned in for craftsmanship. The people there, utilizing all their expert craftsmanship, constructed a bamboo chariot for Matsyendranath, and then eagerly waited for the return of their dear prince by road. That chariot of Dharmarájiká is the oldest ratha of Bengal or eastern India. The current name of Dharmarájiká is Dhámrái (Dharmarájiká > Dharmarájiá > Dhámrái). There are very few people who have not heard of the rathajátrá festival of Dhámrái in Dhaka district.
chapterTitle: Mymensingh, Mahásthángaŕh, Medimimańd́al, Dhámrári, Vikrampur Mymensingh (Bangladesh)

t: Matsyendranath ( 3 ) was the prince of Bengal. His capital in the beginning was Rampal and towards the end it was Maynámati. Maynámati was part of Tripura district during British rule and not far from Comilla. Maynámati was one of the centers of Buddhist yogic practices (baoddha yogácára). Though it was included in the former Tripura district, its distance to the border of Dhaka district was not much. Dhaka district, the Comilla sub-division and the Brahmanberia sub-division of British Tripura district, along with its contiguous areas of the Habiganj sub-division of Sylhet, were once the centre of Buddhist practices. With Buddhism as its focal point, a highly learned society evolved in this area over the last 1500 to 2000 years. This society controlled Bengalʼs cultural life for several hundred years. The sense of civility and courtesy of Dhaka and Tripura, their knowledge and wisdom, culinary arts and social norms, have long inspired Báuṋgálistán. And this was not all! The widely acknowledged center of Sanskrit studies in Bengal, Vikrampur was also situated in this area. Dharmapál Dipauṋkar [981 A.D.], the chancellor of Nalanda University and head of the institution of Tibetan Buddhism, who was known in Tibet as Sriijiṋána Atiish, was also the affectionate scion of Vikrampur. Today that Vikrampur may be gone, but a genuine search might lead to the recovery of its ruins, its skeletal remains. ( 4 )
chapterTitle: Mymensingh, Mahásthángaŕh, Medimimańd́al, Dhámrári, Vikrampur Mymensingh (Bangladesh)

t: Footnotes
chapterTitle: Mymensingh, Mahásthángaŕh, Medimimańd́al, Dhámrári, Vikrampur Mymensingh (Bangladesh)

t: The meaning of the word kerala is a place bound by coconuts. Nowhere in India do coconuts grow so plentifully as in Kerala. Three Sanskrit names for coconuts are prevalent. (1) nárikel (antastha la, that is, lra), (2) náliker (this is also antastha lra) and (3) ker. With the addition of la to the word ker has come the word kerala (this end la is not antastha lra, that is, la). The word la is derived as lá (root verb) + d́a (suffix), meaning one that holds or one that is held. Something that holds ker, that is, coconut, is Kerala. The name of the country that King Mithi conquered is called Mithil. By adding the suffix áp in the feminine gender it has become Mithilá. The expression of the five fundamental factors is called ku in Sanskrit. Thus, ku is one of several names for the earth. In describing various epithets of the earth, it is said:
Bhú – bhúmi – dhará – dharitri – sarvaḿsahá – basumati, Gotra – ku – prthvii – prthvii – kśamábanii – medinii – mahii.
To this ku, in the sense of one holding the quinquele-mental expressions, the addition of la, meaning something that holds, produces the word kula, which means family lineage.

Yes, I was speaking of Kerala. The land of Kerala, decorated with multitudes of coconut groves, is in a sense a heaven on earth. In the south lie the Western Ghat Mountains adjoined by Malabar Bay, and beside it the sea – this is the geographical identity of Kerala. Along with the beauty of nature is an abundance of natural resources and in its people, the highest talent and erudition. The most educated state of India, its northern part was within the former Madras Presidency. In this northern part are Kannanur, Kojikode, Palaghat and Mallapuram districts. In the central region is the former Cochin state, and in the south is the former Travancore state. The word Cochin has come from the very old Dravidian word koccaes, which later was transformed into kocce > kocce, which means small, brilliantly white. The Dravidian expression koccaes has become the Bengali word kaci. The impact of Dravidian language on Bengali is undeniable. The words kacaourii and kacurii [a flat bread fried in ghee] have come from the word koccepuri.

It is in the sense of a small beautiful island that this land was named Cochin. Cochin state was once the central jewel of the land of Kerala. Its capital city, Ernakulam, was at one time under water. The name itself indicates it. Travancore state in the extreme south was once still more extended. The capital city is Tiru-Anandapuram (which is incorrectly pronounced Trivandrum in English). Tiru in Dravidian language is synonymous with the Sanskrit word shrii. That is, Tiruanandapuram means Shriiánandapuram [charming and blissful place]. Similarly one of the holiest of South Indian places of pilgrimage is Tirupati, which would be translated as Shriipati [Lord of charm] in Sanskrit. Apart from Tiruchinapally, there are many places in South India, starting with the word ‘Tiru’, which, as I have explained, means Shrii.

The people of Kerala state are called Malayalis, and their language is called Malayalam. Among South Indian languages, Malayalam has the highest percentage of Sanskrit words. The Nayar community of Kerala (Keralean Kayasthas) are the pride, not only of Kerala, but of entire India. They have no match in education and learning. The predecessors of these Nayars came from Bengal.

This dates back to the distant past, most probably in 534 B.C. The prince of Ráŕh, Vijay Siḿha, came to Sinhala [Ceylon] by sea along with about seven hundred followers. Then the capital of Ráŕh was Siḿhapur (presently Singur of Hooghly district). The port was in an area close to Siḿhapur, and later the port came to be known as Siḿhalpát́an (which is close to Singur). Vijay Siḿha conquered Lanka and, along with his followers, permanently settled there. They are the ancestors of the present-day Sinhalese people. These Sinhalese are very similar to Bengalis in their ways and manners, their customs and behaviour. Their facial appearance bears a close resemblance to that of Bengalis. Until they speak it is difficult to differentiate a Bengali from a Sinhalese. The Sinhalese language is similar to the Bengali language of the Indo-Aryan group, even in its script. Though most Sinhalese are today Hinayánii Buddhists, their traditional styles and practices remain very close to those of Bengal. The Sinhalese have such titles as Senánáyaka, Jayavardhana, Guńatilaka, Bháńd́arnáyaka (many people incorrectly say Bandarnayaka. Bhańd́arnáyaka means one who is in charge of the military depot or who is the storekeeper), Deshanáyaka, etc.

Vijay Siḿha had no children, hence he brought one of his nephews, Pandu Basudeva from Ráŕh and made him heir to the throne. In later times these settlers in Ceylon migrated and occupied the southern part of Malabar Bay (which today we call Kerala) and set up a settlement there. They are the predecessors of the present-day Nayars. In their behaviour and customs, bearing and conduct, and even in their facial shape, they are exactly like Bengalis. They have a very sharp intellect.

Surrounded by hills and the sea, Kerala is somewhat different from its neighbouring states, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka. Whereas in the adjacent Tamil language the percentage of Sanskrit words is very low (in Vipra Tamil about 20% and in ordinary Tamil nearly 5%), in Tulu language the percentage of Sanskrit words is comparatively somewhat more than Tamil, but not much more. (In Vipra Tulu it is 50% and in ordinary Tulu 20%). In the Malayalam language the percentage of Sanskrit words is nearly 75%. This is probably due to its link with Bengal. In Sinhalese language, like Malayalam, the percentage of Sanskrit words is very high.

Separated by hills and the sea, the flora and fauna (plants and animals) of Kerala is different from that of adjacent states. Multiple varieties of flowers and fruits are available, and when forests thrived in abundance, many animal species could be found. Although the elephants of Kerala are a subspecies of the large Indian elephants, there is something distinctive about their appearance. A visit to Tekkari Wild Animal Sanctuary makes this readily apparent. All people in Kerala value the Sanskrit language. Even Christians have assiduously studied and are still pursuing the Sanskrit language. Many educated Muslims know Sanskrit quite well. This means that its use is not restricted to only upper-caste Hindu Brahmans and kayasthas. (Most Kerala Brahmans belong to the Namboodiri and Patti clans; however, adjacent to the districts of Tamil land are Tamil Brahmans who speak Malayalam outside the home but speak in mixed Tamil-Malayalam language inside the home. The Nayars are Kayasthas, I have mentioned it earlier) [Kerala] offers a unique example of natural tolerance among different religious faiths. Jews have lived there since very ancient times – according to some people, for the last twelve hundred years but according to others, even longer. Their mother tongue is Malayalam. They have translated their religious scriptures into Malayalam. Recently many of them have migrated to Israel, and many synagogues [in Kerala] are lying deserted.

Christians came [to Kerala] long ago. The history of Christianity in Kerala began in that distant past when the rest of India did not even hear of Christianity. The Christian religion in Kerala has a distinctly Kerala system of baptism. When Christian missionaries came to Bengal, they created the new Bengali term báptisma for baptism, but in Kerala, since ancient times, they have been using the word jiṋánasnánam.

It can be surmised that Islam first came to India by land, after the invasion of Sindh by Muhammad-Ibn-Kashim or, to be more accurate, after the death of Dahir. However, with regard to the Philippines (whose Sanskrit name is Mahárliká or Mahárliiná), Malaysia, Indonesia, Chittagong and Kerala, Islam came by a different route, by sea via the Arab merchants. At that time Chittagong was chiefly inhabited by Hinayánii Buddhists (also known as pacifists or Theravadins). Arab traders came by sea and preached the religion of Islam, and a large group of Hinayánii Buddhists in Chittagong accepted Islam as their religion. Even today, in their local customs and behaviour, in their spoken language, the affinity between Buddhists and Muslims is very close. In comparison to other Bengali dialects, the Chittagong dialect contains more Arabic words.

Before coming to Kerala, Arab traders had come over to Laccadives, Minicoy, Amindvip, Maldvip and other islands. From there they traveled primarily to the northern areas of Malabar district. The meaning of the word Malabar is water and hills, that is, where the sea and hills merge together. Muslim residents of Kerala, like other residents of the state, speak Malayalam, but compared to other residents, there are a few more Arabic words in their spoken language, just as there are in the Chittagong dialect. The Kerala Muslims are called ‘moplá’ in common parlance.

I was speaking of the cultural link between Kerala and Bengal. On auspicious occasions, people also ululate, uludhvani (in East Bengal it is called giving the cry of jokár ( 1 )). In Kerala some people call this sound mukhavádyam. As in Bengal, Kerala society was matriarchal. Today just as a balance has been struck between the matriarchal and patriarchal systems in Bengal, a similar phenomenon has happened and continues to happen in Kerala. If a marriage is arranged according to the Vedic system, only Brahmans observe it. Others follow one of many recognized systems. Usually among the Nayars, there are titles like Nayar, Panikkar, Menon, Kartta (in Bengal respectable men are also addressed as karttá), Pillai and Kaimal.

The staple food of Kerala is rice and fish. The housewives of Kerala are in the habit of preparing vegetables with coconut milk; however, unlike Bengal, they do not use mustard oil as the cooking medium. Since there are plenty coconut trees, they use coconut oil for cooking. The girls of Kerala have recently started wearing saris, although it is not their normal attire.

In some areas Malayalam is spoken even outside Kerala. Kerala is a small state. It would have been better if all the areas where Malayalam is spoken had been included in Kerala. The currents in the small and large rivers of the state are strong, which makes it possible to produce hydro-electricity at low cost. From the ebb tide and flow tide and from the sea waves, marine electricity can also be generated. Cheaply produced electricity would hasten the development of industries in Kerala. This would strengthen the economic base of the state. In this context I am drawing the attention of rational, progressive people. ( 2 )
Footnotes
Vihár/Bihar
Vi – hr + ghaiṋ = Vihára. Thus the word Vihára/Bihar is derived. Vi is a prefix here. The va of a prefix is never a vargiiya ba. Everywhere it is antahstha va, even it is not wa.
The English spelling of Bihar should start with V, that is, it should be Vihára. Yet, ninety nine percent people would write Behar. The English used to write it as Bihar. That is also incorrect.

In the Pathan era, there were three provinces (subá) in India – the Punjab, Hindustan and Bengal. Akbar broke up these provinces and created a few more provinces. He split Hindustan province into Agra and Oudh provinces (it should have been Avadh; but, in history, it is written in English as Oudh). And Bengal province was split up into Bihar and Orissa provinces. During Pathan regime Orissa was practically independent. But during Moghul era Orissa changed hands quite frequently. Sometimes it was in the hands of Moghuls, sometimes in the hands of Bhoṋsle Marathas, sometimes in the hands of local Hindu kings. In fact, after the Royal Kesari dynasty (in which there were great kings like Ananta Keshari, Jajáti Kesari) the history of Orissa fell into uncertainty. During the rule of Akbar [1556–1605] when the province of Behar was created, then its name was written with the Persian letter Be, it was written as Behar. Later the province of Behar lost its separate identity and was included into Bengal province.

When the then province of Bengal passed into the hands of the English after the battle of Plassey, then in imitation of the Persian word Behar, writing Bihar in English started. In 1912, when, during British rule, with the provinces of Behar and Orissa, the separate states of Behar and Orissa were created, in the beginning it was written as Behar and then later it got transformed into Bihar.

During the Buddhist age in Bihar, especially in Magadha, Buddhism had a firm foothold – there were a large number of Buddhist Vihára which were also called Brahmaviháras. I have said a little earlier that in the local pronunciation there was only ba. When during Shahjahanʼs rule [1628–1658], Urdu was made the state language of the Moghuls in place of Persian, then the Munsis (who worked as clerks in small courts) of Behar, alongside with Persian script, used to write Urdu in a somewhat transformed form of Nágarii script. Although in official works and in the upper levels of the big and small courts, Urdu written in Persian script was in practice, but at the ordinary level Urdu written in changed Nágarii script was more widely used. Even during British era when English came to replace Urdu as the official language in the law courts and at the state level, at the ordinary level that very Urdu in mutated Nágarii script was in use. Since most of these court clerks were Kayasthas by caste, this transformed Nágarii script came to be known as káyethi lipi [a script used mostly by Kayastha scribes]. During our boyhood days, in the court documents and police records that script was in use and it was meant to be learnt compulsorily by the officers. After independence, that script was removed and in its place, the Devanágarii script was installed. In the káyethi lipi there is only one va which should serve both as vargiiya ba and antahstha va. Hence, to write correctly, it must be written as “Vihár”.

I was speaking of the Behar province during Akbarʼs time. Its capital was Ajimabad. The town grew up after the name of the army chief, Azim-us-San. This Azimabad is nowadays called Patna City (recently the name of the railway station has been changed to Patna-Sahib, since it is a holy place of pilgrimage to the Shikhs because of it being the birth place of Guru Govinda Singh [1675–1708]). Later when the Behar province was reunited with Bengal provinces, then Bengal province had only one Nawab but had three different Subedárs [Governors] – one at Dacca, one at Murshidabad and one at Azimabad.

Most of you must be aware of the fact that the governor of Azimabad was Hazi Ahammad, who was a brother of Nawab Alivardi Khan [1725–1740]. During the Afghan rebellion in Patna (Azimabad), he was killed by the Afghan rebel soldiers. The daughter of Alibardi Khan, Amina Begum, was married to Muhammad Jainuddin, the son of this Hazi Ahammad. The elder son of Jainuddin was Mirza Muhammad and the younger son was Mirza Mehedi. Since Alibardi did not have a son, after his demise, his daughter, Amina Begumʼs son, Mirza Muhammad became the Nawab and he came to be known as Siraj-ud-daula [1756–1757]. ( 1 ) People say, Mirza Mehedi was killed by the English.

There were several districts of Behar during Akbarʼs time – (1) Champaran, (2) Saran, (3) Trihut, (4) Shahabad, (5) Behar, and (6) Munger. Later these districts were divided into several parts to create the present districts of Bihar. ( 2 )
Champaran (Bihar)

Campakárańya, described in the Rámáyańa, turned into Mágadhii Prákrta Campárań; in Occidental demi-Mágadhii it became Campáranya. Campakaranya constituted the present East Champaran (Matihari), West Champaran (Bettia) and the adjacent Madeshii [central region] areas of Nepal. (For a short period a Tehshil [sub-district] of Gorakhpur was within Campakaranya.) Important places like Lumbini, Kushinagar (Kashiya), Nandangarh, Lauria and even Kapilavastu were once part of Champaran. The historically famous Lumbini – the Lumbini script was used to write the history of India – also belonged to the western part of Champaran. The Bráhmii letters of the Lauriyá script, in which the history of Buddhist India was recorded, also had their origin near Bettia of Champaran.

The first man to decipher the Lauriá script was Mr. Princep, and consequently a famous ghat́ [river bank] in Kolkata was named after him. This young officer of the East India Company initiated a significant step in Indian history. I do not know when the name of this Kolkata ghat́ named after Mr. Princep will be changed. In my historical search, I went to Lauria. The locals revere this place as sacred. They call it Lor Bábá. It is Champaran which, by an inevitable decree of history, today is in fragments. The major rivers of Champaran, the Rápti (which flows alongside the city of Gorakhpur), Narayańii, Gańd́aka and Dhanavatii (Dhanauti) once kept the land green with plentiful corn, flowers and fruits. Champaka [magnolia] trees are seen in abundance in the area even today. Its natural beauty and forest resources are incomparable.

The spoken language of Champaran is Champaranii Bhojpurii, and in the western part it is Bastiá Bhojpurii [of Basti district in eastern U.P.] However, the language of Dhaka [a place in eastern Champaran] area, situated in the eastern part of the district, is Maethilii. Since it was under the rule of Nepal for a long time, in some parts of Champaran (especially in the Birganj area) there is a marked Nepalese influence. Most landlords belonged to the Ráńá family. People of Nepalʼs Tháru tribe live there in large numbers. The measure of a bighá ( 3 )in Champaran is the same as a Nepalese measure.
Sharan (Bihar)

During the Buddhist era, this area was known as Shákyárańya; it becomes Sharan in Mágadhii Prákrta. Even during British rule the district was known as Sharan district. Its headquarters was at Chapra. Presently the district is divided into three parts: Chapra, Gopalgaunj and Siwan. Except for the area near Shonepur, the language of the entire district is Bhojpurii. Only the language of Shonepur region is Bajjiká Maethilii. This district is very fertile and its people are educated, yet there is endless poverty. The famous village Hatthiigrám (Hathoá) of the Buddhist era is also situated in this district. Lord Buddha moved about on foot in almost every village in Sharan district.

In this context, it is good to remember that the villages where Buddha delivered his important discourses are known as Sońevarśá (that is, where gold rained) and those notable villages where he rested for more than one day are known as Dharhara (Dharáhará). In Bihar, in almost all districts, there are several villages called Sońevarśá and Dharhara.
Tirhut (Bihar)

Tirhut district comprises the present Samastipur, Darbhanga, Madhuvani, Sitamari, Muzaffarpur and Vaishali(Hazipur) districts and, in addition, some adjacent Madeshii (plain) regions. The language of the northeastern part of this district is Paiṋcakroshii Maethilii, and of its southwestern part, Baijiká Maethilii. Even during British rule, Tirhut was a large district. Its headquarters was Muzaffarpur (named after Muzaffar Shah). During the early part of British rule, extensive stretches of forest prevailed in this district. Where many tigers, niilgái [antelope] and even rhinoceros existed, today the forest has vanished, and the wild animals have [consequently] become extinct. In the Tirhut-Vaeshalii region of that period, Vardhaman Mahaviir, the son of a wealthy tradesman named Siddhártha, was born. His motherʼs name was Trishalá.

Later this district was bifurcated. The western part was named Muzaffarpur, out of which the present Sitamari, Muzaffarpur and Vaishali districts were created – and the eastern part was given the name Darbhanga. Its headquarters were set up at Laheriasarai near Darbhanga town. Presently the district has been split into Darbhanga, Madhuvani and Samastipur districts.
Shahabad (Bihar)

Sher Shah was the son of the soil of Shahabad district. In the town of Sasaram (the actual name is Sahasrarám, named after a prosperous gentleman, Sahasrarám Singh; the corrupted form in English is Sasaram) the grave of Sher Shah is located. After Sher Shah, the district was named Shershahabad. Thereafter it was renamed Shahabad. The headquarters of this district was initially at Sahasrám. Later, during British rule, it was shifted to Arrah.

At present, the district is split into two parts. The northern part is called Bhojpur, with its headquarters at Arrah, and the southern part is known as Rohtas, its headquarters being at Sahasrám [Sasaram]. It is said that King Harishchandraʼs son, Rohitáshva, was the king of this region. After his reign, the region came to be known as Rohtas, after his name.

The language of Bhojpur district is standard Bhojpurii, and in the western part it is Kashiiká Bhojpurii (Bhojpurii which is spoken in Kashii district). Gauṋga, Sone and Karmanáshá are the well-known rivers of the district. The water of the Bhabua sub-division in Rohtas district is the best in Bihar. In the Buxar sub-division, various historical relics exist from the medieval period in India. Many places described in the Rámáyańa are also situated in this sub-division. People of this district are industrious and guided by basic intelligence.
Patna, Gaya, Aurangabad (Bihar)

The headquarters of Behar district was Gaya. However, since this was a very important district during British rule, a second headquarters was set up at Biharsharif. In later years the district was bifurcated; the southern part was called Gaya district and the northern part was called Patna district. In the beginning, the district headquarters was Azimabad (Patna City). Later, in 1912, when Orissa and Behar provinces were created, Bankipore was made its capital. Since Azimabad was a very crowded city, it was not possible to make it the capital.

Towards the end of the Moghul era, the chief of the treasury of Suba Bangal [Bengal province] was an up-country gentleman named Bankey Behari Lal. A little towards the west of Azimabad, he established a new town. It was named Bankipur, after himself. In the beginning, even the railway station was called Bankipur. The code of this station was BKP. Later, when the Patna-Gaya railway lines were laid, the name was changed to Patna Junction; but the code of the station remained the same – BKP. Perhaps it is still the same today [very recently it is changed to PNBE].
Slowly and slowly, the name Bankipur vanished into the cavern of time. We now call Bankipur as Patna. The name Bankipur became lost. The city is now called Patna, which is the capital of Bihar.

Behar, which was a very large district during the Mogul period, was split into five different districts – Patna, Nalanda, Navada (Nawada), Gaya and Aurangabad. The sub-divisional town of Zehanabad in Gaya district belongs to the Pathan era; hence, the town is quite old. In those days, Bengal province had two sub-divisional towns, one in Gaya district and the other in Hooghly district. It led to some difficulties in the discharge of official work. Since there was confusion between the Kanthi of Midnapur and the Kandi of Murshidabad [two very similar sounding names], the British used the name Contai for Káṋthi, and for the same reason contemplated changing the name of Zehanabad. As Zehanabad of Gaya district is an old and large town, they thought it wiser to change the name of Zehanabad in Hooghly district. Thus, in accordance with the name of the adjoining administrative division, the town Zehanabad of Hooghly district was renamed Arambag. Today the people of Arambag have forgotten that the original name of their town was Zehanabad.

Behar district was once the cynosure of all eyes during the Buddhist era. When Bakhtiar Khilji conquered Bengal, a number of Buddhist Vihára subsequently came under his control. In the course of his conquests, the first places to come into his grasp were Fullahárivihára (its present name is Fulwarisharif), Ádi-vihára (Bhakhtiarpur), Harinitvihára (Harnot) and Mahávihára (Biharsharif). Idols of the Buddhist era, stone inscriptions, and other such archeological relics lie scattered in the fields and villages of this old Behar district.

In quest of the history of Magadha, I have journeyed to different villages of this area. In the then district of Behar, two small rivers, Nairanjana and Mohania, racing in from the south, met together near Gaya. Their combined name has come to be ‘Falgu.’ On the very bank of this Nairanjana River, Buddha attained baoddhatva [spiritual realization]. He took initiation from a sage named Sanjay in a village called Páháriyá near Nawada in Behar district and learnt from him the lessons of Sáḿkhya yoga. The names of the two inquisitive youths of this district to whom he first imparted spiritual lessons were Sáriputta and Mahamaouggalan Arhan. Rajgiri or Girivraja, which was the first capital of the vast Magadha kingdom, also belonged to this Behar district. Later the capital was shifted to Pataliputra. Pataliputra is in Behar district. On the outskirts of Rajgiri, the great battle took place between Bhima and Jarasandha, the king of Magadha.

It was in Magadha that the famous poet Válmikii was born. Here also the scientist Áryabhatta [A.D. 476] took birth. The great sage Chavan was the son of the soil of Bihar. He was a renowned expert in Ayurveda, and invented chavanprásh, a famous ayurvedic medicine for cough and other bronchial troubles. This medicine is still in use today. The names of Mańd́ana Mishra (Máhiśyatipuri > Máheśii), the great philosopher of Mithila and great interpreter of Nyáya philosophy, and also Maharśii Gautama (Kámtaol), are known to all educated Indians.

With each and every atom and molecule of Bihar is associated the valour, the architecture, refined taste, scholarship and perfumed pollens of history. Páchet́i or Manbhum (Purulia and Dhanbad), Palamou, Chutia Nagpur (Hazaribag, Giridih and Ranchi), Palikot, Bishenpur, Singhabhum, Dhabalbhum (parts of Tatanagar, Jhargram and Bankura) and Porahat (Seraikella and Kharswan) of those days were ruled by the native kings. They used to present token offerings to the courts of the Pathans and Moghuls. Some of them did not even do this much; they only acknowledged their loyalty. Rajmahal and Sahebganj of the Dameen-i-Koh regions were in Murshidabad district. Pakur, Layá Dumka (Dumka) and Deoghar were in Birbhum district, and Jamtura was in the Samantabhum sub-division of Burdwan.

The vast district of Purnea, however, remained within Bengal province (subá Báuṋgál). The administrator of Purnea district was called the governor; that is, Burra Hakim [district judge]. In Birbhum, another large district of Bengal province, there was likewise a governor or district judge. Generally the district judge of Birbhum was called the ‘Rájá’ [king], and possibly for that reason the headquarters of Birbhum was called Rajnagar. Probably because Purnea district was full of natural resources, paddy and intellectual wealth, it was called Purńiká in Sanskrit. According to some, Purnea was very ancient, hence in Sanskrit it was called Puráńiká. I have heard elderly people there pronounce the name of the district as Puráńiá. It is more logical that the name Purnea has come from the word Puráńiká.

During the early part of British rule, the governor of Purnea was Shaukat Jung or Shaukat Ali [1756]. This part of Indian history is not at all ancient; however, its details are murky and somewhat clouded. Most likely certain opportunists, to serve their own interests, have deliberately distorted that history. Yet, as far as can be ascertained, the wife of Shaukat Jung/Shaukat Ali was Maimuna Begum, the Khala Amma (maternal aunt) of Siraj-ud-daula. According to some people, Shaukat Jung/Shaukat Ali was the maternal uncle of the only married wife of Siraj Bubbujan (not the mother of Ummat Jahura). But many people do not support this view. Many believe that Maimuna Begum was in fact the maternal aunt of Siraj, but was not the daughter of Nawab Alibardi. She was the daughter of Begum Sharfunnisa through her first marriage. According to others, however, Begum Sharfunnisa married only once; hence, the question of her first or second marriage does not arise. Regarding Begum Sharfunnisa it is said that Alibardi Khan, when doing each and every noble deed, used to consult her. However, he carried out all his dishonest deeds (many thought Nawab Alibardi was highly reputed in this regard) without her knowledge. Be that as it may, Mirza Muhammad (who later became Siraj-Ud-Daula) was made the heir to the throne in consultation with Begum Sharfunissa. After Siraj became the Nawab, his maternal aunt became filled with vengeance. She wanted her own son to become the Nawab. At her instigation, Shaukat Jung (Shaukat Ali) advanced with an army towards Murshidabad to teach Siraj a lesson. Coming to the southern part of Purnea, the two armies were almost face to face. The water of Purnea did not suit the soldiers of Shaukat Jung. In search of water for them, he dug a huge diirghiká [tank.] Then a fierce battle began between the two armies. In this battle, Shaukat Ali was badly defeated. The local people gave this site the name Diighikát́ihára, meaning, the defeat that was due to the digging of the tank.

Later, when the British set up the B.N.W.R. (Bengal and North Western Railway) railway lines, they gave the railway station the name Katihar. This railway line extended from Katihar to Kanpur, and its headquarters was Gorakhpur. When later it was nationalized, it was called OTR (Oudh-Trihut Railway.) After independence it was renamed N.E.R.(North Eastern Railway). The railway headquarters is still at Gorakhpur. Initially, Katihar was a small village. During the British era, it was a police state of the Purnea subdivisional headquarters. For some years now Katihar has become a district. Now it is a rather large town. Nearby, the village called Diighi is still in existence.

In any case, I was telling you about Magadha. The word Magadha is derived from mag + dhá + d́a = magadha. Mag means anti-Vedic; that is, Magadha stands for a country which is against Vedic rituals. Time and again, Magadha revolted against Vedic ritualistic practices. That is why it was given this name. Between Magadha and Auṋgadesh there was Mokama t́ál [extensive stretches of fertile land near the Ganges.] This t́ál was one of the most important places for producing grams (cholá) not only in India but in the entire world.

In Mágadhii language, cholá is called boot́, which has come from the Sanskrit word bunt́ika. In Hindi, cholá is known as cańá, which comes from the Sanskrit word cańaka. The Bengali word cholá is a Persian word. In both Bengali and Urdu, the word cholá is used, but in Ráŕhii Bengali, the word boot́ is more widely used. In Barendrii Bengali and Sher Shahabadia Bengali as well as in Maethilii, cholá is called badám, and in Bhojpurii rahilá. This t́ál is located partly in Patna district, partly in Mungher district and partly in Navada district. Its old name is Ambabhúmi. This Ambabhúmi is famous in history for its fertile lands. In ancient times, regular battles took place between Angadesh, Magadh and Videha states to determine the borders of this territory. Many of you are perhaps aware of the fact that the Kayasthas of Ambabhúmi are known as ambaśt́ha.
Monghyr (Bihar)

From the Sanskrit word mudgagiri has come the word Muṋgir. The word Muṋgir was transformed into the present Mongher. Mongher is a very ancient town. Even during the time of Rashtrakutas, Mongher was famous. This Mungher town was also the last capital of Moghul Bengal. Mir Kashim was its Nawab. The fort of those days still stands in Mungher. There remains still today the Topkhana Bazar (the cannon manufacturing center), the maidan [large field] for army drills (the Kareya maidan), the Kashim Bazar and the Sujighat. Suja, the son of Shahjahan, went into this ghat́ [river bank used as a boat station] to Arakan via Bhagalpur by waterway to seek refuge with their king. The Sujagang of Bhagalpur was named after him. During the Pal regime, for just a few days, this town was the second capital of Bengal. The major capital was Gaoŕ. The Rashtrakutas [753–973 A.D.] repeatedly attacked Monghyr, probably during the time of Mahendra Pal. Unfolding extensively along the northeast of the Ganges, this district was one of the most important districts of Bihar. The language of northwestern Mongher was Maethilii, in the southwest it was Magahii, while in most parts of Mungher, it was Angika. There is no Maethilii-speaking area in the present, small district of Mungher. Those areas have gone partly to Begusarai and partly to Saharsa district. The British bifurcated this district and called the eastern part Bhagalpur, and the western part Mungher.

Bhagalpur is a very old town. In the pre-Buddhist era, it was called Bhárgavapur (Bhárgavapur > Bhággarpur > Bhagalpur.) During the Buddhist era, it was called Bhagadattapur. In later times, the northern part of Bhagalpur District became the subdistrict Saharsa. Later this Saharsa subdistrict became a full-fledged district. The word Saharsa has come from the word sahasradhárá. The Koshi River, after entering the tender soil of Bihar from Nepal, changed its course several times. That is why it was named sahasradhárá. Before the creation of Saharsa district, the town had a railway station, but no police station. It was jokingly said that the highest government official of Saharsa was the local police officer (daphádár). The old Mungher district has been split into Begusarai, Khagaria, Mungher, Bhagalpur, Saharsa and Madhepura districts. During the time of the Mahábhárata it was called Angadesh. Its king was Karna, and its capital was Champaknagar. (On the outskirts of Bhagalpur town is Champaknagar, within the Nathnagar police precinct).
In Tantra, in describing the boundaries of Angadesh, it has been said:
Vaedyanáthaḿ samárabhya bhuvaneshántagaḿ Shive.

That is, on its southern boundary was Baidyanath, and in the north was Bhubanesh temple (Morang district of Nepal). This was Angadesh. In Angadesh, Maharśi Kalhan used to meditate. The place was named Kalhangram (the present name is Kahalgaon) after him. Here also was located the very famous Vikramshiila Vihára [University] of the Buddhist era (near Antichak village of Kahalgram.) During the Pala era [A.D. 750–1155], at the time of Devapal, one of the two universities of Bengal was Someshvarpur Vihára (in Rajshahii district of Bangladesh) and the other was Vikramshiila. Of the two most ancient universities of India, one, Takśashiiá (Taxila), was in the ancient Gándhára land (Kandahar.) The then capital of Gándhára was Puruśapura, whose current name is Peshawar. The other university(Nalanda Vihára) belonged to Magadhabhúmi in Bihar District.

Among the languages of Bihar, Maethilii and Angika belong to the group of Purva-ardha-Mágadhii [eastern demi-Mágadhii] group of languages. And Bhojpurii, Magahii, Nágpurii belong to the group of Pascimii Ardha-Mágadhii group of languages. The languages of Bihar are not recognized as full-fledged languages even today. Advancement of Bihar in the field of education could have been accelerated had there been the opportunity to study using the mother tongue.

Bihar has plentiful natural resources. In addition there exists the immense wealth of human resources. However, there is endless poverty. The immediate need is to formulate a healthy economic plan for this region and begin its immediate implementation. Bihar, the golden crown of history, must not be pushed into the depths of darkness. ( 4 )

B[V]ihára means to play with joy. If you merrily run for two miles, it could be described as vihára. However if you are browbeaten, with bloodshot eyes, moving even a short distance then it cannot be described as vihára. One whose mind always moves in Parama Brahma is Brahmabihárii. One whose mind is always ensconced in the beauty of Krśńaʼs play, is Krśńabihárii – Brajabihárii. One of my devotees was a great devotee of Tagore. He named his son Rabindrabihárii. Thus Buddha called the Buddhist Saḿgháráms BrahmaVihára. After his demise, his devotees changed the name Brahmavihára to Buddhavihára. That part of India where the largest number of these BuddhaVihára existed was later named Bihárbhúmi by the Buddhists.

When Emperor Akbar split his empire into fifteen provinces, he turned Bihárbhúmi into a new province and called it Behar Suba [Bihar province.] In reality the word Behár is incorrect; it should be Vihára. Its capital at that time was Azimabad (named after commander-in-chief Azim-Ush-Shan), now Patna city. Recently the name of the railway station has been changed to Patna Sahib. After Akbar, Behar province was again included in Bengal province. When in 1912 the British integrated Bihar province with Orissa and, separating it from Bengal, created a new province, it was given a new name, 'United Behar and Orissa.ʼ According to the Government of India Act (1935), when Orissa was made a separate province on the directive of the Oronell Commission, Behar was renamed Bihar. Even then a mistake remained. The ba of Bihar is antahstha va, not consonantal ba. It should be spelled as Vihára. ( 5 )
Footnotes
Manipur

The history of Manipur, the easternmost state of India, is decidedly old. Inhabitants of this region are Indo-Burmese stock. The land is rich in civilization, culture and heritage. Manipur is a beautiful plain surrounded by mountains on all four sides. In ancient times, a large lake existed in the centre of these mountains. Over the course of time, however, [the rains] carried stones, pebbles and alluvial soil down the mountains, until finally the lake was filled, resulting in the creation of an alluvial plain. The lake in miniature form is still present.

The state of Manipur is a very old one. Even in the Mahábhárata this state is mentioned. Some scholars believe that present-day Manipur is not the Manipur referred to in the Mahábhárata. Yet one hardly comes across any supportive arguments in favour of this belief. Unless we have grounds for doubt, we are compelled to accepts that Manipur belongs to the Mahábhárata [era.]

Up till the beginning of British rule, Manipur was a self-governing state. Imphal, its capital is also a very old city. After the downfall of Tikendrajit, the British brought the fertile ‘Kobe’ valley under its direct rule and returned the rest of the kingdom to the king. From that time onwards, Manipur became a native state of British India.

All of you know that once Burma (Brahmadesh) was considered to be a province of British India. The British incorporated the Kobe valley into Burma province. Even after the separation of Burma from India, the Kobe valley remained with Burma. After independence, Manipur – with the exception of the Kobe valley – became part of independent India. The people of Manipur have a special attraction for literature, art, dance and music. They are a peace-loving people and fond of entertainment. In ancient times, they were Theravadi Buddhists. Later, when Mahaprabhu Chaitanya Dev went there, he initiated them into Gaoŕiya Vaeśńava religion. On his way there, he preached Gaoŕiya Vaeśńavism in Tripura, and the local Tripura community likewise embraced Gaoŕiya Vaeśńavism. The Tipras gave up their Burmese names and adopted Sanskrit names. (The first Tipra leader was called Mu-Chang-fa.) From that time onwards, the king came to be called by the Sanskrit name “Máńikya Bahádur”.

After adopting the Gaoŕiya Vaeśńava religion, the life of Manipur witnessed further cultural changes. The residents of Manipur opened new horizons in dance, music and the fine arts. Through their dances, they articulated specific subtle expressions of devotional themes relating to Radha and Krśńa of the Gaoŕiya Vaeśńava religion. As many are aware, the Rása dance of Manipur is famous all over the world.

The Manipuri language belongs to the Indo-Burmese group of languages, which does not signify any particular language, but rather a group of languages, of which the two main languages are Bishenpuria and Mithei. The Bishenpuria language is used by the Manipuris [the Manipuri people] in Bengalʼs Sylhet and in the Chittagong hills of the Tripura-Cachar region and Mizoram. The spoken language of [the capital] Imphal is Mithei, and this language is used in official transactions. In both these Manipuri languages, there is an abundance of Sanskrit words, and both use the Bengali alphabet.

Since Manipuris are adherents of the Gaod́iiya [Gaoŕiiya] Vaeśńava religion, their holiest of sacred sites is Navadvip [birthplace of Chaitanya.] They revere the Chaetanya Caritámrta as their holy scripture – a scripture written by Krishnadas Kaviraj, who resided in Jhamatpur village, Ketugram Police station in the Katwa subdivision of Burdwan district of Raoh.

There is no caste division amongst Manipuris. They are all considered as belonging to the same caste, that is, Kśatriyas. Those regarded as belonging to a different caste are all settlers from outside [Manipur.] The same practice exists among the Sindhis. There is no caste division among the people of Sindh. All are known as Sindhis. The Brahmans of Sindh all came from the Marwar region of Rajasthan. In the only Marwari-speaking district of Thar in Sindh province, they were comparatively in the majority.
The weaving industry of Manipur is world-renowned. The women of Manipur have complete freedom in their social life, and they also play a leading role in the work place. ( 1 )
Aruńácal/Arunachal

This name is a new one. During the rule of the Ahom kings, this area was known mostly as Baliapara. When the British conquered Assam, the district of Assam was known as Baliapara Border District. Yes, scholars do differ regarding the name “Assam.” In ancient times, this region was known as Prágjyotiśpur. In later times, with regard to spiritual thought and Tantra, it became known as Kamrup. The name Kamrup was in use only during the Buddhist era and during the era of the post-Buddhist Nátha religion. In a twelve-hundred year old Bengali poem, it is said:
Divasai bahuŕii kágai d́are bháy,
Ráti bhaele kámru jáy.

The Sankrit letters ka, ta, pa, d́a are transformed into a in Prákrta. Hence Kamrup became, “Kamrua,” “Kamru.” The superficial meaning of the poem is: “Our wife fears even the cry of the crow during the day. However, the same wife goes to distant Kamrup at night to practice Tantra.” In a later period, the storm between Shákta Tantra and Vaeśńava Tantra swept Kamrup. Just as this storm brought catastrophe to the social life of Kamrup, it also ushered an intellectual awakening through cultural conflict. In this context it could be correctly stated that nothing in this world is unmixed. If we look at the positive aspect of this Shákta-Vaeśńava tussle, leaving aside the pernicious aspect, it in fact resulted in the birth of a new civilization in the Brahmaputra valley, which, though it bore the impact of the past, also gave a new direction to the future. From that conflict emerged the present day cultural life of Kamrup. There was a pernicious side to this feud. On the one hand, Kamrup had to face disastrous consequences due to the Moghul invasion; on the other hand, it had to finally concede defeat when attacked by the Ahoms coming from Burma.

Towards the end of this conflict, the Ahoms became the rulers of Assam. However, while many people say that from the name of the Ahoms came the subsequent name ‘Assom’ or 'Ahomʼ of Kamrup, this is not correct. This beautiful land of nature, formed due to a blending of rivers, plains and hills, came to be known as A-sama [A in Sanskrit stands for ‘not’ and sama means 'evenʼ] due to the rugged geography of its soil. It took the corrupted form of ‘Ássám’ in English. Following that distorted English pronunciation ‘Ássám,’ it is now called Ássám in Bengali. It should preferably be called ‘Asama.’ The Assamese language is the eastern borderland language belonging to the eastern Mágadhii group of languages. The style of its pronunciation is chiefly that of the Yajurveda. However, due to being under prolonged rule of the Ahom kings, and also due to the impact of Burmese pronunciation on the Ahoms, north Burmese pronunciation has certainly influenced the Assamese language.

Yes, we were discussing Balipara District. Eventually, by separating Balipara from Assam, a separate province called North Eastern Frontier Agency (abbreviated as NEFA) was formed under the direct rule of the Governor General of India. As a result, its public life was cruelly separated from the mainstream of Assamese life. Thus, even today, [the people of Balipara] know Assamese as their natural second language. From cultural, economic and many other considerations, the relationship of this district (NEFA) with Assam is inseparable. In independent India, the name NEFA was changed to Arunachal. This name of this state [Aruńácal] should be spelled with cerebral ńa. ( 2 )
Haryana

Its Vedic name is Haritadhánya. In Vedic language, dhánya means green vegetation. When the Vedic Aryans came [to Haryana] after entering India, they were drawn to its green beauty and named it Haritadhánya. The Sanskrit letters ka, ta, pa, d́a become a in Prákrta, dha becomes ha (for example, dadhi > dahi > dai – to write dae is incorrect; it is not bao which should be bau; similarly it is not maomáchi – the correct spelling should be maumáchi.) Thus, haritadhánya became hariahánan, and in Demi-Prákrta this became hariháná. In modern language this was transformed into Haryana. Similarly, lodhradhánya has become Ludhiana. In the spelling of dhánya there is the dental na. From that standpoint, it is proper to use the dental na in spelling Haryana and Ludhiana. However, here the vowel e follows the letter ra, after that there is ya, and beside it is a – these are all abádhak varńa [free letters unrestricted by the change of dental na into cerebral ńa.] According to this logic, it would be more reasonable to write it with cerebral ńa, that is haryańá. The local language of Haryana is Ját́t́u or Haryanvi.

The combination of Haryanvi language, prevalent in the region of Delhi, with Persian and Turkish words gave birth to the Urdu language (Urddu) in the army cantonments. That very language which the men in uniform, that is, in varddii (wrongly pronounced urddi in Bengali) used to speak was called Urdu. Putting aside the history of the Urdu language, we incorrectly treat Urdu as a foreign language. Urdu is very much an Indian language spoken in the Delhi area. Its source is the Haryanvi language. Recently, teaching and studying in educational institutions are conducted to some extent in the Haryanvi language. Several films have also been produced in this language.

The very old town of Haryana is “Merát́,” which in English and Bengali is wrongly pronounced ‘Meerut.’ The word Merát́ has come from the Sanskrit Mayráśt́ra. Mayráśt́ra → Mayrát́t́ha → Mayrát́ → Merát́. It was named after a certain non-Aryan king named Maydánava (dánava [demon] is not a creature of bizarre appearance. Aryans used to call a class of non-Aryans of India as dánavas). This Maydánava belongs to the era of the Mahábhárata. The present Harayana is fast advancing in the fields of education, culture and technology. It is a developed state of present-day India. Let various parts of India learn a valuable lesson from the present Haryana. Let me reiterate that the progress of Haryana is worth emulating. ( 3 )
Utkal – Orissa

The word ut means to move upward; kul means sprout. The mass of sand and silt carried by multiple rivers into the ocean that has risen like a sprout (kal) from the seabed is utkala. The southern plains of Orissa are hence known as Utkal.

One must remember that the northern part of Orissa is a hilly region. Its ancient name is not Utkal – it is Koshal or south Koshala. In those days, the Kanyakubja area was known partly as Koshala and partly as Shrávastii. This area is now part of Uttar Pradesh. The entire region is situated to the north of the Ganges; hence, it was also called north Koshala. During the rule of King Bimbisar, the king of Magadha, Prasenjit, was the king of north Koshala. Amongst the queens of King Bimbisar [546 B.C.] was Koshalkumarii, sister of Prasenjit. Ajatshatru [489–516 B.C.], an adherent of the Arya doctrine (the doctrine that follows the Vedas and the Rśis), became king by slaying Bimbisar, a follower of Buddha. Bimbisarʼs brother-in-law, Prasenjit, became angry and attacked Magadha to avenge the murder; however, he failed to win the battle. It should be remembered that Ajatshatru was without doubt the son of Bimbisar, but he was not the nephew of Prasenjit, that is, the son of Koshalkumarii.

At an appreciable distance to the south of the Ganges was south Koshala or Mahákoshala. At one time the western part of south Koshala was divided into many small states. Each state had built up its own fortress or gaŕh. Thus, the western part of south Koshala later came to be known as Chattisgarh (a collection of thirty-six forts). Though there were a number of small and large states on the eastern side of south Koshala or Mahákoshala, this region was for a long time known simply as Koshala. It is situated in the northern region of Orissa. In those days the largest town of the Koshala region in Orissa was Sambalpur. Its spoken language is Koshalii, which is generally known as Sambalpurii Oriya [Oriya as spoken in the Sambalpur area]. This Koshala region of Orissa is considered a part of Áryávarta and the Utkal region as a part of the Deccan.
The fine arts of this area are highly developed; in that sense also, the word Utkal could be used.

The root verb od́ means to draw near, to caress, to embrace, to serve and care for. Od́ + rak = od́ra. The land that takes great care of its guests, drawing the far away people near, is called the land of Od́ra. The coastal area from the mouth of the River Mahánadi to the mouth of the River Subarnarekha is called Od́ra, and the area from the mouth of the river Mahánadi to the mouth of the river Godavari is known as Utkal. The entire coastal area from the mouth of the river Godavari to the mouth of the river Suvarnarekha is Kalinga – that is, the combined name of Utkal and Od́ra. Matters related to this land of Od́ra are called Od́ra, and the language is known as Odri/Aodri. From this Od́rii/Aod́rii has come the word Oriya. The mutated form of Od́rii/Aod́rii does not give rise to the word Uŕiyá – it gives rise to the word Oriya. Hence it is preferable that the word [Oriya] is used. ( 4 )

The suffix rak is used when a person does something habitually. For example, the meaning of the verb ud́ is to entertain, to love and care for, to embrace mutually, to urge on, saying, ‘please eat this’, 'please eat that.ʼ Thus, by combining ud́ + rak we obtain the word Od́ra. Od́ra means one who knows how to love, how to show affection. In ancient times, Orissa was famous for its hospitality. That is why the northern part of Orissa, meaning the left bank of the Mahánadi, was called the land of Od́ra. From this word Od́ra has come the words Orissa, Oriya, and so forth. Even today, you will observe that the people of Orissa are very much accustomed to cooking, entertaining and taking care of people. If someone asks anything of them, they will certainly give it, if at all possible. In those days, the people of Od́ra land used to cultivate dance and fine arts, chiefly to entertain people, to please their minds. Even today, the people of Od́ra retain certain artistic skills, though it has declined to some extent. If their crippled economic status is ameliorated, we can expect them to regain their former artistic skills. The word Utkal means where there is a rise in the faculty of arts or where there is an upsurge of human creative skill (ud́ + kal + ac). ( 5 )
