t: The geographical configuration, water resources and forest resources of Udayan are much like those of Nepal. The developmental plans for this area should preferably emulate those of Switzerland. The same also holds true for Nepal. Udayan is part of present Uttar Pradesh [now a separate state of Uttarakhand.] While some people there belong to the Indo-Aryan community, other people, small in number, belong to the Indo-Tibetan community. There is excellent religious harmony amongst the inhabitants. The people of Udayan are now rapidly progressing in the spheres of education and culture. However if a drive for developmental activities is undertaken with proper planning, the speed of progress would be still greater. There are sixteen categories of Brahmans here. Of these, twelve are Bengali and four are Maharastrian Brahmins. Those belonging to the Bengali group migrated from West Bengal, especially from Burdwan district, during the Pathan and Moghul regimes, and particularly during the time of Aurangzeb. ( 1 )
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: Kinnar (Himachal Pradesh)
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: In very ancient times, Kinnar was an autonomous state. Later it turned into a native state [of British India.] Today it is a district of India. The people of [Kinnar] also belong to the Indo-Tibetan community. Their language belongs to the Tibetan family, with the alphabet being Indo-Aryan; that is a, á, ra, ka, kha – somewhat like the alphabet of Ladakh. The script is known as t́yáḿrá/t́egrá/t́egrii . In ancient India, the people of Kinnar were considered exquisitely beautiful. Hence if one happened to come across a strikingly handsome man, he used to be referred to as beautiful as the people of Kinnar. There is some Buddhist literature in the language of Kinnar. However, there is not much development with regard to modern [forms] of literature. ( 2 )
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: Kiḿ + nr + ac = kiḿnar/kinnar. In the etymological sense, it means, “Is he really a man?” In the colloquial sense, it indicates “a group of people living on the Indo-Tibetan border.” Since these people were very good-looking, questions would haunt peopleʼs minds, “Are they men or gods”? The word kiḿnar/kinnar has emerged in this fashion. At present, Kinnar is a district of Himachal Pradesh, a region where the Himalayas reach a towering height. Most of the mountains are snow-clad.
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: People of the region are simple by nature. In terms of religious practices, they were Maháyánii Buddhists (of the Lama sect). Today, one can discern in them the influence of the Puranic religion. Even some time back, the practice of polygamy was prevalent among the women: however, it is now practically a defunct practice ( 3 )
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: Though there is some impact of Mongoloid features on the appearance of the people there, they are quite good-looking. Hence they were called Kinnars and the region was called Kinnardesh. You all know that the ancient name of Tibet was Kimpuruśavarśa. One meaning of the word Varśa is “country”. For example, BhárataVarśa. The people of Tibet have scant hair. So, at times, there is difficulty in distinguishing the men from the women; the same difficulty is found to some extent in the case of the Bhutias. So, in ancient times people would wonder about the Tibetan men and ask themselves, “Are they males?” For this reason the country was venerably or fondly called Kimpuruśavarśa...
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: In any case, the word devayonii means an entity in whom certain divine qualities are manifested, that is, these are positive micŕovita. Suppose certain spiritual practitioners are good human beings, but have an innate attachment to worldly objects and are drawn to whatever they see; for example, money, jewelry, etc. Or, let us say we have a person who is a good sádhaka and is also is a good human being, but they beg Parama Puruśa for external beauty without desiring Him. They are meditating on Parama Puruśa, so they are human beings of a higher stature, but are seeking something ordinary from Parama Puruśa. After death, such persons will become devayonii [a being with ethereal, aerial, and luminous factors only] called kinnar. A kinnar is a devayoni, so it does not harm anyone. It does not have that disposition. People of ancient times used to seek the help of kinnars to become more beautiful. At one time, the pursuit of beauty or the art of cosmetics was called kinnar vidyá. “The person is extremely good-looking, like a kinnar”! In olden days, a beautiful dancing maiden was honoured with the epithet kinnarii. So you understand, this faculty is the positive microvitum related to the psychology of cosmetic art. Whatever theories exist regarding beauty enhancement, whatever skills exist for beautification, whatever art exists for aesthetic taste – all come under kinnar vidyá. ( 4 )
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: Traelauṋga (Andhra Pradesh)
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: By adding the suffixes ań and byáiṋ to the word triliuṋga the words traelauṋga and traelauṋgya respectively are derived. In a particular locality in the northern part of South India, three special phallic images of Shiva were honoured with reverence. For this reason, the locality was named Traelauṋga or Traelauṋga Bhúmi. The language of this area is Telugu. In the prevalent spoken language, this land is called Telengana. The original name of the place in the southern part of Chandanagar, known as Telenipáŕá, was Teleuṋgiipárá. Since in those days workers coming from Telengana settled there, it was called Teleuṋgiipárá. The present name of Teleuṋgiipárá is Telenipáŕá. ( 5 )
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: Vidarbha/Vaedarbhi/Vaedarbhii (Maharastra)
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: Vi-drbh + ghaiṋ gives us the word Vidarbha. Vidarbha + an gives vaedarbha. Vidarbha means that which cannot be conceived of or that which cannot be conquered. Vaedarbha means anything related to Vidarbha. Etymologically, Vidarbha indicates the eastern part of present-day Maharashtra; that is, the Nagpur-Akola region. In the prevailing language, Vidarbha is called Baráŕ (in English, Berar). In the Moghul era, Baráŕ belonged to the Nizam of Hyderabad state. (The pronunciation of the word Nizam in English is [Naizam], not Nizam. However, in Persian and Arabic, the word is Nizam. The full word is Nizam-ul-mulk.) Later, the British occupied it and, to please the regal Nizam, they offered to address the prince of Hyderabad as the Prince of Berar, just as the prince of England is venerably called the Prince of Wales. Finding his own son compared with the prince of England, the Nizam was highly pleased.
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: Baráŕii is one of the few living daughters of the Maharashtra Prákrit language. Like Marathi, Baráŕii has its own script, Moŕii. However, at present books in Marathi are printed in Devanagarii script. As a result, like people in other parts of Maharashtra, the people of Berar are close to forgetting their own Moŕii alphabet.
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: The word Vidarbha has slightly more historical significance. Many of you might have heard the Puranic story of Nala and Damayanti. Nala was the king of this very Vidarbha. Even in the Vedic age, Vidarbha had some importance. The reason is that the name of Vaedarbhi/Vaedarbhii, the son of the soil of Vidarbha, is remembered along with those amongst the proponents of the Atharvaveda. These include the sages Atharva, Angira, Angiras and Satyavaha. As the great sage Atharva was the earliest of the sages of Atharvaveda, the word Atharva is used to indicate a very old person – “The man has become decrepit (Atharva)”. In this context, it must be mentioned that this Veda was named Atharvaveda after its chief proponent Atharva. For the sake of variation in reading, both the words Atharva and Atharvá can be used. ( 6 )
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: Koḿkań/Kouṋkań (Maharastra)
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: The meaning of the root ku is “to create sound”, “to create high sound”, “ʼto cry loudly”. By adding the suffix ghaiṋ to the root ku, we obtain the word ko, which means “intense sound”. From kań + kac we derive the word kań, meaning “soft and sweet sound”. Kṋo + kań + ac = kouṋkań. In the etymological sense, it means a place where both sweet and strong sounds can be heard. Colloquially it stands for the northern part of the western coast of India. In the Indian sub-continent, there are, in total, six coasts. The coast of Kuch runs from the Indus valley to the Saurashtra. From Saurashtra to Gomantapurii (Goa) is the coast of Koḿkań or the Kouṋkań beach, while the Malabar Coast extends from Gomantapurii to Kannyakumarii. From Kannyakumarii to the valley of Godavari is the Coramandal coast and the Kaliuṋga coast extends from the Godavari valley to the mouth of Suvarnarekha. From the mouth of the Suvarnarekha to the river Naaf is the coast of Bengal. In this land of Kouṋkań, there are the western Ghats or Sahyadri mountains. Alongside them, across a stretch of land, is the Arabian Sea. Mingled with the vigorous roaring of the sea are the gentle murmurings of extensive forestlands. It is from these twin sounds kṋo and kań that the land came to be named Kouṋkań.
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: The language of Kouṋkań is derived from Maharastra Prákrit. Earlier, this language was called the Marathi version of Kouṋkań. Now the language of Kouṋkań is regarded as an independent language, and is prevalent from the south of Mumbai to Gomantapurii. The Chitpávan Brahmans of Maharashtra are slightly different from the Gaoŕ Sárasvat Brahmans of Kouṋkań. The Sárasvat Brahmans of India live in two different regions. Those living in Kashmir, Jammu and Punjab are known as north Sárasvat Brahmans or Káshimir Sárasvat Brahmans. Dogri and Punjabi Brahmans belong primarily to this group. The Brahmans of Kouṋkań are known as Gaoŕ Sárasvats. They are called thus because their ancestors came by land from Gaoŕ and settled there. Like the people of Bengal, they are also non-vegetarians. Hence, they do not care much for the vegetarian Brahmans in the rest of India. The customs and manners, practices and bearing of the Gaoŕ Sárasvat Brahmans are found to closely resemble those of the people of Bengal. They also have titles such as ‘Pái’ and 'Senoy.ʼ ( 7 )
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: The coast which resounds with this sound is called the Kouṋkań coast. Please do not identify Kouṋkań with kauṋkań. Kauṋkań is a type of bangle. Since very ancient times, women in most countries of the world have used these bangles. The earliest Sanskrit derivative form of kauṋkań was kań kań. It transformed into kaḿkań and with further metamorphosis became káḿgań. In North India, the word káṋgan is also prevalent. Once the word khágan was used in Bengali. In twelve hundred year old Bengali, it is said:
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: Háther káḿgań má leo dápań,
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: Áppane appá bujhata nia man.
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: That is, to see the bangle you wear on your hand, do you require a mirror? So, to know what is the nature of your own mind, what is the need to ask someone else? You can yourself know your own mind through meditation. The meaning of the word kouṋkań is the Arabian Sea gale carried to the Sahyadris.
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: People love to identify various sounds with others that are familiar. On an earlier occasion, you will remember I had told you about the movement of a train. When the driver blows the whistle indicating the train is starting, and it just begins to move, you hear its sound, and perhaps [you] think it is saying – gelum go-o-o-o, gelum g-o-o-o, gelum g-o-o-o [Oh friend, I am leaving, Oh friend, I am leaving, Oh friend, I am leaving]. As the train accelerates somewhat, you seem to hear it making the sound – jácchi jábo, jácchi jábo, jácchi jábo [I am moving I must move, I am moving, I must move, I am moving I must move]. Then, as the train moves still more vigorously, you seem to hear the sound – jata debe tata nobo, jata debe tata nobo, jata debe tata nobo [I can take as much you can give, I can take as much as you can give, I can take as much you can give]. When the train accelerates still further, it appears to make the sound – káṋcá teṋtul páká teṋtul, káṋcá teṋtul páká teṋtul, káṋcá teṋtul páká teṋtul [“Raw tamarind, ripe tamarind, raw tamarind, ripe tamarind, raw tamarind ripe tamarind”]. Then as the train moves closer to the next station, it suddenly decelerates and you seem to hear the train saying – esse gechi, esse gechi, esse gechi [I am home, I am home, I am home].
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: Was the train really making all those sounds! No, not at all. You seemed to enjoy identifying those sounds with those the train was making. In any case, you must have now understood what the word kouṋkań means.
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: The spoken language of Kouṋkań is Kouṋkańii. This language is derived from the Maharastra Prákrta. Once it was considered a dialect of Marathi. Kouṋkańii has no alphabet of its own, and presently, in the area of Kouṋkań adjacent to Maharastra, it is written in Devanágariii letters. In Goa, it is written in Roman letters, and in Kouṋkańii-speaking areas of Karnataka, in Kannad́a script. To write a language in three different scripts is not convenient. From the days of the Portuguese, Kouṋkańii has come to be written in Roman script. Even its literary works have been composed in Roman script. However, only the people of Kouṋkań will decide in what script Kouṋkańii should be written – Kannad́a, Roman or Devanagáriii.
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: Prior to Post-Buddha period the Brahmans of Kouṋkań went there from Bengal by land.
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: Presently they are known as Gaoŕa Sárasvat and their surnames are Pai, Senoy, etc. Maharastra Brahmans are vegetarian whereas Kouṋkań Brahmans are used to eating fish. ( 8 )
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: Kányakubja – Kanauj (Uttar Pradesh)
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: When there are calcium deposits in the joints of bones that compose the spine, they become stiff. The pliability of a childʼs spine is not to be found in that of grown-ups. If one works continuously for a long time stooping low, the upper part of the waist bones becomes slightly dislocated from those of the lower part. This increases the stiffness of the waist. Then one cannot stand erect; one tends to stoop or bend. The stiff part of the waist is perceived as burdensome. In Bengali, we call this weight of the waist kubjabhár or kujbhár or kuj [hump]. Manthara, the maidservant, whom the second queen Kaekeyii of king Dasharath brought from her parentʼs house, had a hump, as narrated in the Rámáyańa. So in the Bengali Rámáyańa, she had another name, Kṋujii. The story goes that the Aryans, after crossing Saptasindhu (Punjab), Haritdhánya (Haryana) and Brahmávarta (Brahmarśidesh or Doab,) advanced further to the east, that is, almost to the central region of the present Uttar Pradesh. They were not very familiar with the area. Seeing the Aryan warriors, the local people went into hiding; hence the Aryans had little opportunity to ask anyone for the name of that region. Along the way they happened to spot a woman with a hump. Since she had a hump, she could not run away quickly. The Aryan soldiers sought her help. They asked her, “Oh mother, what is the name of this land of yours?” Failing to understand them, she kept silent. Since they came across a woman with a hump in this land, the country came to be known as Kányakubja.From this [incident] we have derived the name of the historically renowned land of Kányakubja or Kanauj. Now Kanauj is a Tehsil [revenue district]. The Brahmans of Kányakubja are descended from a branch of the Paiṋcagouŕii Brahman community of northern India.
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: If those who have to work for a long time by bending low from the waist regularly practice the Naokásana [boat posture], Pashchimottánásana [back-upwards posture] and Shalabhásana [locust posture], they will be least likely to develop a hump.
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: When a person has a bent waist, the raised part of the fallen waist is called kṋuj. In Bengali, the adjective of this word in masculine and neuter gender is kṋujo. We call the water pot, which somewhat looks like a hump, also kṋujo (the word suráhii is of foreign origin). The feminine gender of the word kṋujo is kṋujii. In chaste Bengali, it is kubja. The woman with a hump may be called kroŕii in standard Bengali or Sanskrit.
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: Next to Asansol of Ráŕh, there is a village inhabited by the Brahmans of Kányakubja. Its name is Kanyápur. This name too has come from Kányakubja. During the reign of King Gádhi, this was the capital of Kanauj. At that time the name of the town was Gadhipur. ( 9 )
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: Footnotes
chapterTitle: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.

t: Angadesh/Angabhúmi (Bihar)

During the time of the Mahábhárata, when Angadesh was first accepted as an independent kingdom, Duryodhana made Karna the king of Angadesh and rather than consider him a vassal, he allowed him to wear the crown of a sovereign king. Since ancient times the Anga region was not considered part of northern India. Neither Anga, Vauṋga, nor Kaliuṋga were considered part of northern India. Starting from this time, Anga was declared an appendix or Auṋga of northern India and hence its name became Angadesh. Vauṋga remained outside of northern India. Kalinga gained acceptance as a part of southern India. Thus, even today, Oriya Brahmans are sometimes known as Dakśińátya Vedic Brahmans in Bengal. At the time of Karna the capital of Angadesh was Champakanagar. ( 1 ) Karna also founded an auxiliary capital in Mudgagiri, on the western border of the kingdom of Anga. Hence Monghyr has a tradition as a capital. ( 2 )

When Gujaratʼs Rastrakuts [a royal dynasty] defeated eastern India then Angadesh came under their jurisdiction. The Khirkhiriya Hills that we are sitting on were the eastern boundary of the Rastrakut kingdom. Thus they established a capital in their border city of Mungagiri. So we see that Monghyr became a capital more than once. At that time the road system of Bengal, as well as India, was not at all developed. The long highway Shershah built that extended from Suvarnagram in Dhaka District to the city of At́t́ak in western Punjab via Teota (Mańikganj subdivision) and Howrah-Burdwan, and passing by Kolkata, did not afford much convenience to Murshidabad, Monghyr or Patna but Monghyrʼs water-route transport system was good. The waterway worked well all the way from Dhaka to Benares/Allahabad passing via Narayanganj, Teota, Rampur, Boyaliya (Rajsahii), Lalagola Ghat, Godagarii Ghat, Chapaghati, Rajmahal (at one time Rajmahal was the capital of Bengal), Bhagalpur, Monghyr, and Azimabad. Benares and Allahabad used to be helped out by the Shershah-built Badshahii road. Thus, since Monghyr was marked as an important centre of water transport, the capital could be established there without there being any communication problems as such.

Miirkashim accepted Vireshvijayʼs reasoning and moved the capital to Monghyr. On Vireshvijayʼs advice, the nawab set out preparing the capital in Monghyr with great speed and began constructing his armoury. A great fortress was built in Monghyr as well as a munitions factory, heavy-weapons arsenal, huge parade grounds (Karheya Maidan or Kora Maidan), and a new cultural centre, Kasimbazar. The East India Company recognized the danger. Seizing on various small pretexts they declared war against Miirkashim. They had economic power and were prepared for war – the nawab had nothing. He had just begun organizing. On the other side, the East India Company had concentrated their power at Fort William in Kolkata and in Alinagar (present-day Alipur, now a part of Kolkata).

The first battle was a trifling affair; it took place in Katwa and the nawab was defeated. The second battle took place in Gheriya and there also the nawab was defeated. The third took place in Udhuyá or in the Udhuyánálá. The East India Company advanced along the Ganges in the direction of Monghyr. A great battle took place in the Dakra canal. With his finger my visitor pointed out to me the Dakra canal which originated on the western border of the Khirkhiriya Hills and joined the Ganges a little to the west of Monghyr. In reality, the Dakra was not a canal but a river. In the East India Company records it is mistakenly called a canal. At the time of the monsoon deluge, the water of the Ganges goes upstream through the Dakra River and floods a wide area in Monghyr District.

[Now] something about the history of Angadeshʼs terrain. In Karnaʼs time the north of Angadesh bordered on the Himalayas. ( 3 ) The southern border was the source of the Chandan river, a little to the north of Deoghar. On the western border was Ramdiri and Shamhodira (Samidha), near Beguserai, and the eastern border was the Rajmahal Hills near Sahebganj where they approach the Ganges. The Rajmahal Hills range occupy a large area in eastern Angadesh. Their eastern branch stops abruptly near Sahebganj and the Ganges; its western branch ends near Monghyr by the side of the Ganges. The western branchʼs Sanskrit name is the Kśirakśiriká Hills. In Angika they are called Khirkhiriya Hills and in English the Kharagpur Hills. These Kharagpur Hills are a branch of the Rajmahal Hills.

Southern Angaʼs chief river is the Chandan which has two companions, the Baruya and the Chiir. In this Chandan-Baruya-Chiir river basin ( 4 ) one finds the Kalhan Hills (near Kahalgaon, named after Maharśi Kalhan), Ajagavii Hills (near Sulatanganj), Mandar Hills ( 5 ) (a little north of the railway station), and these Khirkhiriya Hills on the western border where one can find, scattered here and there, innumerable examples of the culture of ancient Angadesh. Like the Angika culture, the language also belongs to this place.

Those who think that the Khirkhiriya Hills are the western border of Angadesh, however, are mistaken. To the west of the Khirkhiriya Hills lies the Dakra river basin. This Dakra river basin is Angaʼs final western border. Beyond the Dakra river basin lies the Kiul river basin where one can find many examples of Magadha culture, that is, it belongs to the land of Magadha.

The Angika language has three chief dialects: Dharamapuriya, Champanagarii or Chekachekii, and Mangeriya. The Dharamapuriya dialect is spoken on the north bank of the Ganges. The Chekachekii dialect is spoken in far eastern region where the Rajmahal Hills approach the Ganges near Sahebganj, and in the western border area where the Khirkhiriya Hills stop near the Ganges. Miirzachauki, near Sahebganj, was at the border of the provinces of Bengal and Bihar during the time of Akbar. Miirzachauki was a busy checkpost. It occupied a narrow strip of land between the Ganges and the mountains and thus was an ideal spot for a checkpost. The Mongeriyá dialect is prevalent to the west of the Khirkhiriya Hills in the Dakra River basin.

Besides these, there are also two mixed sub-dialects of Angika: The first is the Shriipuriyá sub-dialect which is used in the region lying between Purnea and Kisanganj. Purneaʼs language is Angika, and Bengali is the language of Kisanganj. The Shriipuriyá language that is spoken in the interlying areas is a mixture of Angika and Rauṋapurii Bengali (Súryapurii). The second sub-dialect is the Northern Khat́t́á dialect which is used in the region between Katihar and Malda. The language of Katihar is Angika, and in Malda, Bengali. In certain places between the two one can find this Northern Khat́t́á sub-dialect. It is a mixture of Angika and Shershahabad Bengali. In Mungeriyá Angika one can find some influence of Magahii. Similarly, in the Magahii of the Kiul River basin there is some influence of Angika.

It is a very small cave,“ he continued. ”A few miles to the southwest of this hill is a cave with paintings from the Buddhist era, and to the east is Rśikuńd́a. Nowadays people have forgotten its history, so they say that it is the ashram of the Rśyashrnga Muni mentioned in the Rámáyańa. Actually there was Buddhist monastery here during the Buddhist era. On the western edge of these mountains you will find the grave of Jamal Minya. Jamal Minya came here from Rajnagar in Birbhum and was the first to propagate Islam in this area. This place was named Jamalpur after him.

Rajnagar is now a very small city but at one time it was the district headquarters. During the Mughal era, certain districts in the Province of Bengal were extremely large (Monghyr, Sylhet, Birbhum, Mymensingh, Purnea, etc.). In many districts the district administrator was called the Jilá Hákim but in Birbhum and Purnea he was called the Baŕá Hakim or governor. The governor of Birbhum used to live in Rajnagar. The last governor, Alinakhii Khan II, only ruled Birbhum for a short time, and Purneaʼs last governor, Shaokatjang, ( 6 ) after being defeated in the Katihar war by Siraj-ud-Daola, was removed from the post of Purneaʼs Baŕá Hákim.

In any case, this Jamal Minya came from Rajnagar. Later the area of Birbhum district was reduced and the district headquarters was shifted from Rajnagar to Suri. Various cultural artifacts are scattered throughout our Angadesh but who is there to point them out? Angadeshʼs condition is like that of an orphaned child. What to speak of Angadesh, a great part of India is in the same condition today. Where will the historical materials come from if we continue to neglect these cultural artifacts? Nearby, for example, near Kahalgaon (Áńt́ichak) was the Vikramshila university from the Buddhist age but how much research has been done on it? Yet, nowadays thousands of universities are springing up like mushrooms. ( 7 )

In the Lachmiipur jungle area by the eastern border of the Khirkhiriya (Kśiirkśiriká) Hills, there [are] many cave paintings from the Buddhist era. [There are] some artifacts that dated back to the beginning of humankindʼs history in old Angadesh. In these hills humankind depicted its existence through many different varieties of drawings. From these it can be understood just how far back Angadeshʼs history goes. If Karna is accepted as Angaʼs first king, then Angaʼs political history is over 3500 years old, but these cave paintings are signs of the first stage of prehistoric humansʼ ascension through the annals of history. They are approximately twelve thousand to fifteen thousand years old. No writings are found with them because at that time humankind had not yet invented script.

This Lachmiipur jungle was even bigger during Buddhaʼs time. At that time it extended south to Grdhrakút́a (Gidhaor). To the west and south of this jungle was Magadha and on the north-east border was Angadesh. ( 8 )

In olden days, that country that was situated at the far border of northern India was considered an outgrowth of northern India and so its name was Angadesh [the country of auṋga]. It was between Barendrabhúmi and Mithila which were on the north bank of the Ganges. South of the Ganges was Magadha and the land of Ráŕh, and within them was this Angadesh. Karna was probably a famous king of this Angadesh. ( 9 )
Kaccha (Gujrat)

The meaning of the word ka is water. That which lies extended in ka is kalambii or kalmii leaves. Ka also means the expressed universe. One who nurtures the universe is a kápálika. Kaḿ saḿvrttibodhicittaḿ pályatiiti kápálikah. [One who protects the created universe, one who is engaged in the pálana kriyá of the expressed universe, is kápálika.] Another meaning of the word is the chief deity of the expressed universe, about whom it has been said in the Vedas, Kasmae deváya haviśá bidhema. It means “I propitiate this god, whose acoustic root is ka, by offering havih” [fire-sacrifice]. Here kasmae does not mean “whom” it indicates the god having the form of ka. Ka + chad + d́a = kaccha. Generally after a, á or a-ending word or vowels, and before the form of kta or d́a of the root verb with aspirates, the related non-aspirate is used. For example, in the case of the word kaccha, there is an a sound in the letter ka. Therefore, instead ofka+ cha = kacha, it will be kaccha. Etymologically, kaccha means the land surrounded or covered by water. On one side is the Gulf of Kuch, the Arabian sea, and the Raan of Kuch, which is surrounded by water. Hence the place is called Kuch. At the farthest tip of South India, near the Mannar Gulf, there lies a small island named Kacchatibhu, midway between India and Sri Lanka. The word comes from the expression Kucchadviipa. Here Kaccha means “surrounded by water”. ( 10 )
Mayurbhanj (Orissa)

Often when writing or engraving the name of an object on paper, hoardings, clips and ornaments, one is faced with the problem of space. However a symbol which bears the identity of an organization can easily be denoted. For example, in the ancient Bhanjabhúm kingdom, there used to be the symbol of a peacock on everything – even on the ornaments of the daughters and brides of the family. Thus, the name of the state came to be Mayurbhanj [Mayur means “peacock”]. Situated on the extremities of Ráŕh, Utkal and Koshal, this state has been known as Mayurbhanj for quite a long time. Likewise all official documents of the state of Darbhanga [in Bihar] carried the symbol of a fish. Mithila [Darbhanga is within the Mithila area] is a fish-eating and fish-loving land. Possibly because of this, in all the state affairs of Darbhanga, the symbol of fish was used. That is the reason why Darbhanga was called Miinaketana. Once in an area near the city of Madras, there was an abundance of fish. Fish symbolized the place. That is why in chaste language it was called Miinaketanam. The name of the Madras airport is still Miinambakam. ( 11 )
Magadha (Bihar)
Magadha culture can be divided into four branches, according to river valleys: (1) Shon-Punpun, (2) Naeraiṋjana-Mohaniya-Phalgu, (3), Kiul Valley and (4) Kśuri Valley.

While it is certainly true that the Ganges flows through Magadha and that the civilization that the Ganges brought with it from north India took on a new form when it came to Magadha, Magadha was in no way founded on this Gangetic civilization. The heart of these four branches of culture was in Girivraja or Rájagir. ( 12 )

Today the rivers of Magadha have all but dried up, but it was not always so. At one time the source of its rivers was in the deep forest. There was a great deal of rainfall in those days and the rivers used to flow twelve months a year. Today, as a result of senseless destruction of the forest, Magadha is gradually being turned into a desert. The village where we met was a little outside the Kiul valley. It falls within the jurisdiction of the Ksuri valley. Today the Kśuri river ( 13 ) has dried up but at one time it was a very big river. This can be ascertained by measuring the width of its source.

It is true that, at that time, the Maháyánii Buddhist god Máriici was popular among the people. Some people used to do Máriici pújá [worship] and others used to throw sand in the idolʼs face to get the god to leave the village. Háriiti was also popular in Magadha but one would not usually see both Máŕiici and Háriiti in the same place. At one spot in the Kśuri valley we found idols of both Máriici and Háriiti.

Háriiti was also a Maháyána Buddhist goddess. The difference between Máriici and Háriiti was that Háriiti was worshipped by both the Maháyána Buddhists and the Shvetámbara Jains. We found both Háriiti and Máriici in the Kśuri river basin. One can deduce from this that in this part of Magadha both Buddhism and Jainism existed side by side. Whether as enemies or friends, they lived together.

It may also be, moreover, that this river basin was the original centre of Maháyána Buddhism. It should not be forgotten that Rajagir-Nalanda, Barhgaon, Mahabihar (Biharsharif), Paharhiya (the village of Maharsi Saiṋjaya, the philosophy teacher of Lord Buddha), and Pavapurii (the place where Varddhaman Mahaviira died) are all in the Kśuri river valley. At one time, the river had a very sharp (kśuradhárávat), strong current. Thus in Sanskrit its name became kśuriká. Later that became kśuri in Bengali. Here it should also be remembered that the current dialects of the Magahii language have been spread through the river basins.

Magadha also has very clear, fixed natural boundaries: The Ganges in the north, the Shon river in the west, the Ramgarh Hills in the south, and in the east Sametashikhara or Pareshanatha Mountain, ( 14 ) Cákái Hill and Kiul River valley. In the direction opposite Grdhrakút́a Hill is Angadesh and opposite Cakravartii Mountain is Ráŕh.
[Now] brokers who dealt in idols had stolen them and smuggled them out of the country.

This kind of sad occurrence is a daily event in Magadha. So much archaeological wealth has been and is being smuggled out of Magadha that in the near future Magadha will become destitute and empty. There is no dearth of educated people in Magadha nowadays, but it seems that they are not paying proper attention to this. What the universities are doing about it I can not say, but I will say that both the educated people of Magadha and the universities should come forward without delay in this matter. It is unthinkable that that part of the world which is richest in archaeological wealth should be deprived of everything it has. ( 15 )

History has never done full justice to this land of Magadha. Every dust particle of its villages and markets is mixed with the gold-dust of its heritage but no one has properly recognized it or recorded it. The little that has been written about it has been written by foreign historians – some out of sport, some out of merriment. The shrivelled Phalgu that you see today was not always in this condition. The hills of southern Magadha were once covered with dense forests. Beyond the mountains, from the north to the south, the Mágadhii river valley was also covered with thick forests. Even a portion of the plains and the banks of the river were also forested. This heavily-forested Magadha used to enjoy an abundance of rainfall and thus the rivers were full of water twelve months out of the year. Because of the abundance of forests there was no problem of soil erosion, and because the forests contained the water there was very little severe flooding. Seeing the Magadha of today, it is difficult to imagine the lush green Magadha that once was.

Magadha was once a vast empire. At the time of Ashoka [232-273 B.C.] and Samudragupta [330-380A.D.] it was probably the largest empire in the world but nothing lasts forever. Those glorious days came to an end and a cimmerian darkness descended over Magadha. The most difficult days in Magadhaʼs history drew nigh during the reign of Skandagupta [455-468].

Skandagupta was one in a string of unworthy sovereigns to occupy the throne of Magadha. At that time the empire had disintegrated and the kingdom was on the point of collapse, confined to its ancient borders. To the north was the Ganges and north of that Mithila, which was at one time part of the empire of Magadha and which Ráŕhʼs King Shasháuṋka had wrested from the hands of Magadha. To the east were the Grdhrakút́a and Cakravarttii mountains. In the eastern region of the Grdhrakút́a Mountains was Angadesh and the Magadha Empire. King Shasháuṋka of Ráŕh also took possession of these areas. In the eastern regions of the Cakravarttii Mountains was the land of Ráŕh, which came under Shasháuṋkaʼs direct rule. The southeast cornerʼs border was Sametashikhara. After that was ancient Ráŕh, which the king of Ráŕh had conquered. The southern portion of the Ramgarh Mountains to the south and the western portion of the Shone River to the west were first controlled by the king of Kashii, Citrasena. After his fall, this entire area was controlled by the royal house of Thániishvar. Magadha did not have a direct struggle with Prabhákaravarddhana but rather with Rájyavarddhana and Harśavarddhana.

Magadha had lost all its previous power and glory King Skandagupta was a weak-minded, vacillating drunkard. He did very little of what we normally consider great deeds; rather he led Magadha to the brink of destruction.

Of course, nothing in this world is completely one-sided. No matter how much historians blame him, Skandagupta did some good also. This city of Gaya, which we are standing in the heart of, was designed by him. He founded Sanskrit schools and training centres in various parts of Magadha, such as Dvádashavarddhaká (Váravigha), Brhaddhiká (Vaŕahiyá), Madhukamadhá (Mokámá), Urubilva (Arawal), Grdhrakút́a (Gidhaoŕ), and so forth, which endured for quite some time. He was the first to introduce the use of the Mágadhii language of that time (Western Demi-Mágadhii) in government service alongside Sanskrit. Still, he watched the Magadha Empire crumble in front of his eyes. He died watching an entire empire fall apart due to his own incompetence.

At that time there was a fierce struggle going on for the capture of Magadha between King Rájyavarddhana of the royal house of Thániisvar and Ráŕhʼs King Shasháuṋka [606-Before 637]. Thánisvaraʼs kings used to repeatedly move their capital from place to place, but Shasháuṋka did not. Rather, he would enlarge his capital according to necessity and befitting the times. He founded Paiṋcagaoŕ [the five ancient parts of Bengal] after capturing Anga and Mithila and then North Bengal (Barendra), Central Bengal (Samatat́) and East Bengal (Vauṋga). That is, during his time Bengal was divided into five political divisions: (1) Ráŕh, (2) Mithila, (3) Samatat́, (4) Barendra, and (5) Vauṋga-D́abák (East Bengal or Shriibhúmi or Cat́t́al was then included in Bengal) – but he kept his capital at Karńasuvarńa. ( 16 )

There were several reasons for the war between Rájyavarddhana and Shasháuṋka. Rájyavarddhanaʼs aims were to plunder Magadhaʼs wealth and to take possession of Angabhúmi. Shasháuṋkaʼs main aims were to take possession of Angabhúmi and to root out the Buddhist religion and culture from Magadha. Although Rájyavarddhana put on a show of liberality he was really narrow-minded. In actual fact, he never treated the Shaivite religion as equal to the Buddhist religion. Shasháuṋka was a staunch follower of Shaivism and completely against Buddhism. He openly declared that as long as one drop of blood remained in his body, he would not allow Buddhism the right to enter either Ráŕh nor Paiṋcagaoŕa ( 17 ), or Bengal.

Ambabhúmi, is situated in the western part of our Magadha. Ambabhúmi was the ancient name of that fertile region (modern name Mokáma T́ál) composed of the western areas of what is now Monghyr District – Surajagaŕá, Lakśmiisarái, Váravighá, Vaŕahiyá, and so on; the eastern portion of Patna district, especially Mokámá and surrounding areas; the eastern part of present-day Nalanda District; and the northeast areas of present-day Nawada District. There was no other region in all of India which was as fertile and as affluent at that time. Thus everyone had their greedy eyes set on Ambabhúmi ( 18 ). Rájyavarddhana and Shasháuṋka were no exceptions.

Their style of attack, however, differed. Rájyavarddhana wanted to plunder wealth, so he would set fire to peopleʼs houses and ransack them. Shasháuṋkaʼs aim was to destroy Buddhist monasteries (what are now called gaŕa in modern Magahii) and Maháyána Buddhist images and idols. You are certainly aware of the fact that, according to social and religious regulations, idols can no longer be used for worship once there is any defect or deformation in them. So Shasháuṋka had the different statues of Buddhist gods and goddesses deformed with a chisel. Today you will find that most of the ancient Buddhist religious statues still in existence have had their noses broken off.

Foreign historians claim that they were damaged during the time of Baktiar Khiljii, or Kálápáháŕ [1565]. ( 19 ) Although there is a grain or two of truth in this, it is, for the most part, a false assertion. They were actively fostering conflict between the Hindus and Muslims of our country, because they followed the policy of ‘divide and rule’. Actually Shasháuṋka was responsible. He was not interested in looting. In this way, with Rájyavarddhana burning his way from the west and Shasháuṋka applying pressure from the east, the two of them brought Magadha to its last gasp.

The sacred banyan tree was not the real Bodhi Tree where Siddhartha attained enlightenment. Ashokaʼs son, Mahendra, took a branch from the original tree and brought it to Sri Lanka. That branch grew into a second Bodhi Tree in Sri Lanka and a branch was taken from that second tree and brought here and planted. This Bodhi Tree was produced from that branch. Shasháuṋka not only extirpated that ancient Bodhi Tree, he also dug a deep ditch around it afterwards and filled it with honey so that the ants would come and eat whatever remained of the roots while they devoured the honey; as a result that Bodhi Tree could not grow back again.

There was no clear or formulated system of studying or teaching history in those days. The study and teaching of history in India was first provided for by Emperor Násiruddiin during Pathan rule and by several foreign travellers during the Mughal era. Thus there were no history books in either Sanskrit or any of the Prákrta languages. The real beginning of the teaching and study of history came during the time of British rule.

As a result of the clash between Shasháuṋka and Rájyavarddhana, the amount of harm that Magadha suffered was doubled. It would be a mistake to say that neither one wanted to see the other; neither one of them could even stand hearing the otherʼs name. Shasháuṋka, in an unexpected development, captured Kányakubja, slew its king, Cakráyúdha (in some peopleʼs opinion, Inráyudha), the husband of Rájyavarddanaʼs sister, Rájyashrii, and installed his own nephew from Ráŕh, Keshariivijaya, on the throne, giving him the name Indráyúdha (some say Cakráyúdha). Rájyashrii returned to her fatherʼs house and instigated her brothers, Rájyavarddhana [605 A.D.] and Harśavarddhana [606-64 A.D.], to turn against Ráŕh. As a result, Magadha, which lay between those two lands, had to suffer many outrages. This is our Magadha.

Mag means 'he who moves about independentlyʼ, that is, one who does not follow the Vedic injunctions. Dha means ‘follower’. The land which follows the anti-Vedic, Buddhist doctrine is magadha. The Sanskrit dha is transformed into dha in Prákrta. Thus magadha becomes magaha – the name of the language is magahii. Following the Buddhist era, the language of all of eastern India was this Mágahii Prákrta. Lord Buddha, The Enlightened, made his appearance in this land.

Our Magadha is situated in the northeast corner of the prehistoric Gondwanaland. Since Gondwanaland is the oldest land on earth, it is also the original home of human beings, the birthplace of human civilization. Ráŕh is in eastern Gondwanaland. In the prehistoric era, human beings came from Ráŕh to make their home in Magadha and they brought with them the current of their civilization and culture. Just as the geography of Magadha slopes downwards from north to south and the rivers flow from north to south, similarly the culture and civilization flowed from south to north. Thus the people of Ráŕh and Magadha are fundamentally one. Like the people of Ráŕh, the common people of Magadha are dark-skinned. Magadha borders Ráŕh along its south-east border. The skin and bodily structure of the people of Ráŕh and Magadha are identical. There is also a noticeable similarity between their languages.

In those days Magadha was full of forests and had abundant rainfall, so there was no need of irrigation. The pre-Aryan people of Magadha used to believe that their land received rainfall due to the grace of the sun-god. Thus they used to worship the sun-god according to their ancient local customs, once during the autumn paddy harvest and again during the spring sun harvest (chaetii harvest). This sun-worship of pre-Aryan Magadha is known today as chat́ pújá. This worship was not performed according to Aryan rules. It was a completely local Magadha practice. The people of Magadha did not bow their heads and submissively accept any of the Aryan practices. For that reason the Aryans called the land magadha. They were afraid of Magadha and used to pay it respect. Thus, to satisfy their grudge and vent their spite, they declared Magadha an unholy land. They said that if a man died there he would not go to heaven and they made efforts to forcibly impose their language, culture and civilization on Magadha. It is up to the historians and social scientists to consider just how successful they were in their efforts.

Magadha did not accept the Aryan civilization. In ancient Magadha there was no custom of racial or caste divisions. The caste system in Magadha came much later due to the influence of the Aryans. Even after the advent of the caste system, the Kraoiṋcadviipii and Magadhaʼs Shrotriya Brahmans did not like the severity of caste divisions. For this reason the Kraoiṋcadviipii and Magadhaʼs Shrotriya Brahmans were not recognized by the Brahmans of northern India.

It was an unbelievable and unforgettable happening. Nearly two and a half thousand years ago two great spiritual leaders appeared on the earth at about the same time on the soil of Magadha to sow there the seeds of their spiritual teachings. One was Vardhamana Mahaviira and the other was Gaotama Buddha. Gaotama Buddha was the son of the feudal king of the central terai, Shuddhodana (Malla dynasty, Shákya branch of the Kśatriyas), and his wife Máyádevii. He practised austerities for a long time in Magadha in the areas of the Barábar, Brahmayoni and Grdhrakút́a mountains. His Guru in Sáḿkhya philosophy, Ácárya Saiṋjaya (Nawada district), was also from Magadha. Although what is called avidyá in his philosophy is not the same as pradhána or prakrti in Sáḿkhya, there is some similarity between the Buddhaʼs concept of avidyá and the Sáḿkhya concept of pradhána.

The Buddha attained enlightenment in the village of Urubilva, located on the bank of the river Naeraiṋjaná (Urubilva is called Bodhgaya today). That Sujátá who fed him kśiira [rice pudding] and saved his life at that moment when the period of his radiant austerities had brought him to the point of death, was Buddhaʼs cousin and the wife of a certain feudal king of Magadha. One should remember here that at that time the Naeraiṋjaná river coming from the south joined the Mohaniká (Mohaniyá) river near Urubilva and flowed together as the Phalgu river from there, later joining the Ganges near Modhukamadhá (Mokámá). About 2000 years ago the two rivers underwent some physical changes due to a huge earthquake and for that reason the Phalgu river of today is much smaller than it was.

At any rate the prince of the Shákyas, Gaotama, attained enlightenment on Magadha soil. Many say that Buddha first introduced the Buddhist dharmacakra [wheel of dharma] and initiated his first disciple near Benares in the Iśipattana Migadába (Rśipattana deer grove, alias Sáranganáth or Sáranáth). Although this is partially correct, it is not the complete truth. It is certainly true that he introduced the dharmacakra in the Iśipattana deer grove and that his five disciples, KaońDinya (Kaońdilya), Bappa (Vapra), Bhaddiiya (Bhadreya), Mohánáma, and Ashsháji (Ashvajit), were present there. But he gave his first initiations on Magadha soil – to Sáriputta, the son of Rúpasári, and Mahámoggallan Arhan, the son of Mahámoggalii.

In those days Magadhaʼs matriarchal system still retained some influence alongside the patriarchal system. So Buddhaʼs first two disciples in Magadha were known by their motherʼs names. The merchant that the city of Pát́aliiputra was named after due to his philanthropy also carried his motherʼs name in accordance with the matriarchal system. The name of the merchantʼs mother was Pát́alii.

Vardhaman Mahaviira was born in Vaeshálii in a Vaeshya family. His fatherʼs name was Siddhártha and his motherʼs name was Trishalá. Like the Buddha, however, he did not propagate his teachings first in his native land but came to Magadha to do so.

One does not have to go far to find the reason why both of them selected Magadha as the proper place for their work. Magadha was not bound hand and foot with the bonds of the Vedic religion. Their natural liberal mentality gushed forth in all aspects of their lives. Buddha was successful in spreading his spiritual teachings there because they were based more on logic than on superstition and belief. Of course, the spirit of revolt against conventionality was present in Vardhanamana Mahaviiraʼs teachings also, but in the opinion of the Magahii people his doctrine of ahiḿsá [non-violence] did not accord well with reality so they were not able to accept it easily. Of course, some people did accept it, but others considered him an unrealistic theoretician and tried to bring him down to earth by using occult powers.
Thus he felt the need to go elsewhere to propagate his new religion.

At that time the most famous city for progressive thinking, education and culture was Ástikanagar (Atthinagar), the capital of Ráŕh. Vardhaman Mahaviira went there and stayed nearly eight years. There he managed to fit his doctrine of ahiḿsá into a somewhat realistic framework. Some prominent merchants of Ástikanagar accepted his doctrine and they renamed the city Varddhamán [Burdwan] after him. Thus it is said that the Jain religion was first established in Ráŕh.

Thereafter he took the road back to Magadha from Burdwan and stopped for a short time in a small village named Svámiisthána (Svámiisthán > Sáiṋchitthán > Sáiṋchithiinchá > Saiṋthiyá) on the banks of the Mayúrákśii River to preach his gospels. By then he was an elderly man, while Gaotama Buddha was still a young man. He breathed his last in Pávápurii on Magadha soil.

There were many in North India who did not appreciate this free mentality of Magadha. They did not spare any efforts to belittle Magadha in the eyes of the people but Magadha was not discouraged by this.
The seven Prákrta languages that arose after the demise of Sanskrit were as follows:
1. Maháráśt́rii Prákrta which was the forerunner of Konkańii, Márát́hi, Vaedarbhii (Várárii), etc.
2. Málavii Prákrta which was the forerunner of Gujrátii, Saoráśt́rii, Kacchii, Málavii, Mevárii, Haŕaotii and Márovárii.
3. Saendhavii or Saobiirii Prákrta which gave rise to Sindhii and Múlatánii.
4. Páshcáttya Prákrta which was the forerunner of Pashtu, Káshmiirii, Uzbekii, Tázákii, etc.
5. Paeshácii Prákrta which was the forerunner of D́ogrii, Páhárii, and Punjabi.
6. Shaorasenii Prákrta which was the forerunner of Hindi, Abadhii, Bundelii, Bághelii, and Vraja.
7. Mágadhii Prákrta which was the forerunner of Magahii, Bengali, Oriya, Angiká, Assamese, Nágpurii, Maethilii, Chatrishgaŕii and Bhojpurii.

This Mágadhii Prákrta had two daughters – Eastern Demi-Mágadhii and Western Demi-Mágadhii. Western Demi-Mágadhii later gave birth to the Magahii language. At one time Mágadhii Prákrta was used not only in eastern India, but in central India as well among the educated community for the exchange of thoughts. Educated people used to show the same zeal for learning Mágadhii Prákrta as they showed for learning Sanskrit. The structure of the Mágadhii Prákrta language is both straighforward and easy. The grammar is also not complex. Both Mahaviira and Buddha gave their teachings in the Mágadhii Prákrta of that time which many people today call Páli. A great deal of literature was composed in the Páli language and its successor Occidental Demi-Mágadhii. Magadha also had its own script. Inscriptions in that ancient Mágadhii script can still be found in certain places in Bodhgaya. It is the younger sister of the Shriiharśa script and closely related to modern Maethilii (Tirahutii) script and Bengali script...

Today many educated people in Magadha are ashamed of speaking their mother tongue. They think that it is perhaps a rustic language, unsuitable for respectable society. Yet this Mágadhii – Occidental Demi-Mágadhii – was once the language of state administration...

Just as Magadhaʼs language has its own style of pronunciation and syntax, its popular culture also shines with originality. Today this popular culture is being swept away but do you know what is even sadder? At one time Magadha had a sound economic infrastructure but since the time of Skandagupta that infrastructure has crumbled. Today, wherever you look, you see a stark picture of poverty and distress. There is no plan for economic development. The young people of Magadha do not have any economic legs to stand on. Magadha has not been built up; rather, for 1500 years it has been hammered into the dust.

The war was going on between Ráŕh and Thánishvara, and Magadha, lying between the two, was being destroyed. Shasháuṋka was an intelligent and courageous man. He built a large army through whatever means he had at his disposal and took Rájyavarddhana by surprise when his adversary was temporarily absent from his capital, taking possession of the city. After this he waged a fierce war against Rájyavarddhana in which Rájyavarddhana was defeated and slain. Some people claim that under the pretence of a truce, Shasháuṋka extended an invitation to Rájyavarddhana, and then either stabbed or poisoned him when he came. One can say what one wants in this matter but there is no sound historical evidence that Shasháuṋka killed Rájyavarddhana unfairly.

After Shasháuṋka retuned to Ráŕh, Rájyavarddhanaʼs brother, Harśavarddhana, liberated his kingdom once again and continued the struggle with Shasháuṋka. As long as Shasháuṋka was alive the war against Thánishvara continued without pause. And so there was no end to Magadhaʼs distress.

After Shasháuṋkaʼs death his widow, Jayashankarii (in some peopleʼs opinion, Triguńáshankarii), ruled Ráŕh along with Paiṋcagaoŕa or Bengal after installing his under-age son, Mrgánkashekhara, as the crown prince. Haŕsavarddhana did not let this opportunity go by and struck a powerful blow against Ráŕh. War ensued and after two sanguinary battles at Nalhát́i and Parkat́iipur (Pákuŕ), Ráŕh fell under Harśavarddhanaʼs control. The same Harśavarddhana who has achieved everlasting fame in India, who, as legend has it, was known for his generosity and who, in some peopleʼs opinion, was the founder of the Kumbhamelá and the Mághamelá, also killed Ráŕhʼs Queen Jayashankarii and her under-age son, Mrgánkashekhara, with his own hand, and utterly exploited Magadha, tossing it aside like a worn-out banana peel. According to the scriptures, the elderly, women, the sick, the disabled, conscientious dissenters, under-age men, and emissaries must not be killed. Harśavarddhana blatantly violated this scriptural injunction. Both the people of Bengal and the people of Magadha condemned and censured him for this.

As long as Shasháuṋka was alive he did not allow the Buddhist religion into Ráŕh. After the defeat of Bengal by Harśavarddhana, Buddhism, despite not enjoying his open support, became predominant, due to the tremendous indirect support he gave it. In their hearts the people remained Shaivites but on the outside they became Buddhists. Later on, during the time of Shankaracharya, a small number of Ráŕhʼs Jains and large numbers of Buddhists throughout Bengal accepted the Puranic religion. This may have been because in Ráŕh there was some similarity between the traditions of the Puranic religion and the Digambar Jain doctrine of that time. So Harśavarddhana dealt a strong blow to the religious thought of Ráŕh, as well as Bengal, and by exploiting Magadha brought it to its lowest point.

Magadhaʼs misery is not a recent thing. It dates back to the time of Harśavarddhana. The people of Magadha have tried to pull themselves up from time to time but after so many blows theyʼve had their back broken. Now they can no longer stand up straight at all.

While returning back after defeating Bengal, Harśavarddhana tried to pulverize Magadha into submission even more. He knew about Magadhaʼs tradition and was afraid that Magadha might overthrow his throne. At that time Magadhaʼs last general, Agnimitra, and his younger brother, Chandraketu, were directing its final efforts to resist Harśavarddhana and a great war ensued. In the battle of Barábar Hill, near the city of Gaya, Magadhaʼs army was utterly routed and destroyed. Even then Agnimitra did not accept defeat. His final confrontation with Harśavarddhana was at Brahmayoni Mountain in Gaya; in this battle Agnimitra was killed.

Magadha has a bright future. Magadha will once again break down the walls of narrow-mindedness and hold its head high in the world community. Magadhaʼs past was bright and its future will be radiant. ( 20 )

Gamadha. The word gam means road. The root dhá+ d́a gives the word, dha which means “something that holds something”. You know that in ancient times those who defied the Vedas were called Mags. The etymological meaning of the word mag is to live a fast life [wantonness]; that is, taking food without restraint, moving recklessly, and doing things without any restraint. In the Vedas, activities such as eating, moving and carrying out actions were bound by certain regulations. Therefore, those who did not obey the Vedas were called Mags.

In the popular sense, the Hinayánii Buddhists of Arakan were called Mags. In the broader sense, any Buddhist was called a Mag. The land that followed the path of those who were opposed to the Vedas was called Magadha (maga + dha + d́a = magadha). That is, the land that was treading the path of the Mags. When Caucasian Aryans entered India from the northwest, they were not amenable to crossing the border north of the Shone River in eastern India. Hence, they gave the name Magadha to that border region. Later, during the age of Lord Buddha and Vardhaman Mahaviir, the people of that land accepted Buddhism with an open heart. However, because of Mahaviiraʼs implicit support of nudism, they did not accept Mahaviira so readily, although both the doctrines of Buddha and Vardhaman Mahaviira were anti-Vedic. Buddha had denounced the fire ritual but did not explicitly decry the Vedas. Vardhaman Mahaviira also criticized the Vedas. He utterly disapproved of animal slaughter. Most Vedic sacrificial rites were centered around animal slaughter; hence, he indirectly censured religious sacrifice. In any case, both these anti-Vedic doctrines were first preached from Magadha. Thus the name Magadha became more firmly established in [the history of] logic.

Vardhaman Mahaviira did not receive much support from Magadha. So he moved away to the then capital of Ráŕh, Ástiknagar (Atthinagar). The people there were followers of Tantra since ancient times. Although they did not lend much support to Vardhaman Mahaviiraʼs doctrine of non-violence, they did not oppose nudism, since Tantric practices include instructions to be free of shame and other bondages. This is corroborated especially by the Jain statues of western Ráŕh. Most of the old idols of Shiva found in Ráŕh are of Jain Shiva. Usually, by the addition of ‘Nátha’ to the name of Jain Shiva, the name of the lord of a holy place is determined – just like Baidyanath, Taraknath, Beharinath, et al. The Jain religion that was established in western Ráŕh was closely related to Tantra – it was Digambarváda. In eastern Ráŕh, Buddhism and Jainism flourished side by side. The Digambar doctrine of western Ráŕh ultimately led to naming even Sadashiva as Digambara. In a song of Ráŕh, it is said:
Buŕi tui gṋájár jogáŕ kar.
O tor jámái ela digambar,
Śṋáŕt́á karche hoggá hoggá,
Dekhe sabár láge d́ar.
[Old woman, make preparations of hemp.]
[Oh, your son-in-law Digambar comes.]
[The ox is making noise.]
[Seeing these, people get frightened.]

However, the Jainism of Ráŕh is centered on Tantra and is saturated with Shaivism. Though the followers of the Vedas did not like Ráŕh, they dared not affront the land of Ráŕh by naming it Magadha. There was only one reason for this; the followers of the Vedas did not encounter any major resistance while entering the land of Magadha. The resistance they faced was ideological in nature. (It was differences in cult and ideology and not any political enmity.) However, in Ráŕh, the situation was quite different. The conflict between the followers of the Vedas with those of Tantra already existed. Furthermore, Ráŕh accepted neither the Vedic caste system nor any discrimination on the grounds of skin complexion. The religious social order was solely based on occupation; not on casteism. During that era, in the battle against the Aryans in Ráŕh, intellectual leadership was provided by Vaedyas (The Vaedyas were not a caste, but practitioners of Vaedyaka medicine – which was not the same as the ayurveda of the Vedas). And, with the help of powerful weapons, the Kayasthas of Ráŕh provided the requisite leadership to resist the Aryans. They did not allow the Vedic religion to gain easy access to Ráŕh, and later they likewise resisted Buddhism. Their final efforts failed with the death of Shasháuṋka, the king of Ráŕh. At that point in time, Buddhism managed to enter Ráŕh through the royal dynasty of Thaneshvar.

In any case, what are the reasons for which Ráŕh was not given the name Magadha? In fact, Birbhúm was located on the farthest border of Ráŕh. From gohat́t́ika comes the word gad́d́á. ( 21 ) This means a place where people run a long distance to fight. Gad́d́á [in Birbhum district that time] was in the northwestern extremity of Ráŕh. It means the place where people rush forward while fighting.

The Aryans, however, accepted Angadesh as part of Áryávarta. Of course, that happened much later during the era of the Mahábhárata. Duryodhana crowned his friend, King Karńa, and with his own money built the capital, Champaknagar. ( 22 ) The Austric word biir means forest. Hence, according to some views, Birbhúmi or Birbhúm means the land of forests. However, the Vedic Aryans did not use the word biir in that sense. In the Vedic language, this border area of Ráŕh meant Birbhúmi or Barjyabhúmi. The people there used to defeat the Aryans in battle and send them across to Gad́d́á. Not only that, they would unleash their pet pack of wolves to chase after them (pashcáddeshe ( 23 ) behind their back or posterior). These domesticated Alsatians were the dependable assistants of the Birbhum warriors. Due to fear of these wolves, they did not want to cross over into Gad́d́á. So, pointing from a distance at Birbhum, they would say, “That is Barjyabhúmi, that is the land to be shunned.” Though they certainly knew internally that they had left Birbhum out of fear, they were averse to admitting it in public. That is why they did not dare to name Ráŕh as Magadha. ( 24 )
Mithila (Bihar)

At the fag end of the Vedic age, the Aryans courageously crossed the river Saraju. Before that they had crossed over Saptasindhu (Punjab), Haritdhánya (Haryana), Brahmavarta, Brahmaśidesh (with Surasen and later Doab); the Aryans halted for some time at Prayág. It could be said that it was like a mark of colon in their journey. More fertile and greener lands beckoned them. In the east they founded the kingdom of Káshii. They brought the kingdom of Káshii within the fold of Aryan customs and manners. In the south of Ganges there was a non-Vedic land, Magadha (Maga menas anti-Vedic; magadha means the land which is anti-Vedic in its inclinations). In the east of Káshii, in the north of Ganges remained Videha, (one of the names of Sita, daughter of Janaka, is Vaedehi). They saw that to proceed to Magadha (non-Aryan land) they would have to cross the Shońaka river (Shone River) and to go to Videha in the north they would be required to cross the river Saraju. So they refrained from crossing the river Shone and Saraju and declared that those were non-Aryan lands. Advancing on the eastern side a little they would have reached Gaúṋgá-Ráŕh (Gaúṋgá-Ridi).

On the eastern side of then Kaośiki river [Koshi] was Barendrabhúmi (Goalpara, Coochbehar, Maldaha, etc.). This Barendrabhúmi and also the entire Bengal, remained identified as the non-Aryan land. Except on the occasion of coming to the pilgrimage center of GangaSagar, it was thought undesirable to touch this land. Though the Pandavas went as far as Manipur, yet this Bengal or Gaúṋgá-Ráŕh was later considered to be the land forsaken by the Páńd́avas.

In those days the Kanyakubja Brahmans of Kanyakubja would seldom cross the Saraju River or the Shone River, afraid of being treated as fallen people. Those who entered Magadha by crossing the river Shone were never recognized by the Brahmans of Kanyákubja in their society – but they got a standing in the Magadha society – as Shrottriya, Kraoṋcadviipi, etc. Those who crossed over the Saraju River on the northern side of the Ganges, they were called Sarajupárii Brahmans. They called themselves at that time Sarajupárii Pandeys, Sarajupárii Dubeys (Dwivedi), Sarajupárii Tiwaries (Trivedi), Sarajupárii Choubeys (Chaturvedi), etc. But the attraction for fertile land cannot be trifled with. So one of the commanders of Aryan army, Mithi crossed over the river Saraju in the eastern direction. Advancing eastwards he came up to the river Kaośiki (Koshi). On the western side the Saraju River (some say Gańd́aki), on the eastern side the Kaośiki, the Himalayas in the north, and the Ganges in the south – the lands, so territorially defined, all came under the control of king Mithi. Mithi called this region Mithila.

Jadunandan, the poet of Mithila while describing the geographical boundaries of Mithila says: Gauṋgá bahati dakśińe Janik/ púrbe Kaośiki dhárá [“The Ganges flows in the south, in the east river Kaośiki”]. In ancient times in the north of Ganges was Angabhúmi, in the south of Ganges, the basin of Ciiracandan was also well-known as Angabhúmi. This continued till the age of Mahábhárata. In the Buddhist era though there was no clear boundary of Angadesh, yet there was the recognition of Angadesh. At that time people mentioned both the names, Anga and Vauṋga in the same breath. In the post-Buddhist era Angadesh lost its identity and that continued up to the Pathan, the Mughal and the British eras. Though after the death of Púrvii-Ardha-Mágadhii language the Anga language survived with its own distinctive characteristics, yet, since it lost its fundamental recognition, it still remains quite neglected.

According to the ancient Vedic regulations, king Mithi held a yajiṋa [sacrificial rites] called Trihottriya [comprising three chief performers] Yajiṋa, to purify Mithila, the non-Aryan land or the land held inferior to that of the Aryans. In ordinary sacrificial rites there used to be one hotá [chief performer], but in this Trihotriya Yajiṋa there were three chief performers (hotá). After holding this rites the Aryans declared this was also a sacred land, and a part of Aryávarta or Uttarápath. Thus Videha was well reformed into Mithila which came to be recognized as the land of trihotra, that is tirhut [transformed form of trihotra]. ( 25 )

Gal + lá + d́a = galla. The root lá means “to contain” or “to be contained”. The word la is derived from the root lá + d́a [suffix]. The land that possesses ker, that is, narikel or naliker, is ker+lá+d́a= Kerala. The land that was controlled by King Mithi or the land that upheld King Mithi is Mithila. You must have heard of King Mithi. In ancient times, the river Gandaka (Narayani Gandakii) used to be treated as the eastern boundary of that portion of Áryávarta situated to the north of the Ganges. And the Shońaka or Shone River was taken to be the eastern border of the portion situated to the south of the Ganges. On the eastern side of Narayani Gandakii, north of the Ganges, is Mithila or Videha. South of the Ganges, on the eastern side of the Shone, is Magadha. The land of Magadha is on the eastern border of Aryavarta. That is why Magadha is belittled as non-Aryan or Mags. In the sense that it was ruled by Mags, the land was therefore called Magadha. The Aryans used to treat this land with contempt. They thought that if one dies in this land of non-Aryans, one would have to be reborn as a donkey in the next life. Hence, in normal situations, no one in those days wanted to go to farther east, crossing the River Shone and coming to Anga, Vauṋga, or Kaliuṋga. Similarly, they did not like to encounter Videha, Anga, Vauṋga and Prágjyotiśpur [Assam] by crossing the river Narayanii Gandaka to the north. Even now, the people of Magadha, Videha (Mithila), and Bengal firmly believe that if one dies in Káshii, one will go to heaven. For a long time, the old people of Bengal thought it best to live in Káshii, so as to count their days till death. Giving up their land and property to their descendants, they used to settle down in Káshii. Another reason for doing this, they thought, was that Káshii, though not exactly on the eastern border of Áryávarta, was somewhat close to the border. A little walk further to the east of Káshii would find one in the land of non-Aryans.

Yes, King Mithi had to make amends for this [so-called] disgrace. He came to occupy [territory] up to the Koaśiki (Koshi) River to the east of Narayani Gandaka (Shonepur is in the ancient kingdom of Káshii; Hajipur is in Videha) and, to purify the land, he held a trihotriya [having three chief priests] religious sacrifice. You know, the chief priest of sacrificial rites is called hotá. One whose role is even greater that that of the chief priest, who makes all accompanying arrangements for performance of the rites, and informs all and sundry about it, but does not himself play a direct role, is called purodhá (pioneer/vanguard).

The chief supervisor of the yajiṋa [ritual sacrifice] had to be well-versed in the four Vedas. He used to have four assistants. One was a scholar in Rgveda; he was called rtvika. Another was a pundit in Sámaveda; he was called udgátá. The third was well-versed in Yajurveda; he was called adhvaryyu. And the fourth was an expert in Atharvaveda; he was called Brahman. Along with the chief priest, five Brahmans used to perform the rites. The huge sacrifice that King Mithi organized had three stout, sturdy and imperious chief priests (hotá). That is why the rites were called trihotriya yajiṋa, and the site where it was held came to be called Trihotriyabhúmi, Trihutpránta, in English Trihut. Since the Moghul period, the land continued to be called Trihut. The name Mithila was essentially of Puranic origin. The use of the name Mithila received an impetus after the Rámáyańa was written. The meaning of the word Mithila is the land controlled by King Mithi, or the land which sustained King Mithi. Before the Rámáyańa was written, the land was more widely known as Videha. In the Puranas, just as Sita was known as Maethilii, likewise she had the other name, Vaedehii. The Maethilii script is also known as Tirhutá script. Below have write some letters on Tirhutá script in order to satisfy your inquisitiveness. ( 26 )
Puńyashloka ńalarájá, puńyashloka hi Yudhiśt́hira,
Puńyashloka ca vaedehii, Puńyashloka Janárdanah.
