chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: Kuc + ghaiṋ = koc The meaning of the root kuc is to “attract”, “to give shelter”, “to attract so as to give shelter”. For example, “the vicinity of hills”, “sandy ocean shore”, “long wavy stretch of forests”, “ a girdle of green fields”. This story is from a long time back, though long after the creation of Ráŕh, when the rest of Bengal came into existence – several lakh [hundreds of thousands] years ago – perhaps sometime after the appearance of man – but certainly not too much later. It must be in between the Oligocene and the Mesozoic age – first when eastern Ráŕh emerged from the sand and silt, carried by the rivers of western Ráŕh. Then, just as the rivers of western and eastern Ráŕh in a similar process created the Samatat́ in the south, in the same way the formation of the land of Barendra began out of alluvium and sand, carried by the rivers Ganga and Brahmaputra. (The literal meaning of the word Barendra is unparalleled or the best of all.)
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: (Bar + indra = Barendra.) The last [regions of Bengal] to be created were Shriibhúmi (Sylhet) and Chat́t́al and, along with Upavauṋga, the entire Vauṋga (D́abák) or East Bengal. The soil of Samatat́, Barendra and Vauṋga is extremely fertile. Within a short period, there sprung up verdant forests. The people of Ráŕh headed eastwards with spades and axes to Samatat́ and across Samatat́ to Vauṋga. While Aryan civilization came to a halt at Samatat́ and Vauṋga (as far as their cultural uniqueness and their blood, Bengalis are not Aryans), eventually Bengalis were impacted by the mudrávarńa (the seal of skin colour) of Aryan culture. Not only Bengalis, the same applies to the rest of India east of Káshii. It was the people of Ráŕh who, crossing over the Ganges, went to Barendra. Thus, when Ráŕh accepted the Brahminic religion, this cult spread primarily from Ráŕh to Samatat́ and Vauṋga . After a few preliminary inquiries, you will come to know that Samatat́ has no intellectual society of its own. It was simply the transplanted culture of Ráŕh. The original Kayasthas and Vaedyas of Bengal are the people who migrated there from Haripal of Hooghly district and Shriikhand́a of Burdwan district. The Brahmans of Vauṋga migrated from so many places in Ráŕh that no specific names can be mentioned. That is why in East Bengal there is no so-called Brahman born in Vauṋga. Even today, those who have been living there for generations introduce themselves as Brahmans of Ráŕh. In sociological language this is called cultural transplantation. Even with regard to Barendra, largely similar events transpired.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: After crossing the rivers Ganges and Padma, when the people of Ráŕh migrated northward instead of east, with spades and axes in their hands, accompanied by cows of the zebu group, and with ploughs and yokes on their shoulders, there came from the north a substream of Mongolian culture. Through a sweet blending of these Ráŕhii and Mongolian cultures evolved the Bengali society of Barendra. While a little paler in complexion than the Bengalis of Ráŕh, with somewhat flatter noses, they were very cultured, gracious and simple human beings. At that very point in time, we obtained the original Bengali Kaevartas of Barendrabhúmi as vital resources for the Bengali race. I have mentioned elsewhere that originally every Bengali was a Kaevarta. Just as the Kaevartas moved from Ráŕh to Samatat́, they also migrated northwards from Ráŕh to Barendra. The Namashudras, who are the essence of the Bengalis of central Bengal, were merely an ornament of the Kaevartas. The people of Barendra have likewise descended from the Kaevartas. The subterranean flow of Kaevarta culture mingled together with Máhiśya culture of south Bengal or Midnapur, meaning that their bloodstream reverberates with the tender and adamantine traits of the original Bengalis. In the last phase of the Buddhist era, the Kaevartas of Barendra became vocal against the tyranny of King Devapal II. In the history of the world, such a well-organized peopleʼs resistance movement is rare – it may be that there has not been any other [comparable movement in history.] The Kaevarta rebellion [Eleventh century] ushered a unique renaissance of the Bengali race – it infused in them an intense consciousness to discover new horizons of ideas.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: These very Kaevartas moved to the north and northwest. Those who moved northwest settled down in Mithila and initiated a new way of life. Even today, thousands of original Bengali Kaevartas live in the Purnea – Saharsa region. Those who went northeast advanced throughout the entirety of the region of Bengal. In Kaevarta society, men slightly outnumbered women. Those who went towards the northeast corner, were compelled to marry Mongolian women in order to preserve their society, thus creating a new branch of Bengali ethnicity. These very people, moving gradually northwards, advanced near the peaks of the Himalayas. They settled down on both sides of the River Saiṋkoch, which originated from Bhutan. This new generation of Bengalis came to be named Koch after the river Saiṋkoch. In their days of woes, when Bengali life was battered by the impact of the descent and explosion of gigantic meteors, the Kaevartas were the greatest refuge and asset of Bengal. That is why they were named Koch, not only after the River Saiṋkoch, but also due to their characteristic of providing shelter to the shelterless. When an idealistic youth of the Koch race saw that the social life of Bengal was heading towards disaster, and had degenerated in its cultural life, he came forward as the living symbol of the sceptre of Bengalʼs revival. This Bengali youth of the Mech dynasty established Kámtápur state in the Saiṋkoch valley with the help of only two hundred dedicated young men. (According to another opinion, the Mech people had not yet been recognized as a branch of the Koch society; they were treated as part of the Koch race.) The name of that youth was Haridas Mondal [Thirtteenth century]. (There is, of course, some difference of opinion on this question.)
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: Since the pre-Buddhist era, Bengal had remained divided into five parts for reasons of geographical diversity and administrative convenience: (1) Ráŕh, to the west of the Bhagirathi River, (2) the central region, comprising the Bhagirathi and Madhumati Rivers (Bágŕii), (3) Barendra, to the north of the Padma River, (4) Vauṋga, on the eastern side of the river Madhumati, and (5) Mithila, to the north of Padma and west of the river Koshii (Kaoshikii). Compared to other regions, Ráŕh and Barendra were slightly larger in area. The other parts each had a bhukti [administrative district]; that is, Bágŕii bhukti comprised the entire Samatat́. The entire Vauṋga area constituted Vauṋga bhukti, and the entire Mithila formed Tirhut bhukti. Yet Ráŕh and Barendra, being comparatively larger in size, each had two bhuktis. The northern part of Ráŕh (north of where the Damodar River used to flow but no longer does today), meaning the present Dhanbad, Burdwan, Birbhúm, Deoghar, Dumka, Gad́d́á, Sahebganj, Ráŕh and Murshidabad, comprised Burdwan bhukti. (In those days Hooghly and Howrah were included in Burdwan.) Medinipur, Bankura, Manbhum, East Ranchi, Singbhum and Bhanjabhúm comprised Dańd́abhukti (Medinipur). Similarly, in the southern part of Barendrabhúmi was Paondrabardhan bhukti, and its northern part formed Kámtápur bhukti. The Bengali Kaevartas of those days, infused with vitality, selected Haridas Mondal as their leader and at the same time made him the king of Kámtápur. From the time of Haridas Mondal, the Kaevartas of this region came to be called Koch. In the course of time the Koch people came to be divided into four characteristic branches: (1) Mech, (2) Rajbaḿshii, (3) Rájguń, and (4) Koliá (Kolliká – Koliá). Needless to say, all four branches were the original Bengalis, and they accepted as the quintessence of their existence the task of upholding, conveying and nourishing the original Bengali culture, and continued to provide evidence of their worthiness as “the shelter or koch of Bengali culture”.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: Later, Kamtapur split into two fragments – its eastern part was called Bijnii and the western part was named Coochbehar. The Koch people were Shaivites since ancient times. Though Jainism and Buddhism had some influence upon them, it was not extensive. However, in the southern part of Barendrabhúmi, that is, in Paondrabardhanbhukti, the impact of Buddhism was widespread. Later, the people of Paondrabardhanbhukti, who had been influenced by Buddhism, accepted Islam as their religion. The same thing happened in Kámtápurbhukti; but compared to Kámtápurbhukti, the number of Muslims was far greater in the Paondrabardhanbhukti. The names of Baneshvar, Bangarh, Jateshvar and Jalpeshvar remind us of the Shaivite influence on these areas even today.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: The Ahoms who came from Burma occupied the upper part of the Brahmaputra valley, but they were not able to set their foot in the lower part; that is, Barenderbhúmi. So, though the impact of the Ahoms on Assamese culture was vast and pervasive, there was not one iota of their influence on Kámtápur or Barendra. In the pronunciation of vowels and consonants in Assamese language, the influence of the Ahoms is universally acknowledged. However, there is not the slightest Ahom influence on Barendra. A look at the spoken language of Kamrup and Goalpara makes this as clear as daylight.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: The British fully occupied the entire eastern part of Kámtápur; that is, Bijnii, and transformed it into their estate under the Permanent Settlement Act. They also brought the western part, that is, a large part of Coochbehar, under their control and allowed only eight police precincts as native areas to be under the king. The large state of Kámtápur was finally reduced to eight police precincts with the name of Coochbehar. These eight police precincts are Coochbehar, Tufangung, Dinhata, Mathabhanga, Mekhligang, Sitai, Sitalkuchi and Haldibari. The British brought the greater part of Coochbehar under their control. They added its northwestern part, that is, the D́alimkot area, to the Himalayan mountainous region of Sikkim, to constitute the Darjeeling district. The previous centre of activities for the D́alimkot region was Phansidewa. Later it was shifted to Siliguri.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: At that time the inhabitants of the plains in Darjeeling district were still in Darjeeling; even now, Bengalis of the Koch group continue to live there. The dwellers of the hill regions, that is, Darjeeling, Kalimpong and Kharsan (which is incorrectly called Kurseong) are Lepchas and Bhutias. (They are Buddhists of the Lama sect). After it was conquered by the British, many Nepalese migrated there from Nepal to earn their livelihood. These Nepalese speak in diverse languages and are of different religious faiths. They are primarily Hindus and Buddhists.) Most of them speak the Rai language. Also among them are people who speak in Gurung, Magar, Newari, Limba, Limpo, Tharu, Kirat and Sherpa languages. The present state language of Nepal is Gorkháli. Though the Gorkhas were not in the majority in Nepal; they were the rulers. Hence their language is now the state language. (Even today, people incorrectly describe Gorkháli as the Nepali language.)
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: Before the advent of the Gorkhas, the king of Nepal was a Newari. At that time, the Maethilii language, written in Maithil (Bengali) letters, was the state language of Nepal. In any case, a few people in the hill regions of Darjeeling speak Gorkháli (which, again, is incorrectly called Nepali language).
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: Just a short while earlier, I mentioned that D́alimkot is now known as Siliguri. Excluding D́alimkot, the majority of Coochbehar was occupied by the British, who named it Rangpur district. Rangpur became its headquarters (karbat́). Since the district was quite large in size, the British split it later on into three parts – the southern part continued to be called Rangpur, with its headquarters remaining at Rangpur. Its northern part was named Jalpaiguri – Jalpaiguri town became its headquarters. Its northeastern part was called northeast Rangpur and its headquarters was set up at Dhubri.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: In 1912, when the state of Assam was created, its poor economic condition was revealed. The annual financial returns of this newly created state of Assam were found to be less than the annual returns of the Kolkata Corporation. To enable the economic condition to become vibrant, Bengali districts such as Sylhet, Cachar and northeastern Rangpur were included in this newly formed state. Rangpur remained in Bengal, and northeastern Rangpur became part of Assam. This was an awkward scenario. That is why the British changed the name of northeastern Rangpur and gave it the new name Goalpara. However, its headquarters remained at Dhubri. Recently, the district of Goalpara has been divided into three parts: (1) Dhubri, (2) Kokrajhar and (3) Goalpara.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: The western part of the present Kamrup district was once in Kámtápur state. Kamakhya hill of Kamrup district was under the control of Kámtápur state for a long time. The Kamakhya Devii temple was also built by the kings of Kámtápur state, and they also repaired it several times. In this connection, the name of King Shukladhvaja of Kámtápur is worth remembering. Those who know the story of the Shákta-Maoásáriá struggle of Assam, must certainly be aware of it.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: Later, Kamrup came under the control of the Ahom kings. According to natural law, the long-standing rule of the Ahom kings brought the influence of the Ahoms on the spoken language and pronunciation of Kamrup (bhát́iá upabháśá of Assamese). However, for obvious reasons, there was no Ahom influence on the spoken language of Goalpara. Therefore, while the cultural life of Goalpara is verily the reverberation of Barendra culture, yet in the wet soil of Goalpara there is only the scent of the warmth of Barendra life. Even today, Goalpara exudes the exquisitely sweet aroma of the warm-heartedness of the Koch people – the story of the rise and fall of their life.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: In any case, you have come to know a brief history of the Koch people. I presume that you now feel very proud of them. ( 1 )
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: Samatat́ – Bágŕi (West Bengal)
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: Ámáder sená yuddha kareche sajjita caturauṋge,
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: Dashánanjayii rámchandrer prapitámaher sauṋge.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: [Our soldiers fought in a a well-equipped, completely fortified manner with the forefathers of Ramchandra, the victor of Ravana].]
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: According to Puranic legend, nearly four thousand years ago there lived a king in Bengal named Sagar. The eastern part (Ráŕh is on the western part) of Murshidabad district during the British [occupation], Nadia (including the present Kustia), Jessore (including the present Banagram), 24 Parganas, Khulna, Faridpur and Bakharganj districts constitute what we call today the delta, Bágŕi or Samatat́. Sagar, the king of Samatat́, was a mighty and influential king. He had a large naval force in the Bay of Bengal. Due to his universally recognized dominion over the Bay of Bengal, and also because the land was occupied by King Sagar, we derive the word ságar = sagar + śiṋa, meaning the sea area ruled by King Sagar. Before King Sagar, the north Indian Aryans, who came from the west, had no influence on Bengal. The Vedic language had no impact at all on Bengali language – the language of Bengal was Sanskrit, which was influenced mainly by the language of the Austric people and partly by the Mongolian [Oriental] language. Sanskrit had its origin in Ráŕh.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: When Samatat́ emerged from the depths of the sea, in that ancient, forest-ridden, newly created Samatat́, its king was Sagar. (Báguŕi: The Mongolian word Báguŕi means small islands that have risen out of the water. From the word Báguŕi has come the Bengali word Bágŕi. In old Bengali, guŕi or guli means collectivity. Examples include, the expression cheleguli khelche [“the boys are playing”]; Maynaguri [the name of a place in the northern part of West Bengal] in the sense of anekguli mynápákhii rayeche [“there are many Myna birds”]. Báguŕi or Bágŕi was given the name Samatat́ in the Sanskrit language of Ráŕh.) Needless to say, the Austric language and the then Mongolian tadbhava báuṋglá [Mongolian derivative word accepted in Bengali] was Bengalʼs original language. Unlike the Vedic language, these languages did not come from outside [Bengal]. Be that as it may, in the earliest era of the history of Bengal, King Sagar was the first to resist Aryan influence, just as in a later era this was done by King Shasháuṋka of Ráŕh.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: According to the story of Rámáyańa, there was a fierce battle between King Sagar and Raghu, the ancestor of Rama.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: The Aryans were not able to take root in the soil of Bengal. They could not reach Samatat́ by crossing Ráŕh. Ráŕh was like an impenetrable fortress to them. The warriors in the army of King Sagar were primarily of the Austric race. In this connection, it is to be remembered that the people of Bengal belong to the Austrico-Mongoloid-Negroid race. The battle was mainly fought by the dark-complexioned youths of Bengali blood with Austric influence, who later, under Aryan influence, were somewhat slighted by being named Háŕi, Dome, Báuri, Koṋrá [Koles], Muńd́á, Kheriá and Malpahari, etc. Among them, the Koles were particularly adept in the art of war. They used to have some sort of respect for the Aryans. King Sagar refused to accept the Koles as a fighting force in his army. This [action on his part] caused the Koles to become complete social outcastes. In some parts of Ráŕh (as in Burdwan), the descendants of Koles are known as Kṋoŕas.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: Even today, the people of Bengal use the word ságar for describing the Gauṋgáságar coast. “I have purchased Ságuri from Sagar” – Ságuri is a kind of brass metal pot, available in Gauṋgáságar. A type of white-complexioned, medium-sized and medium-hot chili known as Ságuri chili grows in the salty soil of the Gauṋgáságar area. Ordinary Bengalis rarely use the word samudra; they use the word ságar. It is a popular Sanskrit word – not Vedic. The etymological meaning of the word ságar is one who has the capacity to swallow everything. ( 2 )
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: Gaoŕ-Vauṋga
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: Gud́ + jan + d́a = gud́aja. The word gud́aja means madya [ale] prepared from raw sugar. This ale is called gaoŕii madya. From this land of guŕ [raw sugar] or [as per another meaning] from this land of intellect and intuition, we obtain the word Gaoŕ [Gaud́] derived from guŕ + ań. The meaning of the word Gaoŕ is Bengal. From a broader perspective, or in the larger sense, the entire North India was called Gaoŕ. Therefore, the entire North India was named Paiṋca Gaoŕ. However, in common parlance Gaoŕdesha stands for Bengal. Generally, Paiṋca Gaoŕ meant the five important parts or limbs of Bengal.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: You may or may not have eaten jilábiis [a sweet] prepared into a coiled shape [and soaked] in the juice of raw sugar. In village markets or fairs, children crowd particularly around shops selling jilábiis. Both boys and girls are to be found in this crowd. Truly, the popularity of jilábiis is not only limited to Bengal. If you visit any district of Uttar Pradesh, even there you will find not one inch of space in front of shops that sell jilábiis. In Sanskrit, jilábiis prepared with the juice of raw sugar were fondly called guŕakuńd́aliká. ( 3 )
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: In ancient times in India and even today, certain metals like copper and tin are very much in demand, even though they are not as valuable as gold, and also not as useful. However, since copper is somewhat scarce in India, it is valued. At one time in Ráŕh, there were copper mines and copious quantities were extracted. The copper was exported abroad from Tamralipta Port (Tamralipta engaged in exporting támra, that is, copper – madhyapadalopi karmadháráya samása [a mode of framing compound words in Bengali grammar by deleting the word in between two other words]). Those mines today are practically extinct. In the copper mines of Manbhum (Purulia), there is hardly any copper today. The copper of Musabani Moubháńd́ár of Singhbhum is also nearly exhausted. At present it is available to some extent in Bankura and in Rajasthan. Hence, since it was much in demand, although not like gold in quality, it was, like brass, called svarńetar [more scarce than gold]. In the Buddhist period, bronze was also called svarńetar. Similarly, a Sanskrit name for tin is rajatetar. Its pure Bengali name is ráuṋg, [derived from] the pure Sanskrit name of bauṋga. Due to its scarcity tin is called rajatetar. Since it is also in demand, some would like to call even lead rajatetar.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: The word gurupatra is used to indicate important metal sheets or lids. Even in ancient times, India used to import tin from Burma, and still today it has to be imported from abroad. The more popular Sanskrit word for tin is bauṋga. Its less popular, alternative Sanskrit word is gurupatra or rajatetar. The land whose children are by nature spiritually thirsty is called Vauṋga.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: Thus you understand that if the name of the country is written in English, it should be written as Vauṋga and not Bauṋga. The Vedic name for this land is Vauṋga, in popular Sanskrit Gaoŕdesha or Vauṋgál. In ancient Bengali, words like Gaoŕdesha, Ráŕhdesha, Vauṋga and Vauṋgál were used to describe Bengal. In Latin, it is called Báiṋjálá; anything related to Bengal is called Banjalitis, in Chinese it is Báiṋál, in Turkish Báuṋgálá, in Persian and Urdu Bauṋgál, and in Bengalʼs own language Váuṋgálá or Váuṋglá [Báḿlá/Báuṋglá /Báuṋlá]. In ancient literature it was called Váuṋgálá using the letter a, and in spoken language Vauṋgála. For example, Bhu su ku áji tu Váṋgálii bhaelii [“Bhu su ku, today you have become a Bengali”], Vauṋge nilo jáyá, Ámi jái Vauṋge, kapál jáy sauṋge [“I go to Bengal and my destiny follows me”], Anuṋga-Vauṋga-Kaliuṋgesu Saoráśt́re Magadheśu ca [“Also in Aungadesh, Bengal, Kaliuṋga and in Saoráśt́ra”]. Remember, in all cases, antahstha va is to be used; if consonantal ba is used, it would mean “tin.” In certain Sanskrit dictionaries, for the word Vauṋga, both Bauṋga and Vauṋga are used in the sense of territory. It is said that both kinds of ba-s are acceptable. No, they are not. Only Vauṋga is acceptable. Respected historian Ramesh Chandra Mazumdar was in favour of using anthastha va when spelling the word Vauṋga. This was appropriate.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: In Buddhist literature, it is said that in the palace of Kapilavastu, Shakyasingha, the son of Shuddhodhan, learnt Bengali in his childhood. From this it is not surprising to say that the Bengali language was not directly the daughter or granddaughter of Mágadhii Prákrt. Still, there was a tremendous impact of Mágadhii Prákrt on Bengali. Buddha came more than two thousand five hundred years ago, and if for this reason he had learnt Bengali, then it must be even older than two thousand five hundred years. Mágadhii Prákrt was alive from 3000 B.C to 1200 A.C. That is, from such estimations it can be said that more than eighteen hundred to nineteen hundred years from today, the Mágadhii language existed. Then came Avahat́t́a, its corrupted form. Ancient Maethilii pundits thought Maethilii was related to Avahat́t́a. Amongst the dialects of Bengali language, as far as we can tell, the most ancient is the Mymensingh dialect, and next to it comes the dialect of Central Ráŕh (the spoken language of Bankura-Purulia). So it could be compellingly stated that Bengali has not descended directly from Mágadhii Prákrta.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: Now, let us come back to our main subject. The name of the land is Vauṋga, not Vauṋga. The ancient land of Gaoŕ means both Ráŕh and Vauṋga. In the limited sense, Vauṋga means East Bengal, but in the larger sense, Vauṋga stands for Gaoŕ combined with Ráŕh-Barendra. The greater part of Bengalʼs glory is the gift of East Bengal, which is the original Bengal. Possibly the word vauṋga, used with a sense of pride, has been used, and even today is being used, to indicate the entire Bengal. ( 4 )
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: Koshala (Orissa)
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: Kosh + lá + d́a = koshala, or kush + kalac also gives the word koshala. The reason why the country was named Koshala was because it was highly advanced in knowledge and resplendent with the jewels of wisdom. In India there were two Koshalas – one was North Koshala, the other South Koshala. South Koshala means the central portion of present-day Uttar Pradesh, whose western part later took the name of Kányakubja or Kanauj. (At present, the small town Kanauj of Farukabad district is a subdivision.) The eastern part of North Koshala later became known as Shrávastii. Still later, North Koshala was given the name Ayodhya – in Saorasenii Prákrta Avadh, in English Oudh, in Urdu also Avadh.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: One of the fifteen provinces of the kingdom of Akbar was Avadh. What the English called Agra province was the Gangetic valley stretching from Mathura to Balia. In those days, Mathura was called Mát́hrá. In English this word came to be spelled “Muthra”. The name of Balia district in the eastern part along the Bihar border has come from the word bahlika. During Akbarʼs time, it was not a district; rather it was a subdivision of Gazipur district. Only very recently, upon separation of Balia from Gazipur, has it been given the status of an independent district, just as Deoria (Devariká) district was created by separating it from Gorakhpur. The British, after separately conquering the provinces of Agra and Oudh, named the union of the two, the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh, or U.P. The expression U.P. became so popular that in order to retain this expression in independent India, the province was given the name Uttar Pradesh. The present Lucknow and Faizabad were part of ancient Koshal, and during the Pathan and Moghul periods were part of Oudh.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: South Koshala means the southeastern part of the present-day Madhya Pradesh and the northern part of the present-day Orissa. South Koshala was also known as Mahákoshala. The western part of Mahákoshala is known today as Chattisgarh (Raipur, Durg, Bastar, Balaghat, Raigarh, Bilaspur, Sarguja, etc.), and the eastern side is known as Koshala and Sambalpur (Sambalpur, Bolangir, Sundargarh, Keonjhar, etc.). Evolving from Saorasenii Prákrta, the present language of North Koshala is Avadhi (the language in which Tulsidas wrote his [version of the] Rámáyańa or Rámcharitamánasa), the language of Chattisgarh in South Koshala [its western part] is born from Mágadhii Prákrta, and the spoken language of east Koshala in Sambalpur area is Oriya (Sambalpurii Oriyá). What is known today as Oriya language has three dialects: (1) that of north Oriya, which is the spoken language of the Cuttuck-Balasore region and also the language used in books. This dialect is very close to Bengali; (2) that of south Oriya, which is prevalent in a large area of Puri district, as well as in Koraput, Ganjam and other areas. It has been impacted by Telugu in its pronunciation and vocabulary. Some words correspond exactly with those of Telugu; (3) that of Koshala and Sambalpur areas of Orissa. Though it is close to Bengali and Nagpuria languages, there exists also the influence of Chattisgarhii language. In addition, it includes a significant number of north Indian words. In any case, you must now have some idea regarding the land of Koshala.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: The la in the word koshala is, when we analyse it according to its suffix (pratyagata vicáre), the initial la, because the root la is the initial la; again the initial la occurs in the suffix kalac. However, people pronounce it like antahstha la, that is, somewhat like koshalra.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: You must have heard of Prasenjit, the king of Koshala. He was the king of North Koshala. Bimbisara, the king of Magadha, was his brother-in-law. His sisterʼs name was Koshalkumarii. Bimbisara was killed by his son, Ajátshatru. However Ajátshatru was not the son of Koshalkumarii. In protest against the murder of Bimbisara, Prasenjit attacked Magadha. Later, at the request of other Indian kings, he halted the battle. The other kings convinced Prasenjit that Bimbisara had forsaken his own religion, revolted against it and become a follower of Buddha. Ajátshatru was a defender of the Aryan religion and was opposed to Buddha. Therefore, disturbing Ajátshatru would not be the right thing to do for any follower of the Aryan religion. Later, of course, Prasenjit even paid obeisance to Buddha. The ashes of Lord Buddha are still preserved in metal urns in various renowned places in India. Prasenjit then took a portion of Buddhaʼs ashes to Koshala. He alleged that, though he had differences with Buddha with regard to religion, yet in one way, they were of the same mold. Buddha was a Kśatriya [warriorclass] and so was he. Thus, ultimately, a compromise was reached between the king of Koshala and Buddha or Buddhism. ( 5 )
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: Kaoiṋca/Akśaycihna not Áksái Cin
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: Many of you know that the king of all mountains, the Himalayas, while very extensive in the east and the west, is no less extensive in the north and the south. The branch of the Himalayas situated on its northern border, which grazes the Tibetan plateau, is snow-covered all year round. These northern Himalayas or upper Himalayas are called Himgiri. Most of the holy mountainous sites in India are located in the Himgiri region. The part of the Himalayas somewhat to the south is covered with forests. However, in the winter season it also becomes covered with snow. This lower Himalaya range is known by its three different segments – in the western, central and eastern parts of India. The ancient name of the westernmost part of the lower Himalayas that extends up to Kashmir, Kimpuruśavarśa (Tibet) and Prameru adhityaká (Pamir plateaux: In very ancient times, the Pamir plateau was part of Kashmiir. Later, it was considered part of Kimpuruśavarśa) was Akśay Cihna [literally “eternal” symbol]. The Rgvedic pronunciation of this mountain was Akśay Ci-h-n, and the Yajurvedic pronunciation was Ak-khay Cihna. The Rgvedic Aryans lived in the region comprising the Akśay Cihna mountain. Later, through oral transmutation, the name of the mountain became distorted and was called Áksái Chin. On further corruption, the word cihna turned into cin. Let this not mislead anyone to consider it as China. The ancient name of the central part of the lower Himalayas was Shivaliuṋga parvamálá (Shivalik range). In Himachal Pradesh, Garhwal and Kumaon regions, this is known as the 'lower Himalayan Shivaliuṋga mountain rangeʼ.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: During prehistoric times, wild animals abounded in the Shivaliuṋga mountain range. The wild animals of ancient India lived in greater numbers in this mountain range than in Ráŕh. This chapter of history was written even before the emergence of human beings on earth. The era when humans first appeared on earth was no longer the era of very large forest animals. It is noticeable that, apart from large-sized mammoths, the majority extremely large-sized animals of prehistoric times lived in the Shivalinga mountain range. Giraffes, dinosaurs, hippos and zebras all lived there. Before Gondwanaland became partially submerged in the sea, and after the rise of the Himalayas from the ocean depths, these forest animals were linked by land with Africa. Later, when large parts of Gondwanaland went under the Arabian Sea and the Indian Ocean, the animals were separated from Africa, their original homeland. Since the Indian climate was not conducive to their survival, and also due to human aggression, they were obliterated from the face of the earth. Animals of the prehistoric era that lived in Ráŕh (Ráŕh was part of Gondwanaland) were likewise massacred by human beings.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: In any case, if proper research is conducted on the Shivalinga mountain range, it is possible to unearth many fossils from prehistoric times. The eastern part of the lower Himalayas (Nepal, Sikkim and Bhutan) was known as Kaoiṋca. The name Kaoiṋca has been buried in the bottomless depths of oblivion. The northern extremity of Kaoiṋca was Kimpuruśavarśa (Tibet) and to the south of it was Bengal, in Chinese language called Báiṋjálá, in ancient Latin Báiṋjál, in ancient Persian Báuṋgálá, in Urdu Bauṋgál and in Bengali Buṋglá. Kaoiṋcagiri was famous for its large-headed and massive mammoths and short-statured humans with highly developed brains. That is why Kaoiṋcagiri and Bengal were known in ancient times as Karii-medhá. Karii means elephant and medhá means intellect. So Karii-Medhá means “land of elephants and intelligent people”.
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: Today, one has to wonder when one realizes that at one time, throughout Manbhum, Bankura, Burdwan and Birbhum, elephants and rhinoceros used to roam in the thousands. Humans have not only forcibly occupied their habitats and turned them into refugees, they have even removed the last vestige of their footprints from the face of the earth.

t: Kaoshámbii (Uttar Pradesh)
chapterTitle: Histories of Kámtápur, Samatat́, Gaod́-Vauṋga, Koshala, Áksái Cin

t: Koshámba + ań + uṋiiś = koshámbii. In the lower part of Brahmavarta or Brahmarśidesh, somewhat towards the upper part of Prayága, there was this town of Kaoshambii in ancient times, renowned in its knowledge and learning. It was so named in the sense of glory. During the time of the kings of Sthaneswar, coins bearing the signature of king Shriiiharśa in Bengali have been found here. After this the historians named the Bengali script Shriiharśa script or Kaoshámbii script. In the history of Bengali language or letters the name of Kaoshámbii is as important as the Shriiharśa script. Although in the later period, the Dálmá script discovered in Ráŕh, whether older than Kaoshámbii letters or not, must be contemporaneous. Of course the nearness of the Dálmá script with the Kaoshámbii script or Shriiiharśa script is quite noteworthy. ( 6 )

t: Kháshi Aiṋcal (Meghalaya)
chapterTitle: Histories of Khási, Aiṋcal, D́ográbhúm, Gurjar

t: khash + ghaiṋ + i = kháshi. The etymological meaning of the word kháshi is the land on which it is a somewhat difficult to move. In the colloquial sense, kháshi means the hilly area on the northeastern border of Bengal. When the British came to India, many small kings ruled this region. They had surrendered to the British according to the British principle of forming subsidiary alliances and were locked into a “tie of friendship.” Among these kingdoms was the state of Miliem located at a towering height yet with some plains lands. After their arrival, the British selected it as an ideal hill town. In 1905, when Bengal presidency was reconstituted comprising West Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, East Bengal and Assam were constituted in the state of ‘East Bengal and Assam.’ It was said that Shillong would be the capital of these states, though Shillong as a town was yet to be sufficiently developed. So Dhaka was made the capital. It was decided that Dacca would be the general capital and Shillong the summer resort or summer capital. In 1912, during the partition of Bengal, the Bengal Presidency was formed with Bengal and West Bengal, while Kolkata remained its capital as before. Bihar and Orissa were separated to form the new province of 'Bihar and Orissa.ʼ But Báṋkipur (the western part of Patna city) was made its capital and Assam became a separate province, with Shillong as its capital. Slowly Shillong grew into a developed city. Many people enjoyed staying in Shillong as a summer resort. The poet Tagore has written:

t: The kings of Jayantia had already surrendered to the Ahom kings. Later, the British included that region as part of their own kingdom. They gave the southern part of Jayantia State to Sylhet district, and its northern part merged with Kháshi district. The Garo hills were formerly part of the zamindary estate of the Susangh kings of Mymensingh. The British separated it, however, and made it a district of Assam. After Ramchandra, the chief king of Kháshi state, completely surrendered to the British, who then killed Govindchandra, king of the Cachars, the entire area was included in Assam province. Cachar state came to be known as Cachar district, and Silchar became its headquarters. However, it must be acknowledged that before they were conquered by the British, the kings of Cachar made a truce with the Ahom kings several times. Cachar was completely routed during the rule of the Ahom king, Sibsingha, after which it again tried to raise its head. After India became independent, the new Meghalaya state was formed, to include the United Kháshi and Jayantia Hills District and Garo Hills. This time too, Silchar was made its capital. Even after this, Shillong continued to remain for some time as the second capital of Assam. Later it was shifted to Dishpur [Guáhát́i]. The northern part of Cachar district was separated and, by giving it special status in the Indian constitution, a new district called North Cachar was created. With its headquarters in Haflong, it is now included in Assam province. In any case, that old Kháshi region is now part of Meghalaya state.
chapterTitle: Histories of Khási, Aiṋcal, D́ográbhúm, Gurjar

t: From a sociological analysis, Kháshi region has distinctive traits. In most parts of India, patrilineal lineage and inheritance systems are in vogue. The only exceptions are Bauṋgálistán, Kerala and Kháshi. In Bauṋgálistán, the family system is patrilineal, but the inheritance system is partly matrilineal and partly patriarchal. As per natural law, a Bengali son inherits the property of a childless maternal uncle according to Dáyabhága [the Bengali system of inheritance]. Yet, in north India, according to the Mitákśará [an ancient Hindu treatise on the laws and rules of inheritance] system, the nephew does not inherit the property of the maternal uncle. In Kerala, both the family and inheritance systems have patrilineal and matrilineal influences. In other words, a child born of a Brahman father and a Kayastha [Nayar] mother would be known by its motherʼs caste [Nayar]. Generally, the child would use the title of its mother. That is, the matrilineal influence is much greater among the Keralite Nayars (in this context, the Nayar regulations are noteworthy) than among the Kayasthas of Bengal.
chapterTitle: Histories of Khási, Aiṋcal, D́ográbhúm, Gurjar

t: The social system of the Kháshi people is entirely matrilineal. In the Shillong region, there are plenty of people whose father is Bengali and mother is Kháshi. Hence, they receive the property of the mother, use the motherʼs title and declare themselves to be Kháshiás. They know both Bengali and Kháshiá languages. This social system of the Kháshi people has accorded them a special distinction in many respects. The Kháshiá king, Ramchandra, has not been given due recognition in history, which is quite regrettable. The circumstances under which he surrendered to the English warrants further research. ( 1 )

t: D́ograbhúm (Jammu and Kashmiir)
chapterTitle: Histories of Khási, Aiṋcal, D́ográbhúm, Gurjar

t: The word kandara could be used in the sense of a cavity, inside of which there is something that is the very life of the cavity itself. For example, the inside of the heart, the inside of the mind, the heart of the heart, cannot be shown, but it is wrapped in bháva and is throbbing with feeling. You have seen that next to many small rivers of Ráŕh, there are very deep gullies. When a flash flood surges down a river, the flood waters breach the embankment, cut through the soil surface and rush downwards. In the course of time, the land on each side of the gully caves in to form this riverside cavity which, in the spoken language of Ráŕh, is called káńdor or káṋdar.
chapterTitle: Histories of Khási, Aiṋcal, D́ográbhúm, Gurjar

t: Also on the slopes of hills when due to rain, storms and landslides large chunks of rocks slide downhill, the road becomes blocked and traffic comes to a standstill. In this manner, due to continuous landslides, one after another, a gartta (gr + kta = gartta) [pit] is formed across the stretch of the hills. In the correct grammatical spelling of gartta, there should be double t-s, but according to the rules of pronunciation or phonetics of ancient times, the rśis used to pronounce the word grttr (g-r-r-r-t-t-a). However, this difficult pronunciation did not last long. In the course of time the pronunciation metamorphosed into gartta. As per the rules for the doubling of letters, the spellings garta and gartta are both equally correct, but not grta, because r or rr, whichever is there in the previous consonant, will be used as r at the top of the second consonant. I hope you have understood quite well this rule of Vedic grammar.
chapterTitle: Histories of Khási, Aiṋcal, D́ográbhúm, Gurjar

t: Later, the Vedic derivative of the word dvigarttabhúmi was duggarbhúmi, and still later it became d́uggarbhúmi. From d́uggarbhúmi came the expression D́ográ desh [land of the D́ogra people], which is another name for Jammu; the language of the land is D́ogri, and the people are known as D́ográ. Thus, in this manner, when cavities are formed across the hillsides, they are called guhás (caves). Another meaning of guhá is a similar place within the mind. Just as people take shelter inside caves, similarly souls obtain refuge inside the caves of the mind.
chapterTitle: Histories of Khási, Aiṋcal, D́ográbhúm, Gurjar

t: Átmáguháyám nihitoʼasya jantoh, meaning “the souls of living beings hide in the caves of the mind.” So guhá means oneʼs “I” feeling. Cosmic Consciousness and the reflected unit consciousness are inherent in this “I” feeling of created beings.
chapterTitle: Histories of Khási, Aiṋcal, D́ográbhúm, Gurjar

t: Dharmasya tattvaḿ nihitaḿ guháyám – the essence of dharma, the life and soul of dharma, lies hidden in the “I feeling” of all creatures, in the mindʼs jewel casket kept hidden in the depths of all beings.
chapterTitle: Histories of Khási, Aiṋcal, D́ográbhúm, Gurjar

t: When hill caves or crevices are decoratively remodeled to serve as religious sites, it is called gumphá. Many caves of the Himalayas are such Buddhist gumphás. The English word for guhá is cave. When a cave, due to continuous earthquakes, or as a result of being struck with axes or chisels by humans, becomes longer and longer in length and gradually takes the form of a long tunnel, it is called cavern in English. People of prehistoric times used to live in caves and gumphás, but they always preferred to live in caverns, because each cavern could not only accommodate several families, it also provided greater security. One of the insignias of human civilization is painting, which is the earliest carrier of its culture, its original identity. Just as the people of ancient times traced line drawings in these caverns and drew images of social and family life, similarly they sketched images with the subtle faculties of their mind. Thence came the ancient cave drawings of Ajanta, Elora, the underground cave sketches in the hills near Kota [Rajasthan] and the drawings in the Khirkhiria hills of Mungher district. The cultural imprint of prehistoric times, when human history had not yet been created, was portrayed through these cave drawings, since there were no books or scripts. Just as there used to be long ports by the rivers, there were also long caverns along and in the hills. These long caverns were called girikandaras. ( 2 )

t: Gurjara (Gujarat)
chapterTitle: Histories of Khási, Aiṋcal, D́ográbhúm, Gurjar

t: Gurj + ac + rak = gurjara. The meaning of the root gurj is “to influence,” “to stir,” “to oscillate,” “to vibrate.” The word gurjara means Gurjar land. Gurjararáśt́ra > Gurjararát́t́ha > Gujrát́/Gujrat. Another meaning of gurjara is the man from the land of Gurjar.
chapterTitle: Histories of Khási, Aiṋcal, D́ográbhúm, Gurjar

t: Gurjara + uṋgiiś = gurjarii. The word gurjarii stands for the daughter of Gurjar land; the other meaning is the musical rága gurjarii. It was a widely used Sanskrit word in medieval times. In the Puranic age, the word Saurashtra was concurrently used for the entire Gurjar. Anga-Vauṋga-Kaliuṋga Saoráśt́reśu-Mágadheśu ca.

t: Tantra has chiefly two branches – the Kashmir branch and the Bengal branch. The Kashmir branch was practiced to the west and north of Kashmir – Gándhár, Áryańyavraja or Iran, Arabia, Mesopotamia, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Mongolia, Outer Mongolia (China) and a large part of Siberia. The Shaeva, Shákta and other schools of Tantras were practiced in accordance with the Kashmirii system in all these places. Even now you will see in these countries instances of phallus worship, meditation on dead bodies, dancing and jumping with dead corpses (in the Kurmun village of Burdwan district, the last vestige of this Shaivite ritual were found centering around the Ishaneshvar temple. In Burdwan and Birbhum, especially in Ajay valley near Katwa, the Bolan festival held there is a Shaivite celebration). The other branch of Tantra, namely, the practice of the Bengal branch [of Tantra] is prevalent in the rest of India and the rest of the world. For example, Jammu, Punjab, Northern India, Western India, Nepal, Tibet, China, Japan, Bhutan, Vauṋga, and Kamrup. Regarding this Gaoŕiiya Tantra or Váuṋglá Tantra above words have been said [in the previous page]. ( 3 )

t: Abhavat, the past, and bhavati, the present, and bhavyam, the future – none of these three is separate and distinct from the others. Nothing suddenly emerges or suddenly disappears; all entities respectfully obey the Cosmic laws in a disciplined way and proceed from the future to the still more distant future in the panoramic flow of the Cosmic Cycle. No one can resist the momentum of this Cosmic flow – no one can contain it – no one can suppress it.

In the annals of human history, many truths and falsehoods have been recorded. Attempts have been made to belittle the importance of great personalities, to erase them from the pages of history, and often small and insignificant people have been magnified and presented as great. But none of these attempts has been successful. Everything is written on the pages of eternal time exactly as it happened; the selfish and vain efforts of petty people have left behind only scornful mirth and derisive laughter on the vast canvas of eternal time.
Uŕiche tomdr dhvajá megharandhracyuta tapaner jvaladarcirekhá,
Karojoŕe ceye áchi úrdhvamukhe – paŕite jáni na, kii táháte lekhá.
[Your banner is flying like a beam of sunlight flashing through the clouds. I am looking with upturned face and folded hands – but I cannot read what You have written there.]

This colourful pageant of history, these unknown pictures of the past, the variegated splendour of this theatrical show, are all every moment rising and falling on the bosom of eternity. History is merely giving a gentle blow, a soft vibration of existence, on the solid rock of time. It has been said, Teśáḿ vilakśańo sákśii [“He is the witness with opposite characteristics”]. Paramashiva, Supreme Consciousness, is intimately associated with all the various scenes of the acts of history, past, present and future: He is their impartial witness. Though the Supreme Entity is not only a witnessing entity – He is much more than that – still He is the uninvolved witness of all the sequences of events. He does not distort history, nor does He give undue importance to any matter or any entity. He is outside the scope of the law of causation, so He is the witness with “opposite characteristics” ( 1 ) to all occurrences. His witness-ship does not involve Him in any event –Kleshakarmavipákásháyaeráparámrśt́ah Puruśavisheśa Iishvarah [“The special Puruśa who remains unassailed by afflictions, actions, reactions, and saḿskáras, is Iishvara, the Lord”]. ( 2 )
